findings.title: kotlin query-string and form-body encoder leaves & = + # / ? [ ] literal (param injection, '+' decoded as space, '#' truncates URL)
findings.description: Kotlin's BaseApi encodes every non-allowReserved query key and value with Ktor `String.encodeURLQueryComponent(spaceToPlus = false)`, and every form-urlencoded key and value with `encodeURLQueryComponent(spaceToPlus = true)`. Ktor's default `encodeFull = false` keeps the whole URL_PROTOCOL_PART set literal: `: / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * , ; = - . _ ~ +`. I ran ktor-http-jvm 3.5.0, the version pinned in the golden build.gradle.kts, on "a b&c=d#e+f/g?h[i]j". The query mode gives `a%20b&c=d#e+f/g?h[i]j...` and the form mode gives `a+b&c=d#e+f/...`. The other 11 SDKs emit `%26 %3D %23 %2B %2F %3F` for these characters. Concretely, `getPetByName("Rex", category = "cats & dogs")` goes out as `?category=cats%20&%20dogs`. The server then sees category="cats " plus an injected parameter " dogs". A value "1+2" arrives as "1 2", and a value containing '#' cuts off the rest of the query as a fragment. The form body has the same problem: `note="a&b=c"` turns into two fields. deepObject keys also keep `[ ]` literal in kotlin only (`filter[name]`), while all others send `filter%5Bname%5D`. Nothing tests this: the kotlin tests only check `category=dog` and a form value with a space. Fix by building both encoders on URLEncoder with `+`→`%20` in the query (as kotlin's own encodePathSegment and encodeQueryAllowingReserved already do), or by calling `encodeURLParameter()`. Add a BaseApiTest row that asserts `a&b=c+d #e/f?` encodes to `a%26b%3Dc%2Bd%20%23e%2Ff%3F` (query) and `a%26b%3Dc%2Bd+%23e%2Ff%3F` (form), mirrored in all 12.

findings.title: kotlin query-string and form-body encoder leaves & = + # ? / : ; , [ ] @ ! $ ' ( ) * unescaped (parameter injection and data corruption)
findings.description: Kotlin's BaseApi percent-encodes query keys and values with Ktor's `encodeURLQueryComponent(spaceToPlus=false)` and form-urlencoded keys and values with `encodeURLQueryComponent(spaceToPlus=true)`. Both are called with the default `encodeFull = false`. In Ktor 3.5.0 that setting leaves the whole URL_PROTOCOL_PART set literal: `: / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * , ; = - . _ ~ +`. I confirmed this against the kotlin golden's own ktor-http-jvm 3.5.0 jar. The string `a b&c=d+e#f?g/h:i;j,k~l*m!n'o(p)q@r$s[t]u"v%w<x` encodes to `a%20b&c=d+e#f?g/h:i;j,k~l*m!n'o(p)q@r$s[t]u%22v%25w%3Cx`. When that output goes through Ktor's own URL parser, which the transport uses via `httpClient.request(currentUrl)`, the query value `R&D=1+1 #x` becomes `/pets?name=R&D=1+1%20`. Ktor parses that as `Parameters [name=[R], D=[1 1 ]]`: the caller's value is split into a second parameter, `+` is decoded as a space, and everything after `#` is dropped as a fragment. The form body has the same defect: a nickname of `c++` is sent as `nickname=c++` and the server decodes it as `c  `. The other 11 SDKs encode `&`→%26, `=`→%3D, `+`→%2B and `#`→%23. One case is reachable from the existing fixture: kotlin sends the deepObject key `filter[color]=…` with literal brackets, while all 11 others send `filter%5Bcolor%5D=…`. Since the non-reserved encoder already keeps every reserved character, `allowReserved: true` has no observable effect in kotlin. Nothing tests this: kotlin's only exact form assertion is `nickname=a+b&tags=x&tags=y` (from a space), and no test in any language puts `&`, `=`, `+` or `#` in a query or form value. Fix: use `encodeURLParameter()`, or a hand-rolled RFC 3986 unreserved encoder like the java/rust ones, for query and form components, then add `+`↔space handling for form. Unit test (kotlin BaseApiTest and PetApiTest): getPetByName category=`R&D=1+1 #x` must produce `category=R%26D%3D1%2B1%20%23x`, and setPetPreferences nickname=`c++&x` must produce `nickname=c%2B%2B%26x`. Add the same test rows to the other 11 BaseApiTests so the escape set is locked in every language.

findings.title: kotlin form-urlencoded body (and query) values leave & = + # / ? : @ $ , ; ! ' ( ) * unencoded: field injection and value corruption
findings.description: Kotlin's BaseApi encodes every application/x-www-form-urlencoded key and value with ktor's String.encodeURLQueryComponent(spaceToPlus = true). Query values go through the same function via encodeQuery(spaceToPlus = false). Both calls leave encodeFull at its default of false, so ktor only escapes characters outside URL_ALPHABET + URL_PROTOCOL_PART. I ran it against the ktor-http-jvm 3.5.0 jar the kotlin golden pins. Input "a&b=c~d*e!f'g(h)i+j k/l:m" came out as form "a&b=c~d*e!f'g(h)i+j+k/l:m" and query "a&b=c~d*e!f'g(h)i+j%20k/l:m"; '#', '?', '[', ']', '@', '$', ',' and ';' also stay literal. The consequences: setPetPreferences(note="R&D") sends `note=R&D`, which the server parses as note=R plus a stray field D. nickname="a=b" splits the field. note="C++" arrives as "C  " because a literal '+' decodes to a space. A '#' in a query value truncates the URL into a fragment. Java uses URLEncoder, csharp Uri.EscapeDataString, python quote_plus, ruby URI.encode_www_form, node URLSearchParams, php rawurlencode, dart Uri.encodeQueryComponent, go url.Values, rust form_url_encode, swift an unreserved-only CharacterSet and elixir URI.encode_www_form. All of them percent-encode & = + #. No kotlin test sends a reserved character through a form or query value: the only form assertion, PetApiTest.kt:1098, uses spaces. Fix: pass encodeFull = true (or use encodeURLParameter) for both the form and query encoders. Then add a unit test asserting `note=R%26D%3Dx%2By` in BaseApiTest.kt, plus the same query-value row in every language.

findings.title: go: optional integer/number/boolean query, header and cookie params are serialized as pointer addresses ("0xc000…")
findings.description: Go's Options structs hold optional parameters as pointers (`*int64`, `*float64`, `*bool`, ...). The api template passes the pointer straight to `serializeStyled` for query (api.mustache:279), header (:293) and cookie (:321) params. In `serializeStyled`, a non-slice value ends up in `stringify(value)`. `stringify` dereferences only `*string`, `*time.Time` and `*models.DateTime`, plus anything that implements fmt.Stringer, such as `*Swatch`. Everything else falls to `default: fmt.Sprintf("%v", v)`, which prints the address of a pointer. I checked with go 1.26.2: `fmt.Sprintf("%v", any(&x))` printed `0x6c3f03bcc180` for `*int64`, `*bool` and `*float64`. So an optional `limit` (integer) query param goes out as `?limit=0x6c3f...`, and an optional integer header carries an address. The other 11 SDKs send `5`, `true`, or `1.5`. Petstore has no optional non-string scalar query, header or cookie param, so no golden test reaches this. Fix by dereferencing in stringify through reflection (`rv.Kind()==Ptr → rv.Elem()`), the same way toStringSlice already does, or by dereferencing in the template. Add stringify table rows for *int64, *int32, *float64, *bool, and an optional integer query param to petstore (for example `limit` on findPetsByStatus).
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. A pointer is go's way to express an optional field, and the serializer can dereference it, as toStringSlice already does.

go.note: stringify default branch now dereferences non-nil pointers by reflection (nil pointer gives empty string), so optional *int64/*float64/*bool query/header/cookie params send their value, not the address.

findings.title: ruby: Faraday decodes and re-encodes the built query, which collapses exploded arrays to the last value, defeats allowReserved, turns '+' into a space, and sorts params
findings.description: Ruby's BaseApi builds a fully encoded query string and passes the whole URL to `connection.run_request(method, url, ...)`. Faraday's `Request#url` splits off the query and runs it through `params_encoder.decode`. That is `QueryParamsEncoder`, which delegates to `Faraday::NestedParamsEncoder`. Faraday then rebuilds the query with `NestedParamsEncoder.encode` (followed by `+`→`%20`). I ran faraday 2.14.2 under Ruby 4.0.5. Input `revision=1+2/a:b&colors=red%7Cblue&tags=a&tags=b` goes on the wire as `colors=red%7Cblue&revision=1%202%2Fa%3Ab&tags=b`. Input `revision=v1.0/beta:rc1&...&a=2&z=1` gives `a=2&...&revision=v1.0%2Fbeta%3Arc1...`. This has four effects. (1) Exploded arrays, which are the OAS default for query arrays (style form, explode true), keep only the last element: `tags=a&tags=b` becomes `tags=b`. That is silent data loss. (2) allowReserved is undone, because `/ : ? [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * , ; =` are re-percent-encoded. (3) A literal `+` in an allowReserved value is decoded as a space (`value.tr('+',' ')`) and sent as `%20`. (4) Params are sorted alphabetically. Ruby's tests only cover `build_query_string` and `encode_query_allowing_reserved` in isolation, so none of this shows up. The petstore spec has no exploded array query param, and no test reads the wire query for `revision`. Fix by bypassing the params encoder: give Faraday the query through a passthrough encoder whose decode returns the raw string unchanged and whose encode emits it as-is, or set the request's URI query directly. Add a DefaultApiClient unit test that sends a URL with repeated keys, a `+`, and the reserved set, then asserts the exact `env.url.query`.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Faraday's params_encoder is pluggable, and a passthrough encoder keeps the bytes that build_query_string produced.

ruby.note: QueryParamsEncoder is now a passthrough: decode wraps the raw query under one key and encode emits it unchanged, so repeated keys, order, allowReserved characters and an encoded plus all reach the wire. Params passed separately still get Faraday encoding with + turned into %20.
ruby.test: test/default_api_client_unit_test.mustache: 'sends a repeated query key once per value', 'keeps the order of the query parameters', 'keeps allowReserved characters literal', 'keeps an encoded plus and an encoded space distinct', 'installs the passthrough query encoder on the connection it builds'

findings.title: Container-typed primitive responses (getInventory map<string,int32>, getMatrix array<array<int32>>) bypass the strict primitive checks in 6 SDKs
findings.description: Model fields get strict scalar checks in all 12, but operation-level container returns of primitives do not. For getInventory body {"available":"abc","sold":1.9,"pending":"5","placed":true}: php's int path returns 0 for "abc" (json_decode('abc') -> null -> intval(null)), 1 for 1.9 (truncation), 5 for "5", 1 for true, 0 for [1]; a malformed int body at top level also becomes 0 and a malformed string/float/bool body becomes ""/0.0/false via settype (verified with php 8.5 replicating the code). node uses `(x: unknown) => x as number` — no validation at all, any JSON value is returned typed as number. python maps 'StrictInt' -> plain `int` in _NATIVE_TYPES_MAPPING and validates via TypeAdapter(dict[str,int]) in LAX mode: "5"->5, true->1, 1.0->1, " 7 "->7, "1_000"->1000 (verified). dart uses lazy `(… as Map).cast<String,int>()`: deserialization succeeds and the TypeError ('String is not a subtype of int?') is thrown later at element access, outside SerializationException (verified dart 3.11). kotlin decodes Map<String,Int> with the default Int serializer, which (per the SDK's own comment) accepts quoted numbers even with isLenient=false — the Strict* serializers are only attached to model properties. java Map<String,Integer> truncates 1.9->1 (ACCEPT_FLOAT_AS_INT). swift types int32 leaves as Int and accepts 1.0. csharp/go/rust/ruby/elixir reject every one of these. Same inputs must be accepted/rejected identically; php's garbage->0 is silent data corruption.

findings.title: python format:byte MODEL fields (pydantic Base64Bytes) reject/corrupt raw bytes on construction and decode malformed base64 leniently
findings.description: Every python model property with format: byte (PetPassport.thumbnail/scans/biometricChip, BinaryVault.seal/shards/labels) is typed pydantic `Base64Bytes`. Base64Bytes VALIDATES its input by base64-decoding it, including when the caller passes raw bytes to the constructor or assigns them (validate_assignment=True). Verified with pydantic 2.12.5: `V(seal=bytes([0,0xFF,0x10,0x42]))` raises ValidationError ('Invalid base64-encoded string'); `V(seal=b'hello world')` raises 'Incorrect padding'; `V(seal=b'test')` silently stores b'\xb5\xeb-' and serializes as "test" (the wire carries the caller's raw bytes as if they were base64); re-assigning a decoded value (`m.seal = m.seal`) raises. In the other 11 SDKs a byte field holds RAW bytes in memory and the serializer base64-encodes them (go test TestByteField_ScalarRoundTripsThroughBase64 constructs raw {0x00,0xFF,0x10,0x42}). On decode, Base64Bytes uses non-validating `base64.b64decode`: '!!!!' -> b'' and 'dG!VzdA==' -> b'test' and 'dGVz dA==' -> b'test' are accepted. This contradicts AGENTS.md Resolved 'python ... reject malformed base64 on decode (b64decode(validate=True))' — that fix only covers ObjectSerializer._deserialize (bare bytes / containers), not model fields. The python tests in TestByteFormatBase64RoundTrip claim to cover 'PetPassport.thumbnail' but only exercise ObjectSerializer.serialize(bytes), never the model field, which is why this is uncaught. Fix: a custom Annotated[bytes, PlainValidator(strict b64decode(validate=True) only for str input; pass bytes through), PlainSerializer(b64encode, when_used='json')] alias like OffsetDateTime/JsonNumber in _types.py.

evidence.quote: python and node reject malformed base64 on decode (python `b64decode(validate=True)`

python.note: python only. New Base64Bytes alias in _types (strict b64decode for str, bytes pass through, JSON-only b64encode) replaces pydantic's Base64Bytes; codegen import now points at the package _types.

findings.title: Request timeout does not cover the response body read in java and dart, though TransportOptions documents it as end-to-end
findings.description: TransportOptions.getTimeout() is documented as an 'End-to-end request timeout... Covers the entire request lifecycle: connection, TLS handshake, sending the request body, and reading the response'. In java the only deadlines are HttpClient.connectTimeout and HttpRequest.timeout. The JDK cancels the request timer once response headers arrive, so a server that sends headers and then stalls the body is never timed out. I verified this on JDK 22 with a 1000 ms timeout: a server sending headers plus 3 of 100 body bytes and then sleeping 8 s made send() block for 8098 ms and fail with IOException('fixed content-length: 100, bytes received: 3'), which surfaces as NetworkException, not NetworkTimeoutException. If the server never closes, it hangs forever. dart has the same gap. Future.timeout wraps only _httpClient.send(), which completes on headers. streamedResponse.stream.toBytes() has no deadline, and dart:io HttpClient has no read timeout (only connectionTimeout is set). The other 10 bound body reads: kotlin socket/request timeout, csharp HttpClient.Timeout over the buffered content, python urllib3 read timeout, ruby read_timeout, php timeout+max_duration, node AbortSignal over arrayBuffer(), go Client.Timeout, rust reqwest timeout, swift timeoutIntervalForRequest/Resource, elixir receive_timeout+Task. Unit tests cannot see this. It needs a fixture route that sends headers then stalls the body (e.g. a chasm 'slow-body' endpoint) and a per-language assertion of NetworkTimeoutError within the timeout.

findings.title: caCertPath pins to the custom CA in most SDKs but only ADDS it to the system roots in rust, dart and ruby
findings.description: java (custom-only KeyStore; doc: 'an SSLContext trusting only the given CA certificate'), kotlin, csharp (CustomRootTrust), go (x509.NewCertPool), swift (SecTrustSetAnchorCertificatesOnly(true)), python (urllib3 skips load_default_certs when ca_certs is set), node (tls 'ca' replaces the roots) and elixir (cacertfile) trust ONLY the configured CA. Three SDKs keep the system roots as well. rust calls reqwest add_root_certificate, which adds to rustls native roots. dart uses SecurityContext(withTrustedRoots: true) then setTrustedCertificates. ruby sets f.ssl.ca_file, but faraday-net_http's configure_ssl always sets http.cert_store to OpenSSL::X509::Store.new.tap(&:set_default_paths) unless ssl[:cert_store] is given (checked in upstream source). So a certificate from any public CA, or a MITM CA in the OS store, is accepted by rust/dart/ruby but rejected by the other SDKs for the same config. php (Symfony 'cafile' -> CURLOPT_CAINFO) may also keep libcurl's compiled-in CAPATH; that needs a check. The TransportOptions doc ('in addition to (or instead of) the system trust store') hides the split. A fixture test would need a server with a cert from a CA in the system store but not the configured CA.

findings.title: csharp drops a multipart body (and a binary body's Content-Type) on a 307/308 redirect, and throws for a Stream body
findings.description: BaseApi hands multipart uploads to DefaultApiClient as a Dictionary<string, object>. In the redirect loop, the follow-up request rebuilds content only for byte[] and string. A Dictionary (multipart) or any other object falls through with next.Content == null, so a 307/308 replays the POST/PUT with NO body. That is a silent loss of the upload. For a byte[] body, the replay uses new ByteArrayContent(bytes2) without the declared Content-Type: mergedHeaders' Content-Type is skipped and never reapplied, so the redirected binary upload carries no Content-Type. A Stream body (what ExtractBinaryPart can return for octet-stream/image uploads) throws ApiException('Cannot replay a streaming request body...'). java buffers InputStream/File and replays them, and python/ruby/php/node/rust/elixir/go/swift replay pre-serialized bytes. A fixture test would need a 307 from a multipart endpoint, since chasm already serves 307s.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Build the HttpContent once into a buffered byte[] (multipart via ReadAsByteArrayAsync, Stream via CopyTo) and re-create it with its Content-Type on each hop.

csharp.note: Multipart (Dictionary) and Stream bodies are buffered to bytes before the first send when redirects are followed, and every 307/308 hop replays them with the original Content-Type (multipart boundary kept). byte[] replay now reapplies the declared Content-Type. The Stream-throws branch is removed.

findings.title: swift (Apple) routes only same-scheme traffic through the proxy; https targets bypass an http:// proxy
findings.description: buildSession chooses the connectionProxyDictionary keys from the scheme of the PROXY URL. In CFNetwork, HTTPEnable/HTTPProxy proxies http:// targets and HTTPSEnable/HTTPSProxy proxies https:// targets. With the common 'http://proxy:3128', only HTTP* keys are set, so every https:// API call goes direct and bypasses the configured proxy (an egress-control bypass). With an 'https://' proxy URL, http:// targets go direct. The other 11 route both target schemes through the one proxy. CI cannot catch this because the Linux build throws proxyUnsupported, so the Apple branch is never run.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Set both HTTP* and HTTPS* keys to the proxy host/port regardless of the proxy URL scheme.

swift.note: Same root cause as F127. proxyConnectionDictionary() now fills both HTTP* and HTTPS* keys from the one proxy URL, so https targets no longer bypass an http:// proxy.

findings.title: swift noRedirect (OAuth2 token) requests ignore the proxy and leak a URLSession per call
findings.description: buildNoRedirectSession builds a fresh URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral for every noRedirect call. It copies the timeouts and protocolClasses but not connectionProxyDictionary, so OAuth2 token-endpoint POSTs (the only noRedirect callers) bypass the configured proxy on Apple while every other request uses it. The session holds a strong delegate and is never invalidated, so each token fetch leaks a URLSession and its delegate. The other 11 send noRedirect requests through the same configured transport.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Build the no-redirect session once, from the same configuration including the proxy dictionary, and invalidate it on close().

swift.note: noRedirect requests now use one lazily built session made from a copy of the primary session configuration. It keeps the proxy, timeouts, stateless settings and URLProtocol classes, and close() invalidates it. The Proxy-Authorization header is still sent on token calls, because the main path sends it too; not changed.
swift.test: DefaultApiClientUnitTests.mustache: testNoRedirectSessionIsReusedAndInheritsThePrimaryConfiguration (same instance, cookie, cache and timeout settings carried over). Invalidation on close() and the proxy carry-over are not tested.

findings.title: swift transport is stateful: URLSessionConfiguration.default stores and replays cookies and serves responses from URLCache
findings.description: The main session uses URLSessionConfiguration.default, whose defaults are httpCookieStorage=HTTPCookieStorage.shared, httpShouldSetCookies=true, urlCache=URLCache.shared and requestCachePolicy=.useProtocolCachePolicy. So swift silently keeps every Set-Cookie and replays it on later requests (process-wide, shared with the app), and can answer GETs from the HTTP cache without reaching the server. The noRedirect session (.ephemeral) also keeps an in-memory cookie jar. csharp explicitly sets UseCookies=false, noting 'The other 11 SDKs are stateless by default'. java/kotlin/python/ruby/php/node/dart/go/rust/elixir install no cookie jar or cache. Two identical calls can differ on the wire, and the second may never hit the server.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Set httpCookieStorage=nil, httpShouldSetCookies=false, urlCache=nil and requestCachePolicy=.reloadIgnoringLocalCacheData.

swift.note: buildSession sets httpCookieStorage=nil, httpShouldSetCookies=false, urlCache=nil and requestCachePolicy=.reloadIgnoringLocalCacheData. The no-redirect session inherits them.

findings.title: dart BasicAuthenticator puts the raw password (and username) into its ArgumentError via ArgumentError.value, so the secret shows up in toString() and logs
findings.description: When the Basic credentials fail validation (CR/LF/NUL in the username or password, or ':' in the username), dart throws `ArgumentError.value(_password, 'password', msg)`. Dart's `ArgumentError.toString()` appends `Error.safeToString(invalidValue)`, which gives `Invalid argument (password): Basic auth password must not contain CR, LF, or NUL characters: "s3c\u0000ret"`. The value is also public as `e.invalidValue`. So any log line or crash report that prints the error contains the plaintext password. The other 11 SDKs throw message-only errors that never include the credential. The authenticators promise that secrets never leak into logs, and this breaks that promise. The same pattern exists nearby: `OAuth2ImplicitAuthenticator.setAccessToken` throws `ArgumentError.value(token, 'token', ...)`, which leaks the access token, and `abstract_api_client` throws `ArgumentError.value(value, 'headers', ...)`, which leaks a header value that can be an API key or token. Fix: use `ArgumentError(msg)` or `ArgumentError.value('***', name, msg)`. Unit test: in dart/test/basic_authenticator_test.dart, assert that `e.toString()` does not contain the password for the NUL-password case.

evidence.quote: throw ArgumentError.value(value, 'headers', 'Header "$name" contains CR, LF, or NUL');

dart.note: BasicAuthenticator (username and password), OAuth2ImplicitAuthenticator.setAccessToken and AbstractApiClient (URL, header name, header value) now throw message-only ArgumentError. toString and invalidValue no longer carry the credential. The header-name leak was not named in the finding but was changed alongside the others.
dart.test: basic_authenticator_test.mustache: 'a rejected password never appears in the ArgumentError' and 'a rejected username never appears in the ArgumentError'; oauth2_implicit_authenticator_test.mustache: 'a rejected access token never appears in the ArgumentError'; default_api_client_unit_test.mustache: 'the header-value ArgumentError never carries the secret value' and 'the URL ArgumentErrors never carry the URL or its query token'

findings.title: OIDC rediscovery after Cache-Control max-age discards the exchanged delegate — every call after expiry throws 'Must call exchangeCode()'
findings.description: When the discovery cache expires (default 86400 s, or the OP's max-age — e.g. Google sends max-age=3600, Auth0 max-age=15), getDelegate/resolveDelegate builds a brand-new OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator (tokenExchanged=false, empty token manager) and replaces the old one. All access/refresh token state and the exchanged flag are lost, so the next getAuthHeaders throws the 'Must call exchangeCode() before making API requests' precondition error (rust/swift CodeNotExchanged). With max-age=0 the very first API call after exchangeCode fails. Rediscovery should only refresh endpoints (or carry the token manager/exchanged state over), not reset the session. Aggravated by discovery not being single-flight outside java/go (kotlin, python, node, dart, swift, csharp, php, ruby race and can create several delegates). No language has any test of max-age parsing or rediscovery (grep for max-age in every OpenIdConnectAuthenticator test returns 0), which is why this survived.

evidence.quote: delegate = new OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator(host, clientId, clientSecret, authorizationEndpoint, tokenEndpoint, redirectUri, scopes);

findings.title: Refresh grant omits client authentication and the 'fallback' re-sends the same refresh grant (auth-code, OIDC, password BODY mode) — flows break permanently at first expiry against confidential-client OPs
findings.description: Uniform defect (not a parity split, but in-lens and not recorded in AGENTS/PARITY_TODO). Once a refresh_token exists, the password authenticator (and always the auth-code authenticator / OIDC delegate) builds params = {grant_type=refresh_token, refresh_token=X} with NO client_id/client_secret and passes that as the 'original grant' to the token manager. The manager's internal refresh copies client_id/client_secret only from `params`, so the refresh POST carries no client authentication in BODY mode (auth-code has no BASIC option at all, so it is always unauthenticated). RFC 6749 §6 requires a confidential client (one that sent client_secret in the code/password exchange) to authenticate per §3.2.1; Keycloak/Google/Auth0 reject such a refresh (invalid_client / invalid_request). The manager then 'falls back to the original grant' — which is the identical unauthenticated refresh params — so it fails again and throws OAuth2ServerError. The password flow therefore never re-runs the password grant (unlike client-credentials, whose fallback is the real grant), and since invalidateAccessToken() never clears the refresh token there is no recovery path short of a new authenticator. The in-code comment ('RFC 6749 §6: the refresh grant carries only grant_type and refresh_token') misreads the RFC. Fix: include client_id/client_secret (BODY) on every refresh in password/auth-code, and keep the real grant params (password grant / error for auth-code) as the fallback. Test: java OAuth2PasswordAuthenticatorTest.usesRefreshTokenOnSubsequentCalls only asserts grant_type/refresh_token presence; add assertions that the refresh body carries client_id/client_secret and that a 400 invalid_grant on refresh re-runs grant_type=password.

findings.title: go/rust/elixir per-scheme OAuth wrappers drop the spec's declared scopes (no scope= on token request / authorize URL)
findings.description: The generated per-scheme authenticators (MachineAuthClientCredentials, LegacyAuthPassword, UserAuthAuthorizationCode, BrowserAuthImplicit) pass the spec scopes in java/kotlin/csharp/php/python/ruby/node/dart/swift (e.g. ["pets:write","pets:read"], ["read"]) but go hardcodes nil, rust vec![] and elixir [] for every OAuth base class. Result: the machineAuth client-credentials POST in go/rust/elixir carries no `scope` parameter, the legacyAuth password grant no scope, and the userAuth/browserAuth authorize URLs no `scope=` — different bytes on the wire and a different granted token (OP default scopes). Root cause is in the codegen superArgs, not the templates. Only elixir has wrapper tests, and they assert URLs but not scopes; add a per-wrapper test (petstore already declares the scopes) asserting the token body / authorize URL contains the spec scopes in every language.

elixir.note: Elixir side only. buildElixirSuperArgs hardcoded [] for every OAuth base class; it now renders spec.scopes() through a new formatElixirScopes (BetterElixirCodegen.java). The golden wrappers now carry ["pets:write", "pets:read"] and ["read"]. Scope names are escaped for a double-quoted literal. The OIDC wrapper takes the same path, but its spec has no scopes so it stays [].
elixir.test: oauth2_*_authenticator_test.mustache: 'scheme authenticator keeps the declared scopes' (client credentials, password, auth code) and '... in the authorization URL' (implicit, auth code)

go.note: BetterGoCodegen.buildGoSuperArgs hard-coded nil for scopes. A new formatGoScopes now passes the spec's scopes, in the same order the java wrapper uses. Go side only.

rust.note: Rust side only. BetterRustCodegen.renderSchemeAuthenticator now passes the spec scopes (new formatRustScopes) for the client-credentials, password, auth-code and implicit wrappers. OIDC keeps vec![], as java does.
rust.test: oauth2_client_credentials_authenticator_test: test_scheme_wrapper_sends_the_scopes_declared_by_the_spec; same-named tests in the password, implicit and auth_code test templates

findings.title: rust OIDC take_delegate() makes concurrent calls rediscover and install an unexchanged delegate (intermittent CodeNotExchanged / permanent token loss)
findings.description: rust's OpenIdConnectAuthenticator moves the delegate out of its Mutex (take_delegate) for the duration of delegate.try_auth_headers()/exchange_code().await. A concurrent call's resolve_delegate() fast path only returns early `if delegate_guard.is_some()`, so while the delegate is taken it falls through to a fresh discovery GET, builds a NEW OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator (token_exchanged=false), stores it and then takes it → OAuth2AuthorizationCodeError::CodeNotExchanged (or ConfigurationError 'OIDC delegate is in use by a concurrent call'). If the first call restores its exchanged delegate before the second call's discovery finishes, the second call overwrites it and the session is lost permanently. The other 11 keep the delegate shared (java synchronized getDelegate, go mutex, etc.) and only the token manager serializes. Any parallel API calls through an OIDC-authenticated rust client hit this. Fix: hold an Arc<delegate> (clone the Arc out of the lock) instead of take()/restore.

rust.note: The OIDC delegate is now an Arc kept in the mutex and cloned out, with no take/restore. A late discovery no longer overwrites a live delegate. A concurrent call during exchange_code reuses the delegate (discovery GET count stays 1).

findings.title: caCertPath adds to the system trust store in dart, rust and (likely) ruby but replaces it in the other 9
findings.description: When caCertPath is set, 9 SDKs trust only that CA: java/kotlin build a KeyStore holding just the CA, csharp uses X509ChainTrustMode.CustomRootTrust, go uses a fresh x509.NewCertPool() as RootCAs, python passes urllib3 ca_certs (default certs are not loaded), node passes `ca`, php uses curl cafile, swift sets the anchor certificates with AnchorCertificatesOnly, and elixir sets cacertfile. java's own Javadoc calls this 'certificate pinning ... trusting only the given CA'. dart instead uses SecurityContext(withTrustedRoots: true) plus setTrustedCertificates, which adds the CA to the system roots; dart's own comment calls it 'TLS pinning'. rust calls reqwest add_root_certificate on a client that already has rustls-tls-native-roots, which also adds. ruby uses Faraday's net_http adapter, which always installs an X509::Store with set_default_paths, so ca_file adds to it too (inferred from the adapter; needs a runtime check). Result: with a private CA configured, dart/rust/ruby still accept any publicly-trusted certificate, for example a MITM with a public cert, while the other SDKs reject it. Same input, different trust decision. The TransportOptions doc in all 12 says 'in addition to (or instead of)', which papers over the split.

findings.title: go trace-context hook always receives context.Background(), so the documented OpenTelemetry setup never injects a traceparent
findings.description: InjectTraceContext calls the registered propagator with context.Background() every time. Go operations take no context.Context (for example GetPetById(petId, server)), so the caller's active span can never reach the propagator. The doc-comment example `otel.GetTextMapPropagator().Inject(ctx, propagation.MapCarrier(headers))` is therefore always handed a span-less Background context, and the W3C propagator writes nothing. Under the documented setup go never sends a traceparent. The other 11 SDKs read the ambient context: java/kotlin Context.current(), csharp Activity.Current, python/ruby/node/php/elixir via OTel's current context, rust Context::current(), and dart/swift callbacks that read Context.current/activeSpan. go's own tests hide the problem: withActiveSpan registers a closure that ignores the ctx argument and captures one span's ctx (`func(_ context.Context, ...) { propagation.TraceContext{}.Inject(ctx, ...) }`). That only works for a single global span, not for concurrent requests, and is not the documented usage. Go's lack of ambient context forces some difference here, but not this one: the hook advertises a ctx it can never supply. Also dead code in the same file: the unexported headerCarrier type (Get/Set/Keys) is never used, and its Get canonicalises the key while Set does not.

evidence.quote: func (a *PetApi) GetPetById(petId int64, server GetPetByIdServer) (*Pet, error)

findings.suspected_forced_reason: Go has no goroutine-local or ambient context; the real fix needs a ctx-accepting operation variant or a documented capture pattern

go.note: The go ctx limitation is stdlib-forced (operations take no context.Context). The unused headerCarrier is already gone and the doc already shows the closure-capture pattern (trace_context_util.mustache). A real fix needs ctx-accepting operation variants.

findings.title: rust caCertPath validation cannot fail under rustls: a non-PEM file is silently ignored, and a PEM block with bad DER panics
findings.description: TransportOptionsBuilder::build validates the CA with reqwest::Certificate::from_pem(&pem). Cargo.toml builds reqwest with default-features=false and rustls-tls-native-roots, so default-tls is off. In that configuration from_pem just stores the bytes (`original: Cert::Pem(pem.to_owned())`) and never returns Err (checked in reqwest-0.12.28 src/tls.rs:167-174). So the 'failed to parse' InvalidCaCertificate branch is unreachable. Any readable file passes: a text file with no PEM block yields zero certs at ClientBuilder::build, the client silently falls back to the native roots, and the fail-fast promise is broken. A file with a valid PEM armour but invalid DER makes RootCertStore::add fail inside ClientBuilder::build; build_http_client then calls `.expect("failed to build HTTP client")`, which panics inside DefaultApiClient::new. That breaks the 'typed Err, never a panic' contract. The other 11 reject an unparseable CA file at construction with their built-in error (java/kotlin/dart have a garbage-PEM test for this; rust does not).

rust.note: TransportOptionsBuilder::build now checks the CA file itself. It needs at least one PEM CERTIFICATE block with valid base64 wrapping a DER SEQUENCE of exactly the stated length. A text file or a corrupt block now returns InvalidCaCertificate. The remaining gap is a block that is DER-shaped but not an X.509 certificate, since webpki alone can reject that inside ClientBuilder::build, where '.expect' still panics. Closing it needs build_http_client to return a Result.

findings.title: swift on Apple platforms rejects a PEM caCertPath because SecCertificateCreateWithData only accepts DER
findings.description: validateCaCertPath and the trust delegate both call SecCertificateCreateWithData(nil, fileData). That API accepts only DER and returns nil for PEM text. On macOS/iOS a PEM CA file therefore makes DefaultApiClient.init throw ConfigurationError.invalidCACertificate("failed to parse ...: no PEM blocks found or unparseable"). That includes the repo's own fixture src/main/resources/fixtures/certs/ca.pem, which starts with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----. The other 11 document and accept PEM. Verified with a local Swift script: SecCertificateCreateWithData on fixtures/certs/ca.pem returned nil. CI runs swift on Linux, where the Security branch is compiled out, and every swift HTTPS test is wrapped in `#if !os(Linux)`, so nothing catches this.

evidence.quote: guard SecCertificateCreateWithData(nil, certData as CFData) != nil else {
let certificate = SecCertificateCreateWithData(nil, certData as CFData)

swift.note: New parseCaCertificates unwraps PEM blocks to DER, with a bare DER file passing through as one certificate. validateCaCertPath and the trust delegate use it, so a PEM caCertPath is accepted on Apple. The Security call itself is Apple-only; parsing is tested on all platforms.

findings.title: elixir inline (property) enums use the sanitized member NAME as the wire value: hyphenated or non-lowercase values are rejected on decode and sent wrong on encode
findings.description: For an inline enum, openapi_types emits `Enum<{{nameLowercase}},...>` (elixir model.mustache:411). nameLowercase is the enumVar NAME lowercased (AbstractBetterCodegen.java:1915-1923: AVAILABLE→available, ON_HOLD→on_hold), not the wire value. convert_to_type(data, "Enum<"...) (object_serializer.ex:736-750) checks `to_string(data) in allowed` against those names, then `String.to_atom`. On encode, sanitize_field_value has no module to resolve for an `Enum<...>` type and falls back to `to_string(atom)` (object_serializer.ex:492-505, 450). For an inline enum with wire values `Available`/`on-hold`, decoding valid wire data raises SerializationError ('"on-hold" not in ["available","sold","on_hold"]'), and an `:on_hold` value is sent as `"on_hold"`. The standalone-enum module path (Availability) is correct because it maps through value/1 and from_value/1. Every petstore INLINE enum (Pet.status, Order.status, Defaults.mode) is a single lowercase word, so name and value coincide and the bug is hidden. Expand petstore with an inline property enum such as `["In-Stock", "OUT_OF_STOCK"]` and round-trip it in all 12.

elixir.note: Real defect: model.mustache:411 emits Enum<nameLowercase,...> and the serializer decodes and encodes against those names, not the wire values. A fix needs the codegen to supply an escaped raw wire value per enumVar (the template's value is a quoted Elixir literal), plus a name-to-value descriptor parsed in convert_to_type and sanitize_field_value. That is too big for this batch, and the model emission cannot be locked without a spec change: the petstore spec needs an inline property enum whose values are not lowercase single words, for example Order.shipmentStatus (type: string, enum: [In-Stock, OUT_OF_STOCK, on-hold]), round-tripped through the elixir model and serializer tests.

findings.title: java maps OAS readOnly/writeOnly to the INVERTED Jackson access mode; the other 11 ignore both keywords
findings.description: java/models/model.mustache:692-697 renders an OAS `readOnly` property as `@JsonProperty(access = JsonProperty.Access.READ_ONLY)` and a `writeOnly` one as `Access.WRITE_ONLY`. In Jackson, READ_ONLY means the property is serialized but ignored on deserialization, and WRITE_ONLY means the reverse. That is the opposite of the OAS meaning (readOnly: appears in responses and is never sent; writeOnly: is sent and never appears in responses). I checked this with jackson-databind 2.19.4 using the golden's mapper settings. For a READ_ONLY `id` plus a WRITE_ONLY `password`, the request body is `{"id":5}`: the readOnly id is sent and the password is dropped. Decoding `{"id":7,"password":"leaked"}` gives id=null and password=leaked: the server's id is lost and a writeOnly secret is accepted. No other SDK changes behaviour. csharp/php/ruby/node only add a doc remark (csharp model.mustache:423-428, php :461-466, ruby :448-453, node :290-295). python only adds `json_schema_extra` metadata (python model.mustache:370-381). kotlin, dart, go, rust, swift and elixir have no handling at all. So java alone has wire behaviour for these keywords, and it is backwards. The petstore spec has no readOnly or writeOnly property, so nothing exercises this. Expand petstore with e.g. `Order.id: readOnly` and a `Credentials.password: writeOnly`, then pick one canonical behaviour (most likely: omit readOnly on encode, ignore writeOnly on decode, in all 12) and pin it with a round-trip test in each language.

java.note: The petstore has no readOnly/writeOnly property, so no test can lock the fix. The Jackson access modes in java/models/model.mustache:692-697 are inverted relative to client semantics (readOnly should be Access.WRITE_ONLY, writeOnly should be Access.READ_ONLY). The canonical cross-SDK behaviour (omit readOnly on encode, ignore writeOnly on decode, in all 12) is still undecided. Spec needed: Account{id:int64 readOnly, username:string, password:string writeOnly} plus a createAccount operation, as in the F055 YAML.

findings.title: java/kotlin default optional arrays and maps to empty containers, so they send `"tags":[]` and `"location":[]`, and an absent key decodes to [] instead of null
findings.description: Optional array and map properties get a non-null empty default: java `public List<Tag> tags = new ArrayList<>();` and `location = new ArrayList<>()` (Pet.java:100,115; same in PetWithOwner, StockItem.matrix, PetPassport.scans, BinaryVault.shards/labels), and kotlin `val tags: List<Tag>? = mutableListOf()` (Pet.kt:59,72). The kotlin default comes from BetterKotlinCodegen.toDefaultValue (lines 531-537), which returns mutableListOf()/mutableSetOf()/mutableMapOf() for every array or map. java's comes from the base java default value. The java mapper is NON_NULL and keeps empty lists; kotlin has `encodeDefaults = true` and stripJsonNulls only removes nulls. So `new Pet(name, photoUrls)` sends `{"name":..,"photoUrls":[..],"tags":[],"location":[]}`, while the other 10 send no tags/location keys. I confirmed with jackson 2.19.4 that a default-constructed model serializes to `{"tags":[]}`. On decode, a response without `tags` gives `[]` in java/kotlin and null/None/nil/undefined in the other 10. Every addPet/updatePet body carries the extra keys, and an empty array can mean 'clear this field' to a server. No java/kotlin test asserts the encoded Pet body. Fix by defaulting optional containers to null (containerDefaultToNull), and add a request-body byte assertion for a minimally-constructed Pet in all 12.
findings.note: done in java; still open for kotlin

java.note: models/model.mustache no longer emits the `= new ArrayList<>()/HashMap/LinkedHashSet` initializer on an optional (non-required) container field; required containers keep it. A new Pet no longer serializes tags/location, and an absent array decodes to null. The kotlin part is outside this scope.

kotlin.note: Kotlin side only. models/model.mustache now emits `= null` for optional array/map properties instead of mutableListOf()/mutableMapOf(), so a new Pet no longer sends tags/location and an absent key decodes to null. Required containers are unchanged.
kotlin.test: ObjectSerializerTest.kt (template test/ObjectSerializerTest.mustache): SerializeTests 'a minimally-built model sends no key for its unset optional arrays', DeserializeTests 'an absent optional array decodes to null, not an empty list' and 'an explicit empty optional array decodes to an empty list'

findings.title: python `pattern` constraint is emitted with `/.../` delimiters, so any property with a pattern rejects every value
findings.description: python/models/model.mustache:373 and :381 emit `pattern=r'{{{pattern}}}'`. CodegenProperty.pattern comes from DefaultCodegen.toRegularExpression, which is `addRegularExpressionDelimiter(escapeText(p))` (confirmed by javap on openapi-generator 7.22.0). That wraps the regex as `/<regex>/` and escapes `/`. BetterPythonCodegen extends AbstractBetterCodegen extends DefaultCodegen and does not override toRegularExpression. The model therefore gets `pattern=r'/^[a-z]+$/'`. I checked this in pydantic 2.12: with that pattern, both `abc` and `/abc/` are rejected, so every value fails, on construction and on deserializing a server response. escapeText also doubles backslashes inside the raw string (`\d`). petstore has no `pattern` property, so the golden never renders this branch. Add a pattern-constrained string property to petstore and a unit test that a matching value is accepted.

python.note: Confirmed real. The model template emits pattern=r'{{{pattern}}}' (model.mustache:373, plus the re.match validator at :490), and CodegenProperty.pattern carries the /.../ delimiters. The petstore spec has no pattern property, so no generated test can lock a fix. Spec needed: add to Pet in src/spec/resources/specs/petstore/openapi.yaml a property 'microchipId: {type: string, pattern: "^[a-z]{2}[0-9]{4}$"}' and test that Pet accepts 'ab1234' and rejects 'ABC'. Fix: strip the delimiters and un-escape in BetterPythonCodegen.postProcessModelProperty (or a template helper), and do the same for the re.match validator.

findings.title: go, swift and dart oneOf union wrappers have no public constructor; callers can only build a oneOf request body by decoding JSON text
findings.description: go's oneOf wrapper is `type PetFood struct { value any }` with an unexported field and no NewPetFood/From* function. The same applies to SetPetAvatarThumbnailRequest, which IS a request body: setPetAvatarThumbnail takes it, and the go test builds it with `json.Unmarshal([]byte(`"/9j/4A=="`), &thumbnail)`. swift's union is `public struct … { private let _value: Any }` with only `init(from: Decoder)`; its PetApiTests also decode JSON to get one. dart's discriminated oneOf template has only the private `const PetFood._(this._value)`; its primitive-union and anyOf templates do expose `.value(...)`/`.ofValues(...)`. The other 9 can wrap a value: java/csharp subclass instance (`new DryFood(2.5)` is-a PetFood), kotlin `PetFood(x)`, php `new PetFood($x)`, python `PetFood(x)`, node `new PetFood(x)` / plain union alias, rust enum variants `PetFood::DryFood(..)`, ruby/elixir pass the bare variant. This is a public API-shape defect for any spec that sends a oneOf body. Fix: add `NewXxx(v)`/`init(_ value:)`/a public dart constructor. The petstore already exposes it via setPetAvatarThumbnail; change those API tests to construct the body directly.

findings.title: java and kotlin send empty arrays/maps for optional container fields the caller never set ("tags":[], "location":[], "shards":[], "labels":{}), and add them on a decode/re-encode round-trip
findings.description: Java gives optional container fields an initializer (`public List<Tag> tags = new ArrayList<>()`, `location = new ArrayList<>()`, BinaryVault `shards`/`labels`, PetPassport `scans`, StockItem `matrix`). Its mapper uses NON_NULL inclusion, which writes an empty non-null list. Kotlin does the same with `= mutableListOf()`/`mutableMapOf()` plus `encodeDefaults = true`; stripJsonNulls only removes JsonNull. So `new Pet("doggie", urls)` goes on the wire with `"tags":[],"location":[]` in java/kotlin. The other 10 leave these fields null/None/nil/undefined/absent and omit them. A GET-then-PUT round-trip in java/kotlin also turns an absent field into an explicit empty one. `location` is a positional tuple (GeoPoint), so an empty one is wrong data, and a server with minItems would reject it. The petstore mock accepts `[]` because NormalizePrefixItemsRule strips arity, so no spec catches it. Fix: null default for optional containers (containerDefaultToNull) in java/kotlin. Tests: assert the serialized body of a minimally-built Pet has no `tags`/`location` key in all 12. Expand the petstore: give an optional array `minItems: 1` so the mock rejects `[]`.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. This is the upstream openapi-generator java/kotlin container default, not a language requirement.

kotlin.note: Same root cause as F026 (kotlin default `mutableListOf()` on optional containers); fixed by the same model.mustache change. Java half was done in batch 1. The minItems petstore expansion is not needed to lock the kotlin side.

findings.title: kotlin: required container properties default to an empty collection, so a payload missing a required array (Pet.photoUrls) is accepted and the constructor does not require it
findings.description: Pet.photoUrls and PetWithOwner.photoUrls are REQUIRED in the schema, but kotlin emits `val photoUrls: Set<String> = mutableSetOf()`. kotlinx-serialization fills a missing field from its default, so `{"name":"doggie"}` decodes as Pet with photoUrls={}, and `Pet(name="x")` compiles without photoUrls. Kotlin has no separate required-key check: its ObjectSerializer only guards explicit nulls. All 11 others reject a missing photoUrls: java `@JsonProperty(value="photoUrls", required=true)` + requireNonNull, csharp `required HashSet<string> PhotoUrls`, php constructor param without default + assertRequiredPresent, python `Field(alias="photoUrls")` with no default, ruby `Types::Required`, node 'photoUrls is required', go 'required field photoUrls is missing', rust plain HashSet (no serde default), swift `decode(Set<String>.self…)`, dart 'Missing required field', elixir required_fields includes photoUrls. They also all require it as a constructor argument. Every Pet decoded in the petstore carries photoUrls, so nothing catches this. Add a missing-required-container row to each language's model deserialize test.

evidence.quote: return fmt.Errorf("required field 'photoUrls' is missing in Pet")

Pet.kt and PetWithOwner.kt no longer have '= mutableSetOf()'. I also updated an ObjectSerializerTest Pet() call that relied on the old default.

findings.title: node: nested model properties skip required-field and primitive-type validation, so only the top-level model is validated
findings.description: deserialize() calls plainToInstance(cls, json) and then re-runs the ROOT model's constructor ('Gap S'). Every nested @Type(() => X) property is built by class-transformer with a no-arg `new X()`, where `data === undefined`, so the nested model's required checks are skipped. The root constructor's Object.assign copies the already-built nested instance without re-validating it. `{"value":"root","child":{}}` as TreeNode, or `{"value":"root","child":{"value":5}}`, decodes in node. The other 11 recurse into nested models and reject both: java creator required, kotlin/swift/rust/go nested decoders, python pydantic, ruby/elixir deserialize_model recursion, dart nested fromJson, csharp required members, php Symfony constructor denormalization. Arrays are not affected (deserializeArray re-enters deserialize per element). The node recursion test (object-serializer.test.ts:595) only uses a valid nested payload. Add table rows in every language's object-serializer test that decode TreeNode with an invalid nested child and expect SerializationError.

evidence.quote: const built = new (cls as unknown as new (i: unknown) => T)(instance);
if (data !== undefined) { if (this.value == null) { throw new TypeError("value is required");

findings.title: node: the discriminated oneOf path never runs the selected variant's constructor, so a variant missing a required field or carrying a wrong-typed field is accepted
findings.description: ObjectSerializer.deserialize routes a discriminated union (PetFood) by calling plainToInstance(targetCls, json) and passing the result straight to `new PetFood(instance)`. class-transformer creates the variant with a no-arg `new DryFood()`, so the required-field and typeof checks in DryFood's constructor (`weightKg is required`, `weightKg must be a number`) never run. `{"foodType":"dry"}` and `{"foodType":"dry","weightKg":"heavy"}` both decode in node. The other 11 reject them: java via the @JsonCreator `required=true` plus requireNonNull, kotlin via kotlinx required fields, csharp via [JsonRequired], php via assertRequiredPresent/assertPrimitiveTypes, python via pydantic, ruby via dry-struct, elixir via assert_required_present, go via the Gap AJ raw check, rust via serde, swift via decode, dart via the fromJson guard. The non-discriminated path in the same function (lines 484-497, the 'Gap S (union)' comment) does run `new schemaCls(instance)`; the discriminated branch never got that fix. No test in any of the 12 decodes a discriminated variant that lacks its own required field, so the petstore cannot catch this. Fix: run `new targetCls(instance)` before wrapping. Add a ComposedSchema unit test in all 12 that decodes `{"foodType":"dry"}` as PetFood and expects the SDK's SerializationError.

findings.title: getPetPhoto (content negotiation, Case 9) returns 7 different things when the server picks application/json
findings.description: getPetPhoto declares image/jpeg, image/png and application/json (a Photo object) for its 200 response. All 12 SDKs send `Accept: image/jpeg, image/png, application/json`, so the JSON variant is a legitimate reply. Every SDK types the return as bytes, and the bytes branch handles a JSON body differently in each one. (1) java (InputStream), csharp (Stream), ruby (StringIO) and dart (Uint8List) return the raw UTF-8 bytes of the JSON. (2) python returns the parsed dict while the signature says bytes: _deserialize returns non-bytes data unchanged when klass is bytes. (3) node returns the parsed plain object cast as Buffer (`(json) => json as Buffer`). (4) php deserializes with returnType 'string', so json_decode produces an array and settype(array,'string') yields the literal string "Array" plus an E_WARNING. (5) kotlin throws SerializationException because it calls deserialize<String> on an object. go (json.Unmarshal of an object into []byte), swift (JSONDecoder into Data) and elixir (convert_to_type(map, "binary()")) also throw SerializationError. (6) rust returns Ok with an EMPTY Vec<u8> (`_ => Vec::new()`), which is silent data loss. No SDK tests the JSON branch: the integration tests only hit the mock's default image variant, and rust's test_pet_api_get_pet_photo discards its result. Pick one contract, for example raw bytes of whatever body arrived (the java/csharp/ruby/dart behaviour) or a typed SerializationError. Then add a per-language unit test that drives getPetPhoto with Content-Type: application/json and a Photo body.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none

findings.title: go and rust send a literal `null` JSON body (with Content-Type: application/json) when the optional request body is omitted
findings.description: placeOrder has an optional requestBody (no `required: true`). If the caller passes no Order, java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, swift and elixir see a null body, send no entity, and strip Content-Type. go stores the typed-nil *Order in an `any` (`var requestBody any = order`). serializeBody's `body == nil` check is false for a typed nil, so json.Encoder emits `null`, and Content-Type is kept because serializedBody is non-nil. rust always calls `object_serializer::serialize(&order)` on the Option<Order>, which serde renders as `null`. Both put `POST /store/order` on the wire with a body of `null` and Content-Type: application/json, while the other 10 send an empty body with no Content-Type. Many servers reject a JSON `null` for an object schema. No SDK tests the omitted-optional-body path. Fix: go should nil-check the typed pointer before boxing (template api.mustache:352); rust should map None to body None (api.mustache:802). Add a placeOrder(nil/None) unit test to every language that asserts no body and no Content-Type.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none

go.note: Go side only. serializeBody now treats a typed-nil pointer, map or slice body as no body, so PlaceOrder(nil) sends no entity and no Content-Type instead of a JSON null. The rust side is untouched.

findings.title: setPetAvatar application/json variant (Case 10) cannot be expressed, and selecting it puts 6+ different bodies on the wire
findings.description: setPetAvatar declares image/jpeg, image/png and application/json, and the JSON variant is the object {data: format:byte, mimeType}. The generator types the body from the first content entry only (binary: InputStream/ByteArray/Stream/bytes/File/Buffer/Uint8List/*os.File/Vec<u8>/Data/binary), so no SDK can build the JSON envelope. When a caller selects requestContentType=application/json, the wire body differs by language. java's Jackson, with FAIL_ON_EMPTY_BEANS disabled, serializes the InputStream as `{}`. go json.Marshal(*os.File) also gives `{}`. kotlin (the `body is ByteArray` passthrough) and rust (the body is already bytes) send the raw bytes labelled application/json. python (b64encode), swift (JSONEncoder Data) and node (Buffer replacer) send a base64 JSON string. dart jsonEncode(Uint8List) sends a JSON int array. csharp System.Text.Json reflects over the Stream object's properties. ruby and php JSON-encode the File/SplFileObject handle. Several SDKs document 'the selector only changes Content-Type; the caller supplies a body the type accepts', but go, java, python, swift, node, dart and csharp re-encode the body, so a caller cannot even pre-build the JSON. Fix: generate one body parameter per declared content type (or a oneOf body type), or pass the body through unchanged whenever a non-binary type is selected. Then lock the wire bytes for the JSON selection in each PetApi test.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none (codegen collapses multi-content request schemas to the first)

findings.title: TLS verification ON (default) is never proven to reject an untrusted/mismatched certificate in 10 of 12 SDKs
findings.description: Only java (DefaultApiClientTest.verifySslTrueRejectsHostnameMismatch / verifySslFalseAcceptsHostnameMismatch) and node (default-api-client.test.ts:59/73) drive a request with verifySsl=true against a cert that must fail (cert names localhost, request goes to 127.0.0.1) and assert it is rejected. The other 10 only assert (a) the TransportOptions flag defaults to true and (b) a request SUCCEEDS with verifySsl=false or with a custom CA. A transport that silently ignored verifySsl (always insecure) would pass every one of their tests, so the single most security-relevant transport property is unasserted in 10 SDKs. The chasm fixture already supports the java/node technique (hostname mismatch with the shipped CA), so this is unit/integration-testable everywhere: add verifySsl=true + caCertPath + 127.0.0.1 => NetworkError (status 0, not ApiError(200)), and verifySsl=false => success, to each DefaultApiClientTest.

findings.title: php and swift put different JSON bytes on the wire ('/' escaped as '\/', php also \uXXXX for non-ASCII) and their tests were bent to hide it
findings.description: php ObjectSerializer::serialize calls json_encode($sanitized, $flags) with flags 0 (or JSON_FORCE_OBJECT): PHP's defaults escape '/' as '\/' and every non-ASCII char as \uXXXX, so a pet name 'café' goes out as "café" and photoUrls as "https:\/\/...". swift's JSONEncoder is created without .withoutEscapingSlashes (available macOS 10.15+/Linux, Package.swift floor is macOS 12), so every '/' (URLs, base64 payloads) becomes '\/'. The other 10 emit literal '/' and literal UTF-8 (csharp explicitly uses UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping, python ensure_ascii=False, go SetEscapeHTML(false)). The tests diverge to match: java/kotlin/csharp/python/ruby/node/dart/go/rust/swift/elixir assert the serialized string CONTAINS the literal 'café'/'日本', but php's peer tests ('accented character serializes and decodes correctly') json_decode the output and compare the decoded value, which passes with escaping; swift's byte-array tests explicitly rewrite expectations with replacingOccurrences(of: "/", with: "\\/"). php's own query path already passes JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES (BaseApi.php:349), so the body path is internally inconsistent too. Fix: php json_encode(..., JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES|JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE|...), swift encoder.outputFormatting = [.withoutEscapingSlashes]; make php assert toContain('café')/'日本' like peers and drop swift's '\/' rewrite; add a shared 'a/b' slash-not-escaped assertion to every ObjectSerializer test.

findings.title: API 404/500 tests accept any error in 6 SDKs instead of the exact status error type
findings.description: For a 404 or 500 returned through PetApi or StoreApi, csharp, php, python, ruby, node and dart assert the exact type (NotFoundException/NotFoundError, InternalServerError...). The other six do not. java asserts `isInstanceOf(Exception.class)` in all five of these tests, and its malformed-body test is equally broad. kotlin asserts the `ApiException` supertype plus the status code. go checks only `err == nil`, rust only `result.is_err()`, swift only `error != nil`, and elixir only pattern-matches `{:error, _reason}`. AGENTS says a test expecting a broad Exception is not a contract test. In these six SDKs a regression that mapped 404 to a generic ApiError, a NetworkError or a SerializationError would pass. Fix: assert the exact type in each (java `assertThrowsExactly(NotFoundException.class)`, go `errors.As(&*NotFoundError)`, rust `matches!` on the variant, swift a typed catch, elixir `{:error, %NotFoundError{}}`).

findings.title: OAuth2 refresh grant: its request body and the fall-back to the original grant on refresh failure are tested only in php (and csharp)
findings.description: In every SDK the token manager sends `grant_type=refresh_token` with the cached refresh token and carries over client_id/client_secret. If that refresh fails, it falls back to re-running the original grant; java also re-throws cancellation instead of falling back. Only php checks both the refresh request body and the fall-back, with 3 captured requests where the 2nd contains `grant_type=refresh_token` and the 3rd the original grant. csharp checks the fall-back by call count only. In the other 10 SDKs the `refreshTokenEmptyStringPreservesExisting` test triggers a refresh but never looks at the refresh request, and no test makes the refresh fail. A regression that dropped the refresh_token parameter, skipped the refresh, or let a refresh error escape instead of falling back would pass in 10 SDKs. Fix: add one test per SDK that copies php's three-response scenario and asserts the body of each request.

findings.title: Operation-level server variants: generated variant URLs, server variables and multi-server ops are untested; elixir's R8-4 typed-variant path has no test
findings.description: The petstore spec declares three operation-level `servers:` cases: getExternalPetInfo (one fixed URL), getStagingPetInfo (a templated URL whose variables have enums and defaults), and getMultiServerPetInfo (two servers, one templated). Only getExternalPetInfo is ever called, and 8 SDKs do not use the generated server type for it. java, kotlin, csharp and php pass the generated variant (`GetExternalPetInfoServer.Server0`) and assert that the requested URL starts with the spec's `https://external-api.example.com/v1`. python, ruby, node, dart, go, rust and swift pass a test-defined subclass or mock that points at the mock server, so the generated variant's URL is never checked. elixir passes a bare `%ServerConfiguration{}` and only asserts `result != nil`. AGENTS R8-4 changed elixir to route through the typed variant module's `url/1`, but the test still uses the bare struct, so that change is not locked. No SDK calls getStagingPetInfo or getMultiServerPetInfo, so variable substitution and enum checks on operation-level servers, and picking among several operation servers, are untested in all 12 (ruby only checks that the constants autoload). Fix: in every SDK, call getStagingPetInfo with the generated variant, with and without a variable override and with one value outside the enum, and assert the resolved URL and the rejection; in elixir use the generated variant module rather than a bare ServerConfiguration.

findings.title: Sending the refresh grant to refreshUrl (not tokenUrl) is untested in all 12 SDKs
findings.description: The password and authorization-code authenticators send the first grant to tokenUrl and the refresh grant to refreshUrl. refreshUrl falls back to tokenUrl when it is null, and the petstore spec declares a distinct `refreshUrl: https://auth.example.com/oauth/refresh` for legacyAuth and userAuth. Every `usesRefreshTokenOnSubsequentCalls` and `includesRefreshTokenOnRefresh` test builds the authenticator without a refreshUrl (or with refreshUrl = null), so tokenUrl and refreshUrl are the same and the routing cannot be observed. The only test that mentions it is elixir's 'scheme authenticator keeps ... the declared URLs', and that only reads the struct field and never checks where the request goes. A regression that sent the refresh grant to tokenUrl, or the first grant to refreshUrl, would pass everywhere. Fix: in each SDK construct with a distinct refreshUrl and assert the URL captured for the first call and for the refresh call.

findings.title: The R8-10 OAuth2 percent-encoding change has no test in any SDK
findings.description: AGENTS R8-10 records that 11 SDKs now keep exactly `-._~` literal and %-encode `* ! ' ( )` in three places: the token-request body, the RFC 6749 §2.3.1 Basic client-auth header, and the authorize URL. No test in any of the 12 SDKs uses one of these characters: grepping every test tree for `%2A`, `%21`, `%27`, `%28` or `%29` in an OAuth context finds nothing. Every `basicAuthUrlEncodesClientIdAndSecret` test uses the same inputs, `id+with/special` and `secret&with=stuff`, so `+`, `/`, `&` and `=` are the only characters exercised. The change can silently revert in any SDK. Swift's authorize URL is the documented exception (R8-F1); its body and Basic header paths are still in scope. Fix: add `~` and `*!'()` to the client_id/secret/scope fixtures in the Basic-header, body and authorize-URL tests and assert the exact bytes.

findings.title: Enum string literals: python/dart/php/ruby silently STRIP a single quote from the wire value; no language escapes backslash
findings.description: AbstractBetterCodegen.toEnumValue builds every string enum value as quoteEnumValue(escapeEnumStringValue(value)). quoteEnumValue either escapes the quote character or deletes it, depending on shouldEscapeQuotationMark(). python, dart, php and ruby use a single quote and return false there, so an enum value such as `o'clock` is emitted as `'oclock'`. The rendered `{{{value}}}` is the wire value in every enum template (python/models/model.mustache:19, dart/models/model.mustache:29, php/models/inline_enum.mustache:11, ruby/models/model.mustache:20/456). Those four SDKs therefore send `oclock` and reject a server's `o'clock` as an unknown variant, while node (also single-quoted) escapes it to `\'` and the six double-quote SDKs keep it. Separately, toEnumValue never calls escapeText (upstream generators do), so no SDK escapes a backslash. A value like `a\d` fails to compile in java/kotlin/csharp, and `a\b` silently becomes a backspace. The kotlin/dart `$name` and elixir `#{}` interpolation sequences are not neutralised either. csharp is the only SDK with its own escape table (getEnumStringEscapes: \n \t \r "), and that table also omits backslash. This is latent because petstore enums contain only [a-z-] characters.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Single-quoted literals can escape the quote with \' (node already does).

findings.title: String default literals use the comment-escaper escapeText, which mutates values and emits invalid single-quoted literals
findings.description: Eleven toDefaultValue overrides wrap a string schema default in the target quote and escape it with DefaultCodegen.escapeText. escapeText was written for comments and double-quoted text: it turns \t, \n and \r into spaces, doubles backslashes, escapes `"` (never `'`), and then runs escapeUnsafeCharacters (`*/`→`*_/`, `/*`→`/_*`; ruby adds `=end`→`=_end` and `#{`→`\#{`). The effects differ by language. (a) ruby/php/dart/node wrap the default in single quotes but leave `'` unescaped, so a default such as `it's` is a syntax error. (b) ruby and php single-quoted strings keep `\"` literally, so the default `say "hi"` becomes the runtime value `say \"hi\"` (and ruby `#{x}` becomes `\#{x}`) and goes on the wire wrong. (c) A newline or tab in a default becomes a space in those 11 SDKs. (d) `a*/b` becomes `a*_/b` in every escapeText user. (e) kotlin `"...$x"` and dart `'$x'` interpolate, and elixir `#{}` does too. python alone uses its own escaping (`val.replace("'","\\'")`), which never escapes backslashes or newlines, so a newline breaks the literal and `\n` is reinterpreted. The same default value therefore produces different in-memory and wire values, or no compiling SDK at all, depending on language. Latent because petstore string defaults are plain words (api, v3, placed, medium, untitled).
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Each language needs a dedicated string-literal escaper (escapeTextInSingleQuotes exists upstream).

findings.title: python maps format: password to pydantic SecretStr, so model bodies send "**********" on the wire
findings.description: BetterPythonCodegen.postProcessModelProperty retypes `format: password` model properties to SecretStr. Model request bodies are serialized with `obj.model_dump_json(by_alias=True, exclude_none=True)` (object_serializer.py:183), and pydantic v2 writes SecretStr as the literal `"**********"` in JSON mode. I confirmed this locally with pydantic 2.12: `{"password":"**********"}`. The `_sanitize_for_serialization` SecretStr branch (object_serializer.py:284) is only reached for non-model objects, and the model template defines no field_serializer to unwrap it. The other 11 SDKs keep the field a plain string and send the real value. The same override also gives python alone validating types for `format: ipv4`/`ipv6` (IPv4Address/IPv6Address) and `email` (EmailStr; node brands Email without validation), so python rejects inputs the other 11 accept. Latent: petstore's only `password` is an OAuth flow name, not a schema field.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None

python.note: Confirmed real. BetterPythonCodegen.postProcessModelProperty:846 maps format: password to SecretStr, which model_dump_json writes as '**********'. petstore has no password-format schema property. Spec needed: add 'password: {type: string, format: password}' to a request-body schema (for example PetWithOwner) and test that serialize() emits the real value. Fix: drop the 'password' case (keep StrictStr). The ipv4/ipv6/email strictness is a separate decision.

findings.title: Enum string literal quoting differs by language: apostrophes are silently stripped in 4 SDKs and '$' / '#{' are interpolated in 3
findings.description:
toEnumValue calls quoteEnumValue. For python, ruby, php and dart, shouldEscapeQuotationMark() returns false, so every `'` is REMOVED from the enum wire value rather than escaped: `O'Brien` becomes `'OBrien'` (`value.replace(qs, "")`). node shares the `'` quote character but keeps the default escape (`'O\'Brien'`), and the 7 double-quote languages emit `"O'Brien"`. As a result, python, ruby, php and dart send a different value on the wire and fail to match the real value in responses. All four languages accept a backslash-escaped `'` inside single quotes, so stripping is not forced.

Separately, no language escapes its interpolation sigil in enum literals:
- kotlin `@SerialName("$eq")` / `EQ("$eq")` and dart `eq('$eq')` interpolate a variable, which fails to compile. Mongo-style operator enums such as `$eq` and `$in` are realistic.
- elixir `do: "#{x}"` interpolates.

The other 9 languages emit these values literally. Backslashes are not escaped anywhere either: python `'a\b'` encodes a backspace on the wire.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Each language has a valid escape for its quote character (\' in all four single-quote languages, \$ in kotlin/dart, \#{ in elixir).

findings.title: Global server and server-variable descriptions are raw spec text placed inside string literals, so one apostrophe breaks 5 SDKs and one double quote breaks the other 7
findings.description:
AbstractBetterCodegen.processServers puts `server.getDescription()` and `sv.getDescription()` (and `sv.getDefault()` / enum values) into the context untouched. They skip escapeText, which the operation-level CodegenServer.description does get through DefaultCodegen.fromServers. They also skip htmlUnescape, because preprocessOpenAPI handles info, tags, schemas and paths but never `openAPI.getServers()`. Every servers.mustache then writes them into a string literal with triple braces.

Which input breaks which SDK depends on the language's quote character:
- Apostrophe (`Bob's sandbox`): php, python, ruby, node and dart emit `'Bob's sandbox'`, which does not parse.
- Double quote: java, kotlin, csharp, go, rust, swift and elixir emit `"..."..."`, which does not compile.
- `$name`: interpolated in kotlin and dart.
- `#{...}`: interpolated in elixir.
- A YAML `|` multi-line description: breaks the single-line literals in python, java, kotlin, csharp, go, swift, dart and node.

I rendered `description: '{{{description}}}',` with `Bob's sandbox` and got `description: 'Bob's sandbox',`. The doc-comment copies of the same description use `{{serverDescription}}` (HTML-escaped) in 10 languages and raw in csharp and python. In csharp that raw copy sits inside an XML `<summary>` with no escapeXml, so `&` or `<` triggers CS1570 under --warnaserror.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. The operation-level server path already runs escapeText, and each language has a valid escape for its own quote character.

findings.title: go: every primary operation method's doc comment (including its `// Deprecated:` marker) is detached from the func by a blank line
findings.description: In go/api/api.mustache the per-param example loop is written as a non-standalone line, `{{#allParams}}{{#vendorExtensions.pluralExamples}}` (template line 108, closing tag on line 110). Each parameter therefore emits an empty line between the doc block and `func (a *PetApi) Op(`. Go only treats a comment as a doc comment when it sits immediately before the declaration, with no blank line in between. As a result all 37 data methods in pet_api.go and store_api.go have no godoc (a scan found 37 detached of 74 API methods; the *WithHTTPInfo variants are fine). This also breaks deprecation: on FindPetsByStatus and GetPetById the `// Deprecated: This operation is deprecated.` line is detached, and it is not its own paragraph either (no `//` separator line before it). So gopls and staticcheck SA1019 never flag callers of the deprecated data methods. That contradicts the AGENTS.md T2-5 entry, which says go puts a `// Deprecated:` doc paragraph on EVERY public variant. The other 11 attach their operation docs and deprecation markers to the declaration.

evidence.quote:
// param pet: Create a new pet in the store

func (a *PetApi) AddPet(pet Pet, options *opts.AddPetOptions) (*Pet, error) {

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. It is mustache standalone-line whitespace. Putting each section tag on its own line, and emitting `//` before `Deprecated:`, fixes it.

go.note: The example loop in api.mustache is split into standalone section lines so no blank line detaches the doc comment, and Deprecated is now its own paragraph, placed last and preceded by a // line.

findings.title: go: golangci-lint is vacuous because every generated .go file carries the `// Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.` marker (contradicts AGENTS 'Not vacuous')
findings.description: All 138 .go files in the go golden, sources and tests alike, start with `// Code generated by openapi-generator-plus. DO NOT EDIT.` (from go/api_info.mustache:1). The shipped .golangci.yml is just `version: "2"`. In golangci-lint v2, `linters.exclusions.generated` defaults to `lax`, which drops every issue in a file carrying that marker (the line also matches the `strict` regex). The `golangci-lint run ./...` step in GoLintingSpec therefore checks nothing. AGENTS.md 'Known-thin gates' claims the opposite: 'Not vacuous: ... golangci adds only errcheck/ineffassign/unused on top'. AGENTS guardrail 3 records that csharp had its `// <auto-generated/>` marker removed precisely to turn analyzers on, so go is the one SDK whose linter is still turned off by a generated-code marker. The go README compounds this: it says golangci-lint 'runs staticcheck, revive, gocritic, gosec, bodyclose, errcheck', and none of those beyond the defaults are configured.

evidence.quote: // Code generated by openapi-generator-plus. DO NOT EDIT.
// Code generated by openapi-generator-plus. DO NOT EDIT.
Not vacuous: the same spec already runs `go vet` and `staticcheck` separately, so golangci adds only errcheck/ineffassign/unused on top.

findings.suspected_forced_reason: The marker is a go convention, but `linters.exclusions.generated: disable` in .golangci.yml turns linting back on, so nothing forces the gate to be empty.

go.note: Lint with generated-file exclusion disabled reports 42 issues (33 errcheck, 9 govet) in the generated code and tests, so it needs an unchecked-error cleanup first; the golangci setting was reverted, README lint wording corrected. AGENTS.md still says golangci-lint is not vacuous and should be corrected.
