findings.title: kotlin: query and form-body encoder leaves & = + # ? / [ ] literal, so values split, truncate or change on the wire
findings.description: Kotlin encodes query keys and values, and the x-www-form-urlencoded body, with Ktor's `String.encodeURLQueryComponent(spaceToPlus=…)`. That call keeps its default `encodeFull = false`, which leaves the whole RFC 3986 reserved set literal: `: / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * , ; = + ~`. I ran ktor-http-jvm 3.5.0 (the version the golden pins) on `a b&c=d+e#f?g/h~i*j!k'l(m)n,o;p:q@r[s]t$u%vé` and got `a%20b&c=d+e#f?g/h~i*j!k'l(m)n,o;p:q@r[s]t$u%25v%C3%A9` (query), and the same with `+` for space (form). Concrete effects: (1) getPetByName(category="a&b=c") sends `?category=a&b=c`, which the server reads as two parameters. (2) A `#` in any query value starts a fragment and drops the rest of the query. (3) A literal `+` (for example nickname="C++" in setPetPreferences) goes out unescaped, and a form/query decoder reads it as a space. (4) deepObject keys go out as literal `filter[k]` instead of `filter%5Bk%5D`. The other 11 SDKs escape all of these: java URLEncoder, csharp Uri.EscapeDataString, php rawurlencode, python quote, ruby CGI.escape, node encodeURIComponent, dart Uri.encodeQueryComponent, go url.QueryEscape, rust urlencoding, swift CharacterSet `-._~`, elixir URI.encode_www_form. No kotlin test sends a reserved character through the query or form path. Only the allowReserved helper and path encoding are tested (ValueSerializerTest.kt:96, :702). Fix: pass `encodeFull = true` to both helpers, or reuse the URLEncoder-based helpers the kotlin ValueSerializer already uses.

internal fun encodeQuery(value: String): String = value.encodeURLQueryComponent(spaceToPlus = false)
internal fun encode(value: String): String = value.encodeURLQueryComponent(spaceToPlus = true)
internal fun encodeQuery(value: String): String = value.encodeURLQueryComponent(spaceToPlus = false)

findings.title: OAS readOnly/writeOnly: java maps them to Jackson access modes with inverted client semantics; the other 11 only add doc comments. Petstore has no readOnly/writeOnly property
findings.description: java/models/model.mustache:692-697 emits `@JsonProperty(access = JsonProperty.Access.READ_ONLY)` for `readOnly: true` and `WRITE_ONLY` for `writeOnly: true`. Jackson defines these from the point of view of the serialized document. READ_ONLY means serialize but ignore on deserialize. WRITE_ONLY means deserialize but never serialize. In a client this is backwards. A server-populated readOnly field (id, createdAt) is DROPPED when java decodes the response and comes back null. A writeOnly field (password, secret) is NEVER SENT in the java request body. I checked this against jackson-databind 2.21.1 with the generator's mapper settings: a READ_ONLY field decoded from `{"r":"srv"}` is null, and serializing an object whose only field is WRITE_ONLY fails with 'no properties discovered'. Of the other 11, python/node/ruby/php/csharp emit doc or json_schema_extra only (python/models/model.mustache:373, node/models/model.mustache:290-295, ruby/models/model.mustache:448-453, php/models/model.mustache:461-466, csharp/models/model.mustache:423-428), and kotlin/dart/go/rust/swift/elixir ignore the keywords. All 11 send and receive both kinds of field normally. The petstore and probe specs declare no readOnly/writeOnly property, so no golden or test notices. Proposed YAML (petstore components.schemas, used by a request/response op such as addPet): `Account: {type: object, required: [username], properties: {id: {type: integer, format: int64, readOnly: true}, username: {type: string}, password: {type: string, writeOnly: true}}}`, plus `/store/account: post: {operationId: createAccount, security: [], requestBody: {required: true, content: {application/json: {schema: {$ref: '#/components/schemas/Account'}}}}, responses: {'200': {description: ok, content: {application/json: {schema: {$ref: '#/components/schemas/Account'}}}}}}`. Assert in every SDK that the echoed `id` decodes and that `password` is on the wire.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none: Jackson can express OpenAPI semantics only with request/response views; the plain annotation inverts them

java.note: Same as F025: needs the Account schema (readOnly id, writeOnly password) and POST /store/account in the petstore spec, plus a cross-SDK decision on canonical behaviour.

findings.title: Schema validation keywords (pattern/minLength/maxLength/minimum/maximum/multipleOf/minItems/maxItems) are enforced only by python; petstore declares none
findings.description: python/models/model.mustache:370-381 turns every constraint into a pydantic Field kwarg (`min_length`, `max_length`, `pattern=r'...'`, `ge/gt/le/lt`, `multiple_of`, `min_length` for minItems). No other language's templates reference `{{#pattern}}`, `{{#minLength}}`, `{{#maximum}}` and the rest (grep over all 12 template trees finds only python/models/model.mustache). Python therefore rejects values the other 11 accept, both when the caller builds a model and when a server RESPONSE is decoded: an out-of-range response field is a python ValidationError/SerializationError and is accepted everywhere else. That breaks the 'same inputs accepted/rejected' rule. It also exposes python-only failures at import time. The pattern is emitted raw inside `r'...'`, so a pattern containing `'` is a SyntaxError. pydantic-core's regex engine rejects ECMA look-around, so a pattern like `^(?!admin).*$` makes the models module fail to import. The petstore spec has 0 occurrences of any of these keywords, so this never renders. Proposed YAML: add to Pet `nickname: {type: string, minLength: 2, maxLength: 8, pattern: '^[a-z]+$'}`, to Order `quantity: {..., minimum: 1, maximum: 100}`, and a probe-only `handle: {type: string, pattern: "^(?!admin)[a-z']+$"}`. Decide one cross-language policy, either enforce everywhere or nowhere (likely nowhere on the response path), and lock it with a response carrying `quantity: 500`.

findings.title: format: time handling: php sends a full RFC 3339 date-time, kotlin has no serializer so its models will not compile, and precision is split between seconds and sub-seconds. Petstore has no format: time
findings.description: Every codegen maps `time` (java/kotlin LocalTime, csharp TimeOnly, php \DateTimeImmutable, python datetime.time, ruby Tod::TimeOfDay, node Temporal.PlainTime, rust NaiveTime, elixir Time.t(); go/dart/swift String), but neither spec has a `format: time` field or param. Divergences found in the templates: (1) php serializes any \DateTimeInterface with DATE_TIME_FORMAT = RFC3339_EXTENDED, both in sanitizeForSerialization and in stringify. A time-of-day therefore goes out as `2026-10-15T14:30:00.000+00:00`, and php's own test only asserts `toContain('2024-01-15T10:20:30')`. (2) kotlin maps time to java.time.LocalTime but registers no contextual serializer (object_serializer.mustache:878-884), and the model template adds @Contextual only for date/date-time/uuid/uri/duration/number. A @Serializable model with a LocalTime field therefore fails to compile. kotlin's stringify also routes LocalTime into `is TemporalAccessor -> DATE_TIME_FORMATTER.format(value)`, which throws for a type with no offset. (3) Precision: python truncates to seconds (`isoformat(timespec='seconds')`), as do ruby `%H:%M:%S`, csharp `HH:mm:ss` and elixir `Time.truncate(:second)`. java ISO_LOCAL_TIME, node PlainTime (its test expects `09:15:30.25`), rust NaiveTime and dart's validated String keep the fraction, and go/swift pass any String through unvalidated. python's test comment claims 'the other 11 SDKs ... all emit HH:MM:SS', which the code contradicts. findings.title: rust OpenIdConnectAuthenticator fails concurrent requests and loses its delegate (exchanged tokens) when a call is cancelled
findings.description: try_auth_headers/exchange_code move the resolved delegate OUT of its Mutex (take_delegate) for the whole token-fetch await and only put it back afterwards. (1) Any second API request on the same Client that arrives during that window gets Err(ConfigurationError::InvalidState("OIDC delegate is in use by a concurrent call")). Two parallel requests through an OIDC-authenticated rust client therefore fail spuriously, where the other 11 either serialize discovery (java synchronized getDelegate, go mutex) or let both proceed. (2) Dropping the future (tokio cancellation or timeout) while awaiting leaves self.delegate = None. The next call re-runs discovery and builds a fresh OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator, so the exchanged code's access and refresh tokens are lost and every later call fails with CodeNotExchanged. resolve_delegate also runs while another call holds the delegate and overwrites it, and the restore then overwrites again. findings.title: Path values "." and ".." pass through encodePathSegment unencoded, and some transports then resolve them as dot-segments
findings.description: In all 12 encoders, `.` is unreserved and stays literal, so `getPetByName("..")` produces `/pet/byName/..?category=x`. What happens next depends on the transport. node (WHATWG) produced `http://h/pet/?category=x`, python's urllib3 `parse_url` produced `/pet/?category=x`, and dart's `Uri.parse` produced `http://h/pet/?category=x`. In those SDKs the request reaches a different endpoint (/pet). rust (url crate, WHATWG), csharp (System.Uri) and php (Symfony resolveUrl) most likely behave the same way; those three were not run. java (java.net.URI), swift (URL) and ruby send `/pet/byName/..` literally, and go and elixir most likely do too (not run). This is a wire divergence with security weight: a user-controlled name reroutes the request. WHATWG treats even `%2E%2E` as `..`, so encoding alone cannot make node or rust agree. The uniform fix is to reject a path-segment value equal to `.` or `..` in all 12, with the language's argument error, or always encode them as `%2E` and accept that node and rust still normalize.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: Partly. node and rust go through WHATWG URL parsing, which resolves `..` and `%2E%2E`. Rejecting these values up front would be uniform.

findings.description: Each value-serializer defect above survives because petstore has no parameter that exercises it. findings.title: allowReserved output is re-encoded by the transport URL parser in 6 SDKs, so reserved characters are not literal on the wire
findings.description: `encode_query_allowing_reserved` produces the same string in all 12, but some transports rewrite the URL after that. I checked each parser on `?r=a:b/c?d[e]f@g!h$i&j=1&k'l(m)n*o+p,q;r~s`. python (urllib3 2.6 `parse_url`, used by `PoolManager.request`), dart (`Uri.parse` in abstract_api_client) and swift (`URL(string:)` on macOS) re-encode `[`/`]` to `%5B`/`%5D`. node (undici fetch, WHATWG URL) re-encodes `'` to `%27`, and rust's reqwest `Url::parse` uses the same WHATWG special-query set, so it does too. ruby (Faraday decode/re-encode, see the separate finding) re-encodes every reserved character. java (java.net.URI), kotlin (Ktor), csharp, go and elixir keep them literal. The only allowReserved wire value petstore tests is `v1.0/beta:rc1`, and only through unit tests of the encoder, never through the transport. So `[ ] '` (and in ruby, all of them) differ on the wire without any test noticing. In node and rust the WHATWG `'` rewrite is unavoidable once a URL object is built, so those two are arguably forced. python, dart and swift could avoid it: urllib3 `request_url` with a pre-encoded url, `Uri(query:)` with `Uri.encodeQueryComponent` disabled, or `URLComponents.percentEncodedQuery`. Add an echo-based PetApi test that sends `revision` with the full reserved set and asserts the received query.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: Partly. node and rust go through a WHATWG URL parser that always encodes `'` in special-scheme queries. ruby, python, dart and swift are not forced.

findings.title: content-based query params (`content: application/json`) skip the SDK serializer in 8 languages, giving different JSON bytes and error types
findings.description: For a query param declared with `content: application/json`, java, kotlin, swift and dart call the SDK ObjectSerializer. The other eight call a raw stdlib JSON encoder. go uses `json.Marshal` and discards the error. HTML escaping stays on, so `<` becomes `<`, which contradicts the AGENTS 'Resolved' note that go serializes with SetEscapeHTML(false). csharp uses `System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer.Serialize` with default options: `<` becomes `<`, `é` becomes `é`, and the SDK converters for dates, enums and duration are skipped. php uses `json_encode` with no flags: `/` becomes `\/` and `é` becomes `é`. I checked this with php 8.5. python uses `json.dumps`, which puts spaces after `:` and `,`, applies ensure_ascii, and raises TypeError on a pydantic model. node uses `JSON.stringify`, so a Date ends in `Z`, not the canonical `+00:00`. ruby uses `JSON.generate`. rust uses `serde_json::to_string(...).unwrap_or_default()`, so a failure sends an empty string. elixir uses `Jason.encode!`, which raises Jason.EncodeError, not SerializationError. For `{"q":"a/b<é"}` the 12 SDKs put at least five different byte strings on the wire. swift's ObjectSerializer also leaves JSONEncoder's default slash escaping (`\/`) in place. Fix by routing every queryContent value through the SDK ObjectSerializer.serialize. Petstore has no content query param, so add one.

findings.title: format: byte parameters are never base64-encoded, and each SDK emits a different wrong form

The parameter path has no base64 step anywhere, so a byte query, header or path param with the value bytes "hi" serializes as follows. java and kotlin: `String.valueOf(byte[])` / `ByteArray.toString()` gives `[B@6d06d69c`, an identity hash. csharp: `byte[]` is an `IList`, so the value is treated as an array: `104,105`, or `p=104&p=105` when exploded. dart: `Uint8List` is a `List`, giving `104,105`. go: `toStringSlice` reflects over `[]byte`, giving `104,105`. rust: serde gives `[104,105]`. python: `str(b'hi')` gives `b'hi'`. swift: `Data.description` gives `2 bytes`. ruby, php, elixir and node send the raw bytes as text (`hi`; node through `Buffer.toString()`). The canonical value is `aGk=`. Petstore has no byte parameter. Fix by giving stringify a byte branch that base64-encodes, put it before the IList/List/slice checks in csharp, dart and go, and add a `format: byte` header or query param to petstore.

findings.title: The 1000-deep JSON nesting cap is not uniform: php accepts at most 999, swift at most 512
findings.description: java (StreamReadConstraints), csharp (MaxDepth), and the byte-scan SDKs (kotlin, python, node, go, rust, ruby, dart, elixir) accept depth 1000 and reject 1001. php passes depth=1000 to json_decode, whose depth counts one level more: 1000 nested arrays fail with 'Maximum stack depth exceeded', 999 pass (verified php 8.5). findings.title: format:byte base64 decode strictness differs on padding, whitespace, alphabet and trailing bits (php model fields not validated at all)
findings.description: Verified per language with each SDK's actual decoder: UNPADDED 'dGVzdA' accepted by kotlin (java.util.Base64.getDecoder) and php (base64_decode strict); rejected by the other 10. Embedded SPACE 'dGVz dA==' accepted by java (Jackson MIME_NO_LINEFEEDS skips whitespace), csharp (.NET 9 STJ), php, node (decodeBase64 strips /\s+/); NEWLINE additionally accepted by go (encoding/json ignores \r\n); rejected by kotlin, python(bare path), ruby, dart, rust, swift, elixir. URL-SAFE alphabet '-_8=' accepted ONLY by dart (base64Decode accepts both alphabets, even '%3D' padding). NON-CANONICAL trailing bits 'dGVzdB==' accepted by java, kotlin, php, python, node, go, swift, elixir; rejected by csharp, ruby, dart, rust. php model byte fields (PetPassport::$thumbnail etc.) are plain strings never validated on deserialize, so even '!!!!' is accepted until getThumbnailAsBytes() is called. Note java vs kotlin (same JVM) disagree on both padding and whitespace. node's comment claims to match 'the strict decoders in ruby/php/python/elixir/go/rust', which is false for php, go and python model fields. Pick one rule (RFC 4648 §3.3: reject whitespace and non-alphabet, require padding, reject non-zero pad bits) and pin it with a shared test vector table.

evidence.quote: diverges from the strict decoders in ruby/php/python/elixir/go/rust.

findings.title: go still HTML-escapes <, >, & inside every model body (contradicts AGENTS Resolved 'go serializes with HTML escaping OFF')
findings.description: serialize() disables HTML escaping on its json.Encoder, but every generated model has `MarshalJSON` returning `json.Marshal((Alias)(o))`, and models.Set marshals via json.Marshal too. json.Marshal always escapes HTML; encoding/json then compacts the Marshaler output without un-escaping. Verified with go 1.26: model {"name":"a<b>&c"} serializes as {"name":"a<b>&c"} while the same string in a map stays literal. So Pet.name, Pet.photoUrls (URLs with '&' query strings), Category.name, Metadata, etc. all go on the wire escaped, unlike the other 11 SDKs. The existing test TestSerialize_MapToJSON only checks a plain map, so the regression is invisible. Fix: build the Alias bytes with a json.Encoder + SetEscapeHTML(false) (shared helper) in model.mustache:218/293/343/437/519 and set.mustache:12; add a model-level assertion.

go.note: New models/json_marshal.mustache (published as pkg/models/json_marshal.go, registered in BetterGoCodegen) provides marshalJSON, an Encoder with SetEscapeHTML(false) that trims the trailing newline. Every model MarshalJSON (alias, additionalProperties, unevaluatedProperties, oneOf, anyOf merge) and Set.MarshalJSON now use it, so <, > and & go on the wire literally.

findings.title: python model bodies emit NaN/Infinity (and Decimal overflow) as null instead of rejecting
findings.description: ObjectSerializer.serialize documents 'Uses allow_nan=False so NaN/Infinity ... raise ... Aligns Python with the 10 SDKs', but for a BaseModel it calls obj.model_dump_json(...), which uses pydantic's default ser_json_inf_nan='null'. Verified (pydantic 2.12.5, LaxFloat alias): PhotoMetadataLocation(lat=float('nan')) serializes as {"lat":null}; inf likewise. JsonNumber widens Decimal via float(), so weightKg=Decimal('1e400') becomes inf and is sent as null. Models accept NaN/inf on construction, and json.loads turns an incoming 1e400 into inf. java (nonFiniteNumberModule), kotlin, csharp, node, go, rust, ruby, php, dart, swift all raise their SerializationError on a non-finite value. Fix: ConfigDict(ser_json_inf_nan='strings' is wrong too) — use allow_inf_nan=False on float fields (Field(allow_inf_nan=False) / FiniteFloat) and reject inf in JsonNumber's serializer.

evidence.quote: Uses allow_nan=False so NaN/Infinity/-Infinity raise ValueError

JsonNumber = Annotated[
    Decimal,
    PlainSerializer(lambda value: float(value), return_type=float, when_used="json"),

python.note: LaxFloat now carries Field(allow_inf_nan=False), so NaN and Infinity are rejected on construction, assignment and decode (1e999 becomes inf). JsonNumber now serializes through _decimal_to_json_number, which raises for a Decimal beyond the double range instead of writing null.

findings.title: Binary body sent with a selected application/json Content-Type (setPetAvatar) gives {}, raw bytes or a base64 string depending on language
findings.description:
setPetAvatar declares image/jpeg, image/png and application/json. Every SDK types its body as a binary stream or bytes, and every SDK accepts `application/json` as the selector, which passes the R7 declared-type check. The body ladder then disagrees:
- java: an InputStream is not byte[], so it goes to objectSerializer.serialize(). FAIL_ON_EMPTY_BEANS is disabled, so the body is `{}`.
- go: *os.File goes to serialize() and becomes `{}`.
- kotlin: the ladder checks `body is ByteArray` before the content type, so raw image bytes are sent labelled application/json.
- rust: Vec<u8> passes through unchanged ('already serialized'), so raw bytes are sent as JSON.
- swift: Data is Encodable, so JSONEncoder sends a base64 JSON string.
- node: the ObjectSerializer replacer sends Buffer as base64.
The same call puts three different payloads on the wire, and none of them is the spec's `{data: <base64>}` envelope. The go template comment admits that 'the caller must still supply a body the selected content-type accepts', but no SDK can, because the signature accepts only the binary type. Fix: either reject a JSON selector when the body is binary, with the same ArgumentError/IllegalArgument in all 12, or generate the envelope. Petstore test: setPetAvatar(…, requestContentType=application/json) must have the same outcome in all 12.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None

findings.title: Binary return type with an absent response Content-Type behaves differently in the 12 SDKs; java's BaseApi contradicts its own transport, and rust silently returns empty bytes
findings.description:
Case: a binary-returning operation (downloadPetDocument and similar) whose response has no Content-Type. java's transport treats an empty Content-Type as TEXT and does not base64-encode it (DefaultApiClient.isTextContentType returns true, citing the 'established cross-SDK convention'). java's BaseApi mirror isTextResponseContentType("") instead returns FALSE, and its comment says this 'mirror[s] the transport'. BaseApi then runs Base64.getDecoder().decode() on a body that was never encoded: it throws IllegalArgumentException for most text, and returns wrong bytes for text that happens to be valid base64. The other languages:
- Return the raw UTF-8 bytes: kotlin, csharp, ruby. dart tries base64 first and falls back to UTF-8, so a base64-looking body is mis-decoded.
- Treat a missing Content-Type as JSON and fail on a raw body: go, swift, node, python, elixir, php.
- rust treats it as JSON, gets a parse error, and silently returns an EMPTY Vec<u8> with Ok (`_ => Vec::new()`). That is data loss with no error.
The same input therefore gives three different outcomes: bytes, an error, or silently empty. Fix: use one rule in every language. Recommended: a missing Content-Type on a binary return type means the transport kept the body as text, so return its UTF-8 bytes. java's mirror must match its own transport, and rust must not swallow the error. Petstore extension: a chasm route for downloadPetDocument that omits Content-Type, plus a unit test per language.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. This is an internal mirror bug in java plus an unharmonized policy.

findings.title: Percent-encoding safe set for normal query values and form bodies is not harmonized (~ * ! ' ( )); the R8-10 fix was applied to OAuth only
findings.description:
R8-10 fixed this exact class (keep only `-._~` literal, %-encode `* ! ' ( )`) in the OAuth token body, the Basic header and the authorize URL. BaseApi's general query and form encoders were not changed. Query values today:
- csharp (Uri.EscapeDataString), php (rawurlencode), python (quote, safe=''), ruby (CGI.escape), dart (Uri.encodeQueryComponent), go (url.QueryEscape), rust (urlencoding::encode), swift (explicit `-._~` set) and elixir (URI.encode_www_form) all emit `~` literal and `%2A%21%27%28%29`.
- java (URLEncoder plus `+`→%20) emits `*` literal and `~`→`%7E`.
- node (encodeURIComponent) emits `! ' ( ) * ~` literal.
- kotlin leaves everything literal (separate critical finding).
Form bodies split along a different line: java (URLEncoder), node (URLSearchParams) and ruby (URI.encode_www_form) use the WHATWG form set (`*` literal, `~`→%7E). csharp, php, python, dart, go, rust, swift and elixir use the RFC 3986 set (`~` literal, `*`→%2A).
I checked these with ruby 2.6, elixir, python3 and node: `a~b*c!d'e(f)g` gives ruby CGI `a~b%2Ac%21d%27e%28f%29g`, ruby www_form `a%7Eb*c%21d%27e%28f%29g`, node encodeURIComponent `a~b*c!d'e(f)g`, node URLSearchParams `a%7Eb*c%21…`, and python/elixir `a~b%2Ac%21d%27e%28f%29g`. A spec-compliant server decodes all of these to the same value, but the bytes on the wire differ and no test pins them. Fix: route query and form encoding through one shared per-language encoder with the rust unreserved set `-._~`, as R8-10 did for OAuth. Unit test: each BaseApiTest asserts that `a~b*c!d'e(f)g` gives `a~b%2Ac%21d%27e%28f%29g` in a query value and in a form value.

evidence.quote: OAuth2 percent-encoding keeps exactly the RFC 3986 unreserved set `-._~` literal

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Each language can use a hand-rolled unreserved encoder, as rust/dart/kotlin already do for RFC 5987 and OAuth.

findings.title: Query, form-body and multipart part ORDER differs across SDKs; go, swift and rust multipart are nondeterministic per run
findings.description:
The order of query parameters, form-urlencoded pairs and multipart parts is not the spec declaration order everywhere. Kotlin (LinkedHashMap), csharp, php, ruby, node, dart and rust (query and form use a Vec) emit declaration order. The others differ:
- java builds queryParams and formBody as `new HashMap<>()`. setPetPreferences sends `note…&nickname…&renewalDate…&tags…`, getPetTag sends `filter&sizes&colors&revision`, findPetsByStatus sends `filter[color]&filter[size]&bornAfter&status`, and the uploadPetDocument parts go in the order `file, notes, documentType`. I computed these with Java's HashMap.
- go ranges over `map[string]any` for the query string and multipart parts, so the order is random on every call. The form body goes through `url.Values.Encode()`, which sorts keys: `nickname&note&renewalDate&tags`.
- swift iterates `[String: Any]` Dictionaries for query, form and multipart. Swift seeds hashing randomly per process, so the order varies between runs.
- elixir builds query_params and request_body as maps. Maps of up to 32 keys iterate sorted, so `bornAfter&filter[...]&status` and multipart `documentType, file, notes`.
- rust multipart is `HashMap<String, MultipartValue>` with RandomState.
- python moves every allowReserved query param after all normal ones (normalized and reserved groups).
Wire bytes therefore differ between SDKs, and for go, swift and rust multipart they differ between runs. That breaks byte-level request recording, signature schemes that do not canonicalise, cache keys, and the governing rule of the same bytes on the wire. No test catches it: every multi-field assertion uses contains/split. The kotlin exact `nickname=a+b&tags=x&tags=y` and go `nickname=a+b&tags=x&tags=y` assertions only pass because those two keys happen to sort in declaration order. Fix: use ordered containers. Java: LinkedHashMap in api.mustache. Go: a slice of pairs, with no url.Values.Encode. Swift: KeyValuePairs or an array of tuples. Elixir: a keyword list or list of tuples. Rust: Vec for multipart. Python: keep one ordered pass. Petstore test: assert the exact full string for getPetTag with all four query params, setPetPreferences with all four fields, and the uploadPetDocument part order, in all 12.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Every language has an ordered container: LinkedHashMap, slices of pairs, KeyValuePairs, keyword lists, Vec.

findings.title: A 3xx with no (or unparseable) Location is reported as 'too many redirects' in java and ruby; the other 10 return the 3xx
findings.description: When a 301/302/303/307/308 has no Location, every loop breaks out. java then runs its unconditional post-loop check 'if (isRedirect(response.statusCode()))' and throws ApiException('Too many redirects (exceeded maxRedirects) following <url>'). ruby raises 'Exceeded maximum number of redirects (20)' after a missing Location or a URI.join failure. Both errors are false. kotlin/csharp/php/python/node/dart/go/rust/swift/elixir gate the check on hops >= max (python even comments 'the no-Location case breaks out and is a legitimate terminal 3xx'), so the 3xx reaches BaseApi's status-to-error mapping with its body. The two outliers raise a different message and drop the body/headers.

evidence.quote: raise unusable_response(response, "Exceeded maximum number of redirects (#{max_redirects})") if redirect_status?(response.status)

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Gate on redirectsRemaining == 0 / hops >= max like the others.

ruby.note: Ruby part only. The redirect-exhaustion raise is now gated on hops >= max_redirects, so a 3xx with no or empty Location is returned as the terminal response with its body.
ruby.test: test/default_api_client_unit_test.mustache: 'returns a 3xx without a Location header as the terminal response' and '... with an empty Location header ...'

java.note: Java part: the post-loop 'Too many redirects' check is now gated on redirectsRemaining <= 0. A 3xx with no Location is returned as-is with its body. The ruby part is outside this scope.

findings.title: A malformed Location header produces a different error type in nearly every SDK
findings.description: A response arrived, so by the error contract this should be an ApiError with the 3xx status, or the 3xx returned. Instead: java/kotlin call URI.resolve, which throws IllegalArgumentException (verified: 'Illegal character in path'). It escapes uncaught as the caller-mistake type. node 'new URL(location, currentUrl)' throws TypeError, which transportError maps to NetworkError with status 0. go gets net/http 'failed to parse Location header' with resp==nil, giving NetworkError status 0. dart's Uri.resolve FormatException hits the generic catch, giving ApiException(statusCode: 0). ruby ends with ApiError 'Exceeded maximum number of redirects'. python's lenient urlsplit forwards the raw value. csharp/php/rust/elixir break and return the 3xx. A chasm route that returns 'Location: http://[bad' can drive one it.each row per client spec.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: go's net/http owns Location parsing, but it can be matched by returning the 3xx (CheckRedirect cannot see a parse failure); the others are unforced.

findings.title: Environment proxy variables (HTTP(S)_PROXY/NO_PROXY) are honoured by some SDKs and ignored by others
findings.description: When TransportOptions.proxy is null, ruby (Faraday reads proxy env unless ignore_env_proxy), php (Symfony HttpClient defaults to http_proxy/https_proxy/no_proxy), csharp (HttpClientHandler UseProxy=true with HttpClient.DefaultProxy reading env on Linux), rust (reqwest system/env proxy on by default; there is no .no_proxy()) and swift (system/libcurl proxy) route through an environment proxy. java (HttpClient), kotlin (Ktor CIO), python (urllib3 PoolManager), node (undici fetch), go (a bare &http.Transport{} without ProxyFromEnvironment) and dart (dart:io default findProxy) connect directly. So the same TransportOptions egresses differently by language on a host with HTTPS_PROXY set. The doc says 'null for direct connections', which the env-honouring five contradict.

evidence.quote: @return the proxy URL, or {@code null} for direct connections

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Pick one policy: disable env proxies (rust .no_proxy(), ruby ignore_env_proxy, php 'proxy'=>'' / no_proxy, csharp UseProxy=false) or enable them everywhere.

findings.title: Proxy credentials are stripped on cross-origin redirect hops in java/kotlin/python (and swift/dart), so authenticated-proxy requests 407 after a redirect
findings.description: Proxy-Authorization authenticates to the configured proxy, which is the same proxy for every hop. java/kotlin/swift/dart inject it as a normal request header (proxyAuthHeader) and also list 'proxy-authorization' in the cross-origin strip set, so the redirected request through the proxy carries no proxy credentials. python deliberately deletes it from the ProxyManager's proxy_headers for the rest of the chain ('Guard 3'). dart-io can recover through addProxyCredentials challenge handling; the others get 407. csharp (WebProxy.Credentials), ruby (Faraday proxy user), php (Symfony proxy option), go (Transport.Proxy userinfo), rust (reqwest Proxy), node (ProxyAgent) and elixir (Mint proxy_headers) keep authenticating every hop. Testing needs the squid fixture with auth plus a cross-origin redirect.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Re-add the transport's own proxy header after the strip (the strip should only remove caller-supplied credentials).

findings.title: Relative Location resolution is not RFC 3986 in java/kotlin/python/php (query-only refs); python/php also skip dot-segment removal
findings.description: For base https://h/v1/pets/1?x=1 and Location '?page=2', RFC 3986 gives https://h/v1/pets/1?page=2. node new URL, ruby URI.join, csharp new Uri(base,rel), go ResolveReference, rust Url::join, dart Uri.resolve, swift URLSession and elixir URI.merge all produce that. java/kotlin java.net.URI.resolve uses RFC 2396 rules and produces https://h/v1/pets/?page=2 (verified on JDK 22), so the follow-up hits a different resource. python's hand-rolled _resolve_url (verified) and php's resolveUrl produce the same wrong URL. python and php also append '../owners/9' and './a' verbatim (https://h/v1/pets/../owners/9) instead of removing dot segments, so the request-target bytes differ from the other 10.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. python urllib.parse.urljoin, php Uri\Rfc3986\Uri (ext-uri is already required), and java/kotlin can special-case query-only refs or resolve with an RFC 3986 resolver.

kotlin.note: Kotlin side only. New internal resolveRedirectLocation handles a query-only Location per RFC 3986 (keeps the base path and replaces the query); java.net.URI.resolve (RFC 2396) dropped the last path segment. Other reference forms still go through URI.resolve.
kotlin.test: DefaultApiClientTest.kt RedirectHandling 'resolves a query-only Location against the base path (RFC 3986)' (MockEngine, expects https://h.example.com/v1/pets/1?page=2)

python.note: python only. _resolve_url keeps absolute-with-scheme verbatim and otherwise uses urllib.parse.urljoin (query-only refs and dot segments now RFC 3986).

java.note: Added resolveLocation: a query-only Location ('?page=2') keeps the base path and swaps the query (RFC 3986). Everything else still uses URI.resolve. Java side only.

php.note: php side only. AbstractApiClient::resolveUrl now resolves a relative Location with \Uri\Rfc3986\Uri::resolve (RFC 3986 section 5.2). A query-only reference keeps the base path and dot segments are removed. ext-uri is already a hard requirement.
php.test: tests/Psr18ApiClientUnitTest.mustache: 'psr18 resolves a relative Location per RFC 3986'; tests/DefaultApiClientUnitTest.mustache: 'resolves a relative Location per RFC 3986' (rows: query only, ../, ./, sibling, absolute path)

findings.title: The HTTPS->HTTP body-replay guard fires on different requests: go refuses bodyless GETs; ruby/swift/elixir refuse bodyless POST/PUT/PATCH
findings.description: Canonical behaviour (java/kotlin/csharp/php/python/node/dart/rust) refuses a 307/308 https->http hop only when a real request body would be replayed. go's CheckRedirect has no body check, so a body-less GET that gets a 307 from https to http is refused with ApiError while the other SDKs follow it. ruby, swift and elixir substitute an empty body for POST/PUT/PATCH with a null body (the Content-Length: 0 workaround): ruby serialized_body='' with guard '!next_body.nil?', swift httpBody=Data() with hasBody httpBody != nil, elixir '' with 'body != nil'. So a body-less POST 307'd from https to http is refused there but followed elsewhere. ruby's guard is also not limited to 307/308. The chasm fixture can express both cases (a 307 https->http for GET, and for an empty POST).

evidence.quote: if downgrade?(url, next_url) and body != nil and

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Gate on a non-empty body (go: req.GetBody != nil && ContentLength > 0; ruby/swift/elixir: treat an empty body as no body) and on status 307/308 (ruby).
findings.note: done in go; still open for elixir, ruby, swift

go.note: Go side only. CheckRedirect's 307/308 https-to-http guard now also requires a real body (req.Body non-nil and not http.NoBody), so a bodyless GET and a nil-body POST follow the redirect while a body-carrying POST is still refused. ruby, swift and elixir are not touched.
go.test: go/test/default_api_client_test.mustache TestDefaultApiClient_RedirectDowngradeIgnoresRequestsWithoutBody (GET and POST, 307 and 308); the existing TestDefaultApiClient_RedirectBodyReplayHttpsToHttpByStatus still locks the refusal with a body

ruby.note: ruby only: the https->http guard now fires only for 307/308 with a non-empty body, so the empty body substituted for a bodyless POST is followed like in the canonical SDKs.
ruby.test: test/default_api_client_unit_test.rb 'follows a 307 HTTPS -> HTTP redirect of a POST that has no body' (existing 'raises ApiError when 307 redirects HTTPS -> HTTP and there is a body' still locks the refusal)

elixir.note: Elixir side only. The replay guard tested 'body != nil', but bodyless POST/PUT/PATCH carry the substituted empty string. The decision is now the public refuse_body_replay?/4: 307/308, a body that is neither nil nor "", and an https->http hop. The other three SDKs are not touched.
elixir.test: default_api_client_unit_test.mustache: '3.3: body replay is refused only for a real body on a 307/308 downgrade'

swift.note: swift side only. The new refusesBodyReplay() treats the explicit empty Data() on body-less POST/PUT/PATCH (or a body stream with an empty original body) as no body, so only a real body is refused on an https to http redirect. A real URLSession redirect is Apple-only, so the decision is tested as a pure function.

findings.title: Timeout scope differs: go/node/swift apply one deadline to the whole redirect chain; the others reset it per hop
findings.description: go's http.Client.Timeout covers all redirects plus the body. node creates one AbortSignal.timeout and spreads the same signal into every redirect fetch and the arrayBuffer() read. swift's timeoutIntervalForResource is per task, including redirects. java (HttpRequest.timeout per redirectBuilder), kotlin (HttpTimeout per request), csharp (HttpClient.Timeout per SendAsync), php (max_duration per request), python (Timeout per pool request), ruby, dart, rust (reqwest timeout per request in the manual loop) and elixir (a fresh Task.yield(total) per recursion) restart the budget on each hop. With timeout=1000 and three 400 ms hops, go/node/swift raise NetworkTimeoutError and the other 9 succeed (up to N*timeout).
findings.suspected_forced_reason: go's Client.Timeout and URLSession's resource timeout are whole-chain by design, so the manual-loop SDKs should carry the remaining budget across hops (the documented 'end-to-end' meaning).

findings.title: go follows maxRedirects-1 redirects (off-by-one); the other 11 follow exactly maxRedirects
findings.description: CheckRedirect refuses when len(via) >= maxRedirects. net/http calls it with via = the requests already sent, so len(via)==k when deciding the k-th redirect. With MaxRedirects(5), the 5th redirect is refused and only 4 are followed. MaxRedirects(1) follows none, and the default 20 follows 19. java (redirectsRemaining loop), kotlin, csharp/php/node/dart/rust/ruby/python (hops < max), swift (count > limit) and elixir (hops+1 > max) all follow exactly N. A chain of exactly N hops therefore succeeds everywhere except go, which raises 'stopped after N redirects'. The go test only covers 1 hop and 20 hops with max=5, never the boundary. Add an it.each boundary row (hops == maxRedirects succeeds, hops == maxRedirects+1 fails) to every client spec.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Use len(via) > maxRedirects.

go.note: CheckRedirect compared len(via) >= maxRedirects, which followed only N-1 redirects. Now len(via) > maxRedirects, so exactly N hops are followed and N+1 is refused.
go.test: go/test/default_api_client_test.mustache TestDefaultApiClient_RedirectLimitFollowsExactlyMaxRedirects (max 1 and 5, hops equal to max succeed, max+1 fails)

findings.title: java (4x) and python (16x) cap zstd output when the frame has no content size; java then mislabels every zstd failure as 'library is unavailable'
findings.description: java sizes the output buffer as data.length*4 when Zstd.decompressedSize is unknown (streaming encoders often omit the frame content size). A valid body compressing better than 4:1, which is typical for JSON, makes Zstd.decompress throw. python passes max_output_size=len(data)*16 and fails above 16:1. kotlin (ZstdInputStream), go/rust (streaming decoders), node zlib and elixir :zstd decode without a cap. In java the failure comes out of a reflective invoke as InvocationTargetException, which the ReflectiveOperationException catch rewraps as 'Received a zstd-encoded response but the zstd library is unavailable'. That message is wrong for a corrupt or oversized stream.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. java: use ZstdInputStream (as kotlin does) and unwrap InvocationTargetException. python: use ZstdDecompressor().stream_reader / decompressobj().

java.note: Java part: zstd is now decoded through ZstdInputStream via the shared decodeViaInputStream, with no data.length*4 cap. InvocationTargetException is unwrapped, so a corrupt stream is no longer reported as 'library is unavailable'. The python part is outside this scope.

python.note: Python part only. zstd now stream-decodes with decompressobj() instead of max_output_size=len(data)*16, and raises 'Truncated zstd frame' when eof is false. pyproject zstandard floor raised to 0.23.0 (3.13 wheels and the eof attribute). The java part belongs to another agent.

findings.title: java/kotlin return a still-encoded br/zstd body when the optional codec library is absent, contradicting the 'unsupported Content-Encoding raises' contract
findings.description: decompressBrotli/decompressZstd (java) and decodeViaInputStream (kotlin) catch ClassNotFoundException and 'return data'. A server that ignores Accept-Encoding and sends br/zstd gets compressed bytes back to the caller as if decoded, which then fail confusingly in deserialization. AGENTS 'Resolved' and R6-2 require raising in that case: php/ruby raise 'Received a br-encoded response but the br ... is unavailable', and python falls through to 'Unsupported Content-Encoding'. elixir and dart-io raise too. java/kotlin are the only manual decompressors that still pass through.

evidence.quote: 'Received a br-encoded response but the br extension is unavailable'

findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Throw IOException('Received a br-encoded response but the br library is unavailable') like php/ruby/elixir.

kotlin.note: Kotlin part only. decodeViaInputStream is now internal, takes the encoding name, and throws IOException 'Received a br-encoded response but the br library is unavailable' (same for zstd) instead of returning the raw bytes. The doc comment was updated.
kotlin.test: DefaultApiClientUnitTest.kt: 'br and zstd without their codec library raise instead of returning the encoded body'

java.note: decompressBrotli/decompressZstd no longer `return data` on ClassNotFoundException; they throw IOException('Received a <enc>-encoded response but the <enc> library is unavailable'). The kotlin part is outside this scope.

findings.title: swift returns an EMPTY body when the bytes are not valid in the declared charset and not valid UTF-8
findings.description: responseBody = String(data:encoding:) ?? String(data:, encoding: .utf8) ?? "". Foundation returns nil for any invalid UTF-8, so a text/JSON body containing one stray byte (e.g. Latin-1 'é' with no charset) becomes "". I verified that {"a":"\xE9"} decodes to an empty string. The error body, message and payload are silently lost. The other 11 decode leniently: java new String (replacement chars), python errors='replace', node TextDecoder fatal:false, rust from_utf8_lossy, dart allowMalformed, go string(bytes), ruby invalid: :replace, php/elixir raw bytes, kotlin/csharp replacement.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Fall back to String(decoding: data, as: UTF8.self), which substitutes U+FFFD.

swift.note: responseBody now falls back to String(decoding:as:UTF8.self) so invalid bytes become U+FFFD instead of an empty body.

findings.title: An ApiError for a response that arrived but could not be decoded has null headers in 6 SDKs and the real headers in 6, contradicting the documented null-headers signal
findings.description: AGENTS.md ('responseHeaders null vs empty is a signal') says null headers mean that no HTTP response arrived, and that null is reachable only through the transport-failure constructor. The decompression-failure error contradicts this. A response did arrive, and the error carries its real status, but java, kotlin, csharp, node, swift and elixir build it with null headers. java and kotlin use the ApiException(int, String, Throwable) constructor, which hard-codes responseHeaders = null. php, python, ruby, dart, go and rust attach the response's real headers to the same failure. A caller reading headers == null as 'no response arrived' gets the wrong answer in 6 SDKs. The two groups also disagree on whether, for example, x-request-id is available on this error. The same split appears on the redirect-limit error: java and kotlin pass null, python passes the real headers, and php passes the empty array [], because ApiException::__construct defaults $responseHeaders = []. The php default, plus node's ClientError and leaf constructors defaulting responseHeaders to {}, also means a php ApiException built without headers signals 'a response arrived with no headers'. Pick one rule, most likely the real headers whenever a status is known, and apply it in all 12. The java/kotlin/csharp (status, message, cause) constructor needs a headers parameter.

evidence.quote: Null is reachable only via the transport-failure constructor, which is exactly the point.

findings.title: The typed-error-body accessor's failure contract differs: go returns a non-SDK error, node throws on an empty body, dart swallows every failure
findings.description: In java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, ruby, swift and elixir, getTypedErrorBody returns null/None/nil for an absent or empty body and raises the SDK SerializationError for a malformed body, because all of them route through ObjectSerializer.deserialize. Three SDKs deviate. (1) go: GetTypedErrorBody calls the package-local unmarshalErrorBody, which returns a raw *json.SyntaxError or *json.UnmarshalTypeError, or a plain fmt.Errorf when the depth cap trips. It never returns *SerializationError, so errors.As(err, new(*SerializationError)) fails, which breaks the 'SerializationError for every encode/decode failure' contract. It also skips the BOM strip that go's own deserialize does. (2) node: getTypedErrorBody treats only null as absent. An empty-string body goes to ObjectSerializer.parseJson(""), and JSON.parse('') throws SerializationError, where every other SDK returns null for "". (3) dart: the accessor catches every exception and returns null, including malformed JSON, a type mismatch and a JSON array body (the `as Map<String, dynamic>` cast), so a decode failure is indistinguishable from 'no body'. The go test only checks that an error is non-nil, never its type, and no node test covers an empty-string body.

findings.title: ruby ApiError#message prints an empty headers hash and an empty body, which the other 11 omit
findings.description: ruby's rendering guards with `if response_headers` and `if response_body`. In Ruby both `{}` and `""` are truthy, so an error with an empty body, which is common on 404/500, renders a trailing 'Response body: ' line. Empty headers render 'Response headers: {}'. I confirmed this with a ruby script: the result was "API returned status code 404\nResponse headers: {}\nResponse body: ". Every other SDK omits a section when it is null or empty: java/kotlin/csharp/dart isEmpty, php !== [] and !== '', python truthiness, node length > 0 and !== "", go len() > 0 and != "", rust is_empty(), swift isEmpty, elixir `in [nil, %{}]` and `in [nil, ""]`. Fix: use `unless response_headers.nil? || response_headers.empty?` and the same for the body. ruby's only rendering test asserts `wont_be_empty`, so nothing catches this.

ruby.note: ApiError#message now omits the headers and body sections when nil or empty, and the old code printed 'Response headers: {}' and an empty body line.
ruby.test: test/api_error_test.mustache: 'omits the headers and body sections when they are empty' and 'omits the headers and body sections when they are nil'

findings.title: rust error-body parsing and typed_error_body bypass ObjectSerializer: serde's ~128 depth limit instead of the shared 1000 cap, and no BOM strip
findings.description: R5-3 aligned rust's success path to the 1000-deep cap: object_serializer::deserialize does a byte-scan, calls disable_recursion_limit and strips the BOM. The error path in errors/api_error.rs still calls serde_json::from_str directly in both parse_error_body and deserialize_error_body. As a result an error body nested 129..=1000 deep fails in rust: error_body is None and typed_error_body() returns Err, while the other 11 parse it, and python, ruby, node, dart and go tests assert that the error-body cap is 1000. A BOM-prefixed error body that rust's own deserialize would accept is also rejected. The error message wording differs too ('failed to deserialize error response body'). Fix: route both helpers through crate::object_serializer::deserialize::<T>(bytes). This is what java, kotlin, python, ruby, node, dart, swift and elixir do for the error path.

rust.note: parse_error_body and deserialize_error_body in errors/api_error.mustache now call crate::object_serializer::deserialize. Error bodies get the 1000-deep cap and BOM stripping, and a failure reads 'failed to deserialize JSON: ...' like the success path.

findings.title: rust is the only SDK with no public parsed error body (error_body is pub(crate))
findings.description: Eleven SDKs expose the parsed JSON error body that fromResponse computes: java getErrorBody, kotlin errorBody, csharp ErrorBody, php getErrorBody, python error_body, ruby error_body, node errorBody, dart errorBody, go ErrorBody(), swift errorBody, and the elixir :error_body field. rust computes it, but it is pub(crate) on both ApiError and ApiErrorFields, and neither has a public accessor. The stated reason is to keep serde_json out of the public API, but the crate already ships the public JsonValue wrapper for exactly that purpose (json_value.rs, whose doc comment cites this field). Rust callers can only get a typed view by deserializing again through typed_error_body, which also has the depth-cap issue above. Nothing in rust forces this. Fix: add `pub fn error_body(&self) -> Option<JsonValue>` on ApiError and ApiErrorFields.

evidence.quote: `error_body` is kept crate-private precisely so a `serde_json::Value` AST

rust.note: Added pub fn error_body(&self) -> Option<JsonValue> on ApiError and ApiErrorFields. The field stays pub(crate), so serde_json is not exposed.

findings.title: swift ApiError.fromResponse drops a scalar JSON error body (JSONSerialization without .fragmentsAllowed)
findings.description: swift's fromResponse calls JSONSerialization.jsonObject(with: data) with no options, which rejects a top-level fragment. An error body of `"Not found"`, `123` or `true` therefore leaves errorBody nil in swift. The other 11 parsers accept top-level scalars: java Jackson Object.class, kotlin parseToJsonElement, csharp JsonDocument.Parse, php json_decode, python json.loads, ruby JSON.parse, node JSON.parse, dart jsonDecode, go json.Unmarshal into any, rust serde_json::Value and elixir Jason. All of them populate errorBody with the scalar. I confirmed this with a swift script on this host: each of the four fragment inputs threw, and only `{"a":1}` parsed. Fix: pass `.fragmentsAllowed`, or route through ObjectSerializer the way the other SDKs do. Unit-testable through ApiError.fromResponse(statusCode: 404, headers: [:], body: "\"Not found\""). No test in any of the 12 SDKs covers a scalar error body.

swift.note: ApiError.fromResponse parses with .fragmentsAllowed, so a scalar body populates errorBody. A bare null stays nil rather than NSNull.

findings.title: ApiKey/Basic/Bearer unit-test coverage differs by language, and no SDK tests non-ASCII (UTF-8) Basic credentials
findings.description: Missing cases by language. dart Bearer: no prefix-dedup test at all (already-prefixed, lowercase, mixed-case). dart ApiKey: no empty or whitespace rejection test, no CR/LF/NUL test for query or cookie, no cookie-location test; its test 'non-header locations accept arbitrary chars' is misleading, because CR/LF/NUL are rejected at every location. node ApiKey: no cookie-location test and no CR/LF/NUL query or cookie test. node Bearer: no mixed-case dedup test. java Bearer: no CR/LF or non-ASCII rejection test. java ApiKey: no cookie happy path, no header non-ASCII rejection, no query-accepts-non-ASCII test. Most suites assert `throws` or a substring instead of the exact message for every branch, which is how the java order divergence and the go/rust wording drift went unnoticed. No language has a Basic test with non-ASCII credentials: all fixtures use 'alice:s3cret' or 'user:pass'. Nine SDKs transcode to UTF-8 by construction. php, elixir and ruby base64 the raw string bytes, and ruby strings carry their own encoding: an ISO-8859-1 `"café"` yields Latin-1 bytes (`Y2Fm6Q==` instead of `Y2Fmw6k=`), and mixing UTF-8 and Latin-1 parts raises Encoding::CompatibilityError. Fix: add a shared table to every language's Basic test, e.g. `('ünïcødé','pässwörd') -> Basic w7xuw69jw7hkw6k6cMOkc3N3w7ZyZA==`. Consider `.encode(Encoding::UTF_8)` in ruby.

findings.title: Generated per-scheme authenticator wrappers are almost untested: only java and kotlin construct any, and no SDK tests an API-key wrapper
findings.description: The 8 non-OAuth wrappers carry spec-derived behaviour: fixed key names X-API-Key, X-Internal-Key, api_key and SESSION_ID, fixed locations header/query/cookie, and constructor signatures. Only java/kotlin PetApiTest construct a wrapper, and only PetStoreBearer and AdminBasic. No test in any of the 12 constructs ApiKeyHeader, InternalApiKey, ApiKeyQuery or SessionCookie, or checks that a wrapper emits its key at the right location, still validates eagerly, or redacts. This is how three wrapper problems went uncaught: the rust wrapper modules were dead source until T2-8 and then shipped a missing import (AGENTS documents both); ruby wrappers take keyword args while their bases take positional args; and the java wrapper toString falls back to Object.toString. Fix: add one wrapper case per base class to each language's existing ApiKey/Basic/Bearer authenticator unit test file, using the petstore schemes that already exist: `SessionCookieAuthenticator(host,k).cookieParams() == {SESSION_ID:k}`, `ApiKeyQueryAuthenticator` puts api_key in query params, the wrapper rejects an empty key, and the wrapper repr masks the key.

findings.title: go authenticators leak secrets through %#v because they implement Stringer but not GoStringer
findings.description: go redacts by giving `*ApiKeyAuthenticator`, `*BasicAuthenticator` and `*BearerAuthenticator` a `String()` method. `fmt` ignores `String()` for the `%#v` verb and prints every struct field by reflection, unexported ones included. So `fmt.Sprintf("%#v", auth)` gives `&auth.BearerAuthenticator{..., token:"super-secret"}`. The same happens for the per-scheme wrappers, which embed the base pointer, and for `%v` on a dereferenced value, because `String` has a pointer receiver. `%#v` is a common debugging and test-failure verb. The other SDKs' standard debug formatters (rust `{:?}`, python repr, ruby inspect, node util.inspect, java/kotlin/csharp/dart toString) are all redacted. The go test checks only `String()`, `%v` and `%+v`. Fix: add a `GoString()` method that returns the redacted form. OAuth authenticators (client_secret, refresh token) have the same gap. Unit test: add `%#v` to the format list in go/test/*_authenticator_test.go RedactsSecret.

Not fixed: %v on a dereferenced value still leaks because String has a pointer receiver.

findings.title: java checks API-key and Bearer input in a different order, so a newline-only or control-only value gets a different error message than in the other 11
findings.description:
The other 11 SDKs check 'empty/whitespace-only' first, then CR/LF/NUL (ApiKey) or printable ASCII (Bearer). java folds both into one character loop that throws on the first bad character, and only decides 'all whitespace' after the loop. Concrete cases: ApiKey (any location) "
" or "
" gives java `API key value for 'X' contains forbidden control characters (CR/LF/NUL)`, while kotlin/csharp/php/python/ruby/node/go/dart/rust/swift/elixir give `API key value for 'X' must not be empty`. Bearer "
", "\x0b" or "
" gives java `Bearer token must contain only printable ASCII characters (RFC 7230 §3.2.6)`, while the other 11 give `Bearer token must not be empty`. A blank line read from an env file is a realistic input. The kotlin template on the same JVM checks `isBlank()` first, so the order is not forced. Fix: run the whitespace-only check before the character loop, as in kotlin. Unit tests: ApiKeyAuthenticatorTest and BearerAuthenticatorTest in all 12 should assert the exact message for "
" and "
".

java.note: ApiKeyAuthenticator and BearerAuthenticator now run isBlank() before the character scan, so '\n', '\r\n' and VT report 'must not be empty'. NUL alone still reports the control-character message.

findings.title: php authenticator constructors do not mark secret parameters #[\SensitiveParameter], so secrets appear in exception stack traces (the docblock claims they do not)
findings.description: `__debugInfo` masks secrets for var_dump and print_r, and the docblock says the class is safe for 'stack traces / error logs'. That is not true for traces. PHP records call arguments in exception backtraces whenever `zend.exception_ignore_args` is Off. Off is the built-in default and the php.ini-development setting, and official Docker images ship without a php.ini. So when validation in `BearerAuthenticator::__construct($host, $token)` throws, the token (truncated to 15 bytes) appears in `getTraceAsString()`. The per-scheme wrappers forward the secret through `parent::__construct`, so it can appear twice. composer requires php ^8.5, where `#[\SensitiveParameter]` is available, but no file in the SDK uses it. `var_export()` also bypasses `__debugInfo`. No other SDK puts call arguments into its error traces. Fix: mark `$token`, `$apiKey`, `$password` (and the OAuth `$clientSecret` and `$password` parameters), including the wrapper constructors, with `#[\SensitiveParameter]`. Unit test: in php/tests/BearerAuthenticatorTest.php, set `ini_set('zend.exception_ignore_args','0')`, construct with an invalid secret, and assert that `getTraceAsString()` does not contain it.

php.note: #[\SensitiveParameter] is on Bearer $token, Basic $password, ApiKey $apiKey, the four OAuth authenticators' $clientSecret, and OAuth2 password's $password. The generated scheme wrappers with their own constructor are flagged through a new SENSITIVE_PARAMS set in BetterPHPCodegen. A trace-based test (BearerAuthenticatorTest) checks that the secret is absent from getTraceAsString() with zend.exception_ignore_args=0.
php.test: tests/BearerAuthenticatorTest.php: 'rejected token is not recorded in the exception stack trace' and 'secret constructor parameters are marked sensitive'. The same reflection test is in BasicAuthenticatorTest, ApiKeyAuthenticatorTest, OAuth2ClientCredentialsAuthenticatorTest, OAuth2PasswordAuthenticatorTest, OAuth2AuthCodeAuthenticatorTest and OpenIdConnectAuthenticatorTest.

findings.title: swift authenticators leak secrets through dump()/Mirror because they redact description but have no customMirror
findings.description: Swift redacts only `description` and `debugDescription`. Swift's standard `dump(_:)` and `Mirror(reflecting:)` walk the stored properties, private ones included. I checked this with a local swift script that copies the generated pattern: `dump(BearerAuthenticator(...))` prints `- token: "super-secret"` under the redacted header line. php handles its equivalent debug dump (`var_dump`) explicitly with `__debugInfo`, but swift does not handle `dump`. Fix: conform ApiKey/Basic/Bearer (and the OAuth authenticators) to `CustomReflectable` with a mirror whose secret children are `"***"`. Unit test: in BearerAuthenticatorTests.redactsSecret, capture `dump(auth, to: &out)` and assert the token is absent.

swift.note: BaseAuthenticator now conforms to CustomReflectable with an empty mirror. One change covers ApiKey, Basic, Bearer, all four OAuth2 authenticators and OpenIdConnect, so dump() and Mirror show no secrets.
swift.test: dumpDoesNotLeakSecret in each of the 8 authenticator test files, next to redactsSecret

findings.title: Implicit flow: empty access token accepted (sends 'Authorization: Bearer ') in 7 SDKs, rejected as unset in 5
findings.description: setAccessToken("") passes the printable-ASCII check everywhere. getAuthHeaders then: java/kotlin/csharp/php/python/ruby/elixir test only for null/nil and emit 'Authorization: Bearer ' (empty credential on the wire); node (`!this.accessToken`), go (== ""), rust/swift/dart (isEmpty) throw 'Must set the access token before making API requests'. BearerAuthenticator (which the implicit validation claims to mirror) rejects empty tokens ('Bearer token must not be empty'), so the 5 are right and the 7 should reject "" at set or use time.

findings.title: OIDC authenticator never requests the `openid` scope
findings.description: Uniform gap. Every SsoAuthAuthenticator wrapper passes empty scopes (listOf()/[]/nil/vec![]), and OpenIdConnectAuthenticator adds nothing, so the authorize URL has no scope parameter. OIDC Core §3.1.2.1 requires scope to contain 'openid'; without it the request is plain OAuth2 (no id_token) and OPs such as Google reject a missing scope. The generator ignores the scopes listed on `security: - ssoAuth: [...]` requirements and does not default to 'openid'.

findings.title: RFC 6749 §5.2 error parsing: go loses `error` when error_description/error_uri is non-string; kotlin stringifies numeric `error` and loses it on object/array description
findings.description: For {"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":123} (or an object/array/bool uri/description) java/csharp/php/python/ruby/node/dart/rust/swift/elixir return code=invalid_grant, description=null. go unmarshals into a typed struct; json.Unmarshal reports UnmarshalTypeError, err != nil, so it falls back to code="" (message becomes the raw body). kotlin uses `?.jsonPrimitive?.contentOrNull`: an object/array description throws IllegalArgumentException, caught by `catch (_: Exception)` → code=null; and a numeric/boolean `error` (e.g. 400) becomes code "400" where every other SDK requires a string. (go also renders an empty-string description differently since absent and "" collapse.) R7-13 documents go/swift typed decoding only for the 2xx token body, not this error path.

A numeric or empty error, or a non-object body, still falls back to the raw body.

findings.title: Token-response and OIDC-discovery error messages are not harmonized (rust lowercase, kotlin/php/swift/elixir/go variants; python/ruby accept non-string endpoints)
findings.description: R8-7 harmonized many messages but not these. Canonical (java/csharp/python/ruby/node/dart): invalid JSON → 'Token response is not valid JSON: <detail>', non-object → 'Token response is not a JSON object', missing → 'Token response missing or empty access_token field'. Divergent: rust 'failed to parse token response: …' and lowercase 'token response missing or empty access_token field', and no non-object check (a JSON array yields the missing-token message); kotlin 'Token response is not a JSON object: <detail>' for invalid JSON; php no 'not valid JSON' message, and a JSON list passes is_array so `[]` reports missing access_token; swift and elixir 'Token response is not a valid token JSON object' for both cases; go reports a JSON array as 'Token response is not valid JSON: json: cannot unmarshal array…' and `null` as missing access_token. OIDC discovery: java alone has 'OIDC discovery document field is not a string: <f>'; kotlin 'not a JSON object: <detail>' for invalid JSON; php/elixir/swift report invalid JSON as 'not a JSON object' (swift also for a non-string endpoint, go as 'not valid JSON'); python (`if not authorization_endpoint`) and ruby (`.to_s.strip.empty?`) accept a non-string truthy endpoint (e.g. 123) and build a delegate with it; whitespace-only endpoints are rejected by rust/go/swift/ruby/elixir but accepted by the rest.

evidence.quote: "token response missing or empty access_token field"
"Token response is not a JSON object: ${e.message}"
if (!is_array($responseBody)) { throw new OAuth2TokenException('Token response is not a JSON object');

findings.title: Unclamped expires_in / discovery max-age arithmetic: swift traps, rust panics, java/csharp/ruby throw raw runtime exceptions, kotlin/go silently wrap
findings.description: A server-supplied huge/infinite lifetime is not clamped before date arithmetic. swift: Int(d.rounded(.down)) traps the process for expires_in > Int.max (e.g. 1e20, verified with a probe: 'Double value cannot be converted to Int'). rust: f64→u64 saturates, then Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs(u64::MAX-30) panics ('overflow when adding duration to instant'); same for OIDC max-age. java: textual branch of parseExpiresIn has no NaN/Infinity guard, so "Infinity"/"1e400"/1e20 become Long.MAX_VALUE and Instant.plusSeconds throws ArithmeticException: long overflow (probed); values > ~3.1e16 throw DateTimeException; OIDC max-age likewise. csharp: DateTimeOffset.AddSeconds throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for ~2.5e11..9.2e18. ruby: Float("1e400").floor raises FloatDomainError (not rescued; probed). kotlin: (expiresIn-30)*1000 overflows → expiry in the past → refetch on every call; go: time.Duration(n)*time.Second overflows for > ~9.2e9 s. dart: Duration/DateTime.add range (unverified). python/node/php/elixir cache normally. These escape as non-SDK exceptions (or a crash) instead of the OAuth2TokenError/'stale' contract every other edge case follows. Fix: clamp expires_in and max-age to a sane ceiling (e.g. 1 year) in all 12 and add a unit row for 1e20 and "Infinity".
findings.note: done in rust; still open for csharp, dart, go, java, kotlin, ruby, swift

rust.note: Rust side only. expires_in and Cache-Control max-age are clamped to 31,536,000 s (one year) before the Instant arithmetic, which used to panic for huge values.

findings.title: csharp normalizes redirect_uri through System.Uri.ToString() (trailing slash, default port, host case, unescaping) — bytes differ from the configured value
findings.description: csharp types redirectUri as System.Uri and emits `_redirectUri.ToString()` in both the authorize URL and the code-exchange body. Uri.ToString() returns the canonical unescaped form: a host-only redirect 'http://localhost:8080' becomes 'http://localhost:8080/', ':443' is dropped, the host is lower-cased, and percent-escapes are unescaped before EscapeDataString re-escapes them. OPs compare redirect_uri by exact string (RFC 6749 §3.1.2.3), so csharp can fail with redirect_uri_mismatch where the other 11 send the string verbatim. R8-F2 only covers the OIDC endpoint being a Uri. Use OriginalString (or keep redirect_uri a string). PLAUSIBLE: .NET behaviour stated from documentation, not executed here.

csharp.note: Both redirect_uri sites (authorize URL and code-exchange body) now use Uri.OriginalString instead of ToString(), so no trailing slash, default-port drop or host lowercasing.
csharp.test: OAuth2AuthCodeAuthenticatorTest.mustache: AuthorizationUrlSendsRedirectUriVerbatim and CodeExchangeSendsRedirectUriVerbatim (host-only URI, and :443 with mixed-case host)

findings.title: elixir auth-code/OIDC: exchange_code returns a new struct the Client never sees, so API calls keep raising 'Must call exchange_code'
findings.description: In the other 11, exchangeCode on the authenticator instance the client holds completes the flow. In elixir, OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.exchange_code returns `%{self | token_exchanged: true}` — the flag lives in the struct, not in the shared token-manager Agent — and Client.new stores its own copy, so every API call through the Client raises 'Must call exchange_code before making API requests'. For OIDC, set_api_client returns `%{self | api_client: client}` only on the Client's copy, so calling exchange_code/build_authorization_url on the user's struct hits the `api_client: nil` clause and raises 'ApiClient has not been injected'. The elixir tests only exercise these by calling set_api_client manually and auth_headers directly, never through Client.new. Not forced: the SDK already shares mutable state via Agents (token manager, discovery_cache); the exchanged flag/api_client should live there too.

evidence.quote: def auth_headers(%__MODULE__{token_exchanged: false}) do raise "Must call exchange_code before making API requests"

elixir.note: The token_exchanged flag now lives in the shared OAuth2TokenManager agent (mark_exchanged/1 and exchanged?/1), so any copy of the auth-code authenticator is ready after exchange_code. OIDC set_api_client also stores the ApiClient in the shared discovery_cache agent, and resolve_delegate adopts it when a copy has api_client nil. Dialyzer needed a no_return spec on the new raise helper.
elixir.test: test/oauth2_auth_code_authenticator_test.mustache: 'exchange_code readies the authenticator without using its return value'; test/openid_connect_authenticator_test.mustache: "exchange_code on the caller's copy readies the client's copy"

findings.title: exchangeCode() is silently ignored when a token is cached or a refresh token exists (goes through the caching getAccessToken)
findings.description: Uniform defect. exchangeCode/exchange_code calls tokenManager.getAccessToken(tokenUrl, codeParams), which first returns any still-valid cached token, and otherwise tries the refresh_token grant (and returns its result on success) before ever POSTing grant_type=authorization_code. A second exchangeCode (user re-login / account switch / scope upgrade on a long-lived authenticator, or OIDC) therefore never sends the new code: the old identity's token keeps being used and tokenExchanged is set to true. The code exchange should bypass the cache and refresh path (direct fetch, replacing access/refresh tokens).

findings.title: java auth-code getAuthHeaders NPEs when the OP issued no refresh_token and the access token expired
findings.description: java puts tokenManager.getRefreshToken() (null when the OP returned no refresh_token) straight into the params map; once the access token expires, fetchToken form-encodes the null value and URLEncoder.encode(null) throws NullPointerException out of getAuthHeaders. kotlin/csharp/php/python/ruby/node/dart/go/rust/swift/elixir substitute "" and POST refresh_token= which surfaces as the typed OAuth2ServerError (400). Fix: `?: ""` parity (or better, all 12 raise a typed 'token expired and no refresh token' error instead of sending an empty refresh grant).

java.note: OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.getAuthHeaders now puts '' when getRefreshToken() is null. The OP's 400 surfaces as a typed OAuth2ServerException instead of a NullPointerException from URLEncoder.

findings.title: A zero or negative timeout means something different in each SDK; only rust validates it
findings.description: Every builder takes the timeout with no range check except rust, whose build() returns ConfigurationError::InvalidTimeout for a negative value. The other 11 pass the raw number to their HTTP library, giving library-specific results (from library semantics, not run here). java: Duration.ofMillis(<=0) passed to HttpClient.Builder.connectTimeout and HttpRequest timeout throws a raw IllegalArgumentException at client construction or request time. kotlin: Ktor HttpTimeout requires values > 0, raw IAE. csharp: HttpClient.Timeout throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for 0, but -1 equals Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan, so timeout(-1) silently means no timeout. python: urllib3.Timeout(total<=0) raises ValueError on every request rather than at configuration. node: AbortSignal.timeout(-1) throws RangeError per request (verified locally), and 0 aborts immediately, giving NetworkTimeoutError. go: http.Client sets a deadline only when Timeout > 0, so 0 and negative both mean no timeout. rust: 0 is a zero deadline (immediate timeout), negative is rejected at build. php: max_duration=0 is Symfony's 'unlimited'. dart: Future.timeout with a negative duration fires immediately. Same input, different accept/reject and wire outcome. Under the error contract a negative timeout is a caller mistake and should be rejected at configuration, as rust does. A shared rule (reject < 0, decide whether 0 means no deadline) is needed.

evidence.quote: public Builder timeout(@Nullable Integer timeout) { this.timeout = timeout; return this; }
timeout: non_neg_integer() | nil (typespec only, not enforced)

findings.title: Per-operation server codegen emits duplicate types when two servers of one operation share a variable or a description
findings.description: AbstractBetterCodegen.enrichOperationServers builds serverVariables per variant and never de-duplicates. Every api template emits the variable's enum inside the `{{#variants}}` loop. An operation with two servers that both declare an enum variable `region` is a normal pattern, for example `https://{region}.a.com` and `https://{region}.b.com`. It produces two declarations of the same enum type: compile errors in java (nested enum), kotlin, csharp (CS0101), go, dart, rust and swift; a TS duplicate identifier in node; silent last-wins redefinition in python and php (separate file overwritten), which is wrong if the enum sets differ; and a redefining-module warning in elixir and ruby, which elixir's --warnings-as-errors turns fatal. Variant names come from PascalCase(description) or `Server<index>`, so two servers with the same description, or one starting with a digit, also collide or produce invalid identifiers. The petstore only has getMultiServerPetInfo, where just one of the two servers has a variable, so this is untested.

findings.title: Test gaps: no test covers CA sole-anchor, garbage-CA rejection outside 3 SDKs, proxy failure classes, timeout <= 0, or a shared per-operation server variable
findings.description: These gaps let several findings above go unnoticed. (1) An unparseable CA file is tested only in java (garbagePemCaCertPathThrowsIllegalArgumentException), kotlin (ClientTest) and dart. The other 9 test only a missing file, so rust's lazy from_pem passes. Add a garbage-PEM row to every DefaultApiClient unit test. (2) Nothing checks that caCertPath is the sole trust anchor, so the dart/rust/ruby add-to-system-roots split goes unseen. Petstore/fixture expansion: point a client with caCertPath=fixtures/certs/ca.pem at a TLS endpoint signed by a different CA (a second chasm cert, or the publicly trusted proxy path) and expect NetworkError. (3) Proxy validation tests use one garbage string, except go (ftp, 'http://', socks5) and node (ftp). Missing-host, non-http scheme, upper-case scheme and empty-string cases are untested in 10 SDKs, and no SDK asserts the message. Add it.each/table rows to each TransportOptionsTest. (4) Negative/zero timeout is tested only in rust (test_transport_options_negative_timeout_is_rejected). (5) Server-variable message: no full-message assertion anywhere. (6) Petstore spec expansion: add an operation with two servers that share an enum variable (for example `https://{region}.a.example.com` and `https://{region}.b.example.com`), one with an undescribed server (a second `Server0` across operations, for csharp), and a URL template that repeats a variable. That catches the duplicate-type codegen defect, the csharp namespace collisions and node's first-occurrence replace. (7) swift: all HTTPS/CA/proxy integration tests sit under `#if !os(Linux)` and CI runs Linux, so the PEM-vs-DER, Linux-silent-TLS and HTTPSProxy-key bugs have zero coverage. A Linux-runnable unit test should at least assert that verifySsl(false) and caCertPath throw like proxyUnsupported.

findings.title: csharp declares per-operation server types un-prefixed at namespace level (cross-operation collisions) and emits a duplicate <summary>
findings.description: The other 11 scope per-operation server types: java/kotlin nest them in the sealed interface; python/go/node/ruby/php/dart/rust/swift prefix them with the operation (GetMultiServerPetInfoServerRegional, GetStagingPetInfoServerEnvironment); elixir nests modules. csharp emits `Server0`, `Primary`, `Regional`, `StagingServer`, `RegionValue`, `EnvironmentValue` and `VersionValue` as top-level types in PetstoreClient.Api. Two operations that each have an undescribed server both produce `public sealed class Server0`, which fails with CS0101. The same happens for two operations with an `environment` enum variable or servers with the same description, and a model of the same name causes CS0104 ambiguity through `using PetstoreClient.Models;`. Separately, for an undescribed server without variables the template prints the summary twice (lines 48-50 and again at 74-76), so the golden has two identical `<summary>` lines on Server0.

csharp.note: Per-op server variants and variable enums are now prefixed with serverTypeName (GetExternalPetInfoServerServer0, GetMultiServerPetInfoServerRegion), and the duplicate summary on described-less variants is removed. Caveat: two variants of the same operation that share a variable name still collide (same as php/go).

findings.title: dart's only tracing opt-in (TraceContextUtil.propagator) is not exported from the public library
findings.description: dart cannot detect OpenTelemetry at runtime, so tracing works only if the application sets `TraceContextUtil.propagator = ...`, as the class doc says. The package barrel lib/petstore_client.dart exports configuration, server_configuration, servers and transport_options but not src/trace_context_util.dart. Users must import `package:petstore_client/src/trace_context_util.dart`, an implementation import that the implementation_imports lint flags, and the SDK's own test does exactly that. go (SetTraceContextPropagator) and swift (public enum TraceContextUtil.propagator) expose their registration hook publicly. node and rust keep their helper internal, but they need no registration (runtime detection and a cargo feature).

evidence.quote: static void Function(Map<String, String> headers)? propagator;

dart.note: Added export 'src/trace_context_util.dart' to the barrel. The trace test now imports the public library, so it will not compile without the export.
