findings.title: java, kotlin and swift trust only the first certificate in a caCertPath bundle
findings.description: java and kotlin load the CA with CertificateFactory.generateCertificate(fis), which reads one certificate, and store a single 'ca' entry. swift calls SecCertificateCreateWithData once and anchors one certificate. The other 9 trust every certificate in the file: csharp ImportFromPemFile collection, go AppendCertsFromPEM, python load_verify_locations, ruby/php/elixir ca_file/cafile/cacertfile, node `ca` buffer, dart setTrustedCertificates, and rust (reqwest add_to_rustls iterates all PEM certs). A bundle with a root and an intermediate, or two roots during a CA rotation, works in 9 SDKs and fails TLS in java/kotlin/swift whenever the server chains to any cert but the first. The fix is generateCertificates() with every entry added to the trust store.

findings.title: swift (Apple): an http:// proxy only covers http destinations, so HTTPS API calls bypass it
findings.description: swift builds connectionProxyDictionary from the proxy URL's own scheme. For https://proxy it sets only HTTPSEnable/HTTPSProxy/HTTPSPort; for http://proxy it sets only HTTPEnable/HTTPProxy/HTTPPort. In CFNetwork, the HTTP* keys select the proxy for http:// requests and the HTTPS* keys select it for https:// requests. So with the usual http://proxy:3128, every https:// request goes direct, bypassing the proxy. With an https:// proxy URL, http:// requests go direct instead. Every other SDK sends all traffic through the configured proxy (java ProxySelector.of, go http.ProxyURL, node ProxyAgent, python ProxyManager, etc.). Only on Apple platforms; Linux throws proxyUnsupported, so CI never runs this path. Not runtime-verified here; based on CFNetwork key semantics.

swift.note: Same root cause as F012.

findings.title: swift on Linux silently ignores verifySsl=false and caCertPath, while a proxy on Linux throws
findings.description: The whole URLSession server-trust challenge handler is inside `#if canImport(Security)`. On Linux (FoundationNetworking) there is no handler, so verifySsl(false) does not disable verification and caCertPath is not applied. Only the file's readability is checked, and the system trust store is used. Both settings are dropped without any error. For the comparable platform limit, swift throws ConfigurationError.proxyUnsupported when a proxy is configured on Linux. So swift is internally inconsistent, and on Linux it accepts settings that do nothing; the other 11 honour both. The platform limit is forced, but staying silent is not: it should throw like proxyUnsupported. Linux is the platform CI uses, and all swift HTTPS tests are excluded there.

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, didReceive challenge: ...

findings.title: A required discriminator property that is absent (DryFood/WetFood.foodType) is accepted by 8 SDKs and rejected by 4; elixir's and go's comments contradict their code
findings.description: `foodType` is `required` in DryFood/WetFood. The generator gives it a synthetic default from the discriminator mapping (applyDiscriminatorDefault, AbstractBetterCodegen.java ~5640). Decoding a DryFood with no `foodType` key is then accepted and filled with 'dry' by java (field initializer, not a creator param), kotlin (`= "dry"`), csharp (not `required`), php (assertRequiredPresent skips defaulted ctor params), python (`default="dry"`), ruby (`Types::Required.default('dry')`), node (constructor fills it) and elixir (required_fields excludes it). It is rejected by go (dry_food.go:68-71), dart (dry_food.dart:25), rust (no serde default, dry_food.rs:16) and swift (`container.decode`, DryFood.swift:38). elixir's required_fields doc says the exclusion matches 'the Go / PHP / Kotlin reference behaviour', but go rejects. go's own comment at dry_food.go:78 ('An absent field carrying a schema default is populated with that default') is dead, because the function already returned an error. Decide one rule (most likely: accept, because the default satisfies the requirement) and add a 'DryFood without foodType' decode test in all 12.

matching the Go / PHP / Kotlin reference behaviour.

findings.title: Integer fields: java silently truncates 1.5 to 1 and accepts 42 for a string field; node accepts non-integers for int32/int64
findings.description: java's mapper disables ALLOW_COERCION_OF_SCALARS (ObjectSerializer.java:387) with the comment 'Matches the other SDKs, which reject wrong-typed primitives', but leaves DeserializationFeature.ACCEPT_FLOAT_AS_INT on (Jackson's default) and does not disable int-to-String coercion. Checked with jackson 2.19.4 and the golden's settings: `{"id":1.5}` gives id=1 (silent truncation) and `{"name":42}` gives name="42". node's model.mustache:555-563 only checks `typeof === 'number'` for isInteger/isLong, so `{"id":1.5}` is accepted and re-sent as 1.5. kotlin (StrictLong/StrictIntSerializer), csharp, python StrictInt/StrictStr, go, rust, swift, dart casts, ruby `is_a?(Integer)`, php assertPrimitiveTypes and elixir `is_integer` all reject both inputs. Fix: java should disable ACCEPT_FLOAT_AS_INT and set a CoercionConfig that fails Integer/Float to Textual; node should add `Number.isInteger` (or isSafeInteger) checks.

findings.title: `format: uri` is a validated type in 6 SDKs and a plain string in 6; python's validator accepts only absolute http(s) URLs
findings.description: Type mapping for URI: java java.net.URI, kotlin io.ktor.http.Url, csharp System.Uri, php \Uri\Rfc3986\Uri, python UrlStr, node branded URI (only a typeof check), and String in dart/go/rust/swift/ruby/elixir. AGENTS does not record this as forced, and swift (Foundation URL is Codable), dart (core Uri), ruby (URI) and elixir (URI) all have a stdlib URI type. The visible behavioural effect is in python: UrlStr validates through `TypeAdapter(HttpUrl)` (_types.py:25,62), which rejects valid RFC 3986 URIs. In pydantic 2.12, `urn:isbn:0451450523`, `mailto:a@b.com`, `ftp://x.org/f` and `/relative` are all rejected, so a Pet whose homepageUrl uses any non-http scheme fails to deserialize only in python. java URI.create rejects strings with spaces, while the string-typed SDKs accept anything. kotlin's `Url(String)` (KtorUrlSerializer, ObjectSerializer.kt:803) goes through URLBuilder.takeFrom, which normalizes relative or default-port inputs, so a re-encoded value may not be byte-identical. That last point is plausible but unverified here.

findings.title: `type: number` (weightKg): python and node are lossy on decode (python on encode too) and accept quoted strings, contradicting AGENTS' 'FIVE preserve full textual precision'
findings.description: AGENTS.md:246 lists python (`Decimal`) and node (branded `Decimal` + `JSON.rawJSON`) among the FIVE SDKs that preserve full precision. That is not true of the code. python decodes with a plain `json.loads` without `parse_float=Decimal` (object_serializer.py:220), so the value is a binary float before pydantic builds the Decimal. In pydantic 2.12, `{"weightKg": 0.1234567890123456789}` gives `Decimal('0.12345678901234568')` and 12345678901234567890.5 gives `Decimal('12345678901234567000')`. Encoding goes through `float(value)` (_types.py:87-90). node decodes with a bare `JSON.parse` (object-serializer.ts:274), so the number is already rounded before the Pet constructor applies `String(this.weightKg)` (pet.ts:161-162). Both also accept a JSON STRING for a `type: number` field. python's Decimal is lax, so `"12.345"` is accepted. node accepts ANY string (`"abc"`), because the only check is `typeof !== "string"` (pet.ts:163), and it then re-emits it quoted. java/kotlin/csharp reject a quoted number (jackson 2.19.4 with ALLOW_COERCION_OF_SCALARS=false gives MismatchedInputException; kotlin's BigDecimal(element.toString()) fails on the quotes). The python README even claims the field 'deserializes to decimal.Decimal' as the precision-safe path. Either fix decoding (python `parse_float=decimal.Decimal`; node a JSON.parse reviver using `context.source`) or move both to the lossy list in AGENTS.
findings.note: documents corrected; the code or template part is still open

findings.title: node's global Decimal-field registry turns string values in free-form objects into JSON numbers when their key matches any model's decimal field name
findings.description: ObjectSerializer.serialize's replacer (object-serializer.ts:360-372) checks the holder's constructor for `__decimalFields`. When the holder is a plain object (constructor Object), it falls back to `decimalFieldNames()`, a global union of every model's decimal field names (lines 184-200). This catches more than request-body literals: it also applies to any plain object nested inside a model, such as EdgeCases.freeFormAny, a free-form map, or additionalProperties values. Any string in there whose key is `weightKg` (Pet's decimal field) and whose text looks numeric is sent unquoted. I reproduced this in node 24: `{freeFormAny:{weightKg:"12",note:"x"}}` serializes to `{"freeFormAny":{"weightKg":12,"note":"x"}}`, which changes a JSON string into a number. The other 11 SDKs never change the JSON type of a free-form value. In a real spec with a common decimal name (`amount`, `price`), every free-form payload using that key is corrupted.

node.note: The serialize replacer now tracks objects that sit beneath a generated model instance and skips the name-based Decimal fallback for them. Free-form strings under a model keep their JSON string type, and plain-literal request bodies still emit Decimals unquoted. Residual: a free-form value inside a plain-literal body is indistinguishable from a model-shaped literal, so it can still be affected.

findings.title: An additionalProperties entry whose key collides with a declared property is written three different ways: declared wins, extra wins, or duplicate JSON keys
findings.description: Take a Metadata with createdAt set and additionalProperties["createdAt"]="x", which every SDK's constructor or bucket allows. Serializing it gives: declared wins in kotlin (`if (!merged.containsKey(key))`), python ('Declared fields win') and elixir (`Map.merge(sanitized_extras, declared)`). The extra wins in php (`$normalized[(string)$extraKey] = …` after normalize), ruby (`hash[json_key] = …` after the declared loop), dart (`json.addAll(additionalProperties)`) and swift (second keyed container overwrites). Both keys are emitted, producing duplicate-key JSON, in java (@JsonAnyGetter after fields), csharp ([JsonExtensionData]), go (byte-splices both objects) and rust (#[serde(flatten)] HashMap). node keeps extras as own properties, so they cannot collide. Decode never produces a collision; caller construction can. Pick one rule (declared wins), enforce it in all 12, and add a model unit test per language.

findings.title: Non-discriminated oneOf/anyOf variants are tried in alphabetical (TreeSet) order in 7 SDKs but in declaration order in 5, so ambiguous payloads resolve differently
findings.description: openapi-generator's CodegenModel.oneOf/anyOf is a java.util.TreeSet (confirmed by disassembling openapi-generator-7.22.0 CodegenModel.<init>), so `{{#oneOf}}`/`{{#anyOf}}` iterate alphabetically. java (model.mustache:219, 325), csharp, kotlin, node (model.mustache:68/145), go (model.mustache `{{#oneOf}}` trial loop), swift (model.mustache:398) and elixir build their trial lists from that set. python, php, ruby, rust and dart iterate `composedSchemas.oneOf/anyOf`, which keeps declaration order. The petstore already shows the split: SetPetAvatarThumbnailRequest is declared [byte, array-of-byte], yet java tries `List<byte[]>` first, csharp `List<byte[]>`, go `[][]byte`, elixir `[binary()]`. python/rust/dart/ruby/php try the scalar first. It goes unseen only because those two variants are disjoint, and Medication<Surgery happens to be alphabetical. With overlapping variants declared out of alphabetical order, the 12 SDKs pick different first-match oneOf variants, put a different `actualInstance` first for anyOf, and pick different winners on an anyOf merge key collision. The python template comment ('the other 11 SDKs all resolve it to the first declared variant') is false. Expand the petstore with a non-discriminated oneOf declared [Surgery, Medication] (non-alphabetical) and an op returning it. Then add a test decoding `{"drugName":"a","procedureName":"b"}` that asserts the first declared variant wins in all 12. Fix by driving every template from composedSchemas.

findings.title: additionalProperties are lost on nested models (and in kotlin, on list elements): only a top-level model captures and re-emits extras
findings.description: kotlin calls populateAdditionalProperties(decoded, raw) and mergeAdditionalProperties(encoded, unwrapped) only on the root object. A Metadata nested inside another model, or inside a List<Metadata> response, decodes with ignoreUnknownKeys and drops its extras; on encode, a nested model's @Transient bucket is never merged back. node re-attaches extras via `__additionalPropertiesDeclaredKeys` only after the root plainToInstance; nested @Type models built by class-transformer use excludeExtraneousValues and lose them. Arrays re-enter deserialize, so they are fine. php calls captureAdditionalProperties only on the class handed to deserializeInternal. Nested objects are denormalized by Symfony directly, so extras are dropped, and the sanitizeForSerialization flatten (lines 193-205) only lifts the ROOT object's `additionalProperties`. java (@JsonAnySetter/@JsonAnyGetter), csharp ([JsonExtensionData]), python (model_validator/serializer), ruby/elixir (recursive deserialize_model/sanitize), go/rust/swift/dart (per-type (Un)MarshalJSON/flatten/Codable/fromJson) handle nesting. The petstore never nests an additionalProperties model (Metadata is not referenced by any schema or operation), so nothing catches this. Expand the petstore: add `metadata: $ref Metadata` to Photo or PetPassport and an op returning `array of Metadata`. Then round-trip a nested extra key in all 12.

findings.title: go matches JSON object keys case-insensitively: it accepts mis-cased keys the other 11 ignore, and double-captures them as additionalProperties
findings.description: Every go model's UnmarshalJSON decodes into `type Alias X` with encoding/json, which matches struct tags case-insensitively. `{"name":"d","photoUrls":[],"STATUS":"sold"}` therefore sets Pet.Status. A mis-cased key is unknown to them: ignored, or captured only as an additional property. findings.title: A bare JSON `null` 200 body on a body-returning operation behaves four different ways: silent null (csharp), raw TypeError (dart), silent nil/zero success (go collections/maps), SerializationError (rust/go structs), versus the empty-body ApiException elsewhere
findings.description: kotlin's ObjectSerializer documents the intended rule: a top-level `null` is an absent body. That makes data null, and the convenience method throws the canonical `Expected a response body for <op> but received none` ApiException. java/python/ruby/php/node/swift/elixir reach the same result because their parsers map `null` to null/nil/None. csharp's convenience method gates on `string.IsNullOrEmpty(result.RawBody)`. RawBody is "null" (non-empty), so it returns `result.Data!`, a null Pet from a non-nullable `Task<Pet>`, with no error. dart's generated deserialize closure is `(body) => deserialize(body, Pet.fromJson) as Pet`. ObjectSerializer.deserialize returns null for `null`, and `null as Pet` throws a dart TypeError, a non-SDK type, from inside invokeApiForResult, before the convenience check that exists to avoid exactly that TypeError. go's WithHTTPInfo sets `dataPtr = &data` whenever Body != "". json.Unmarshal(`null`) is a no-op for slices/maps/scalars, so FindPetsByStatus/GetInventory return a non-nil pointer to a nil slice/map as success. Pet fails in its custom UnmarshalJSON with a 'required field missing' error instead. rust's serde rejects null for Pet/Vec, giving a SerializationError rather than the empty-body ApiError. The test suites only cover an empty `""` body, never `null`. Fix: treat a bare `null` as an absent body in csharp (also check Data is null), dart (make the closure null-tolerant), go (leave dataPtr nil when the payload is `null`) and rust (map Value::Null to None). findings.title: All 12: a server-variable enum type is emitted once per VARIANT, so two variants of the same operation that share a variable name (or a description) generate duplicate types
findings.description: AbstractBetterCodegen.enrichOperationServers builds `serverVariables` per variant, and every template emits the enum inside `{{#variants}}{{#serverVariables}}{{#hasEnumValues}}` as `{{serverTypeName}}{{pascalName}}` (or a nested `{{pascalName}}`), which does not include the variant. For an operation with servers `https://{region}.a.example` and `https://{region}.b.example` (a common multi-region pattern), each language emits the region enum twice. The result is a compile error in java (duplicate nested enum), kotlin, csharp, go, rust, swift and dart, and a duplicate `export enum` in node. elixir gets a module redefinition, fatal under --warnings-as-errors. php regenerates the same file and the last write silently wins. ruby/python silently redefine the module/class. variantName is derived only from the description (else `Server<i>`), so two variants with the same description also collide in all 12. The petstore never has two variants sharing a variable, so nothing catches this. Fix: dedupe variable enums per operation in the codegen (merge enum values or name per variant) and disambiguate duplicate variantNames. findings.title: csharp: per-operation server variant and variable-enum types are emitted at namespace level without an operation prefix (Server0, Primary, Regional, RegionValue, VersionValue…), so two operations with unnamed or same-named servers or variables fail to compile; plus a duplicate <summary> tag
findings.description: In 11 languages a per-op server variant is scoped to its operation: java/kotlin/elixir nest it (GetExternalPetInfoServer.Server0), and go/python/ruby/node/dart/rust/swift/php prefix it (GetExternalPetInfoServerServer0, GetStagingPetInfoServerVersion). csharp emits `public sealed class {{variantName}}` and `public sealed class {{pascalName}}Value` directly in namespace PetstoreClient.Api. The same happens for two ops whose servers share a description ("Primary") or a variable name (`version` → two `VersionValue`). A variant named like a model (e.g. a model `Primary`) also shadows the model inside the Api namespace, because a type in the enclosing namespace wins over `using PetstoreClient.Models`. The petstore passes only because its four server ops happen to use distinct names. Separately, for an undescribed variant without variables the template emits the `<summary>` line twice (lines 49 and 75), visible at PetApi.cs:25-26. findings.title: go: every operation's primary doc comment is detached from its func (blank line), so godoc/gopls/staticcheck never see it — including the `// Deprecated:` marker on FindPetsByStatus/GetPetById, which is also not its own paragraph
findings.description: The go api template ends the data-method doc block with `{{#allParams}}{{#vendorExtensions.pluralExamples}}` on one line (two tags, so jmustache does not treat it as standalone). That emits a blank line between the `//` comment block and `func`. Go only treats a comment as a doc comment when it sits directly above the declaration with no blank line, so every data method (AddPet, GetPetByName, FindPetsByStatus, GetPetById, all StoreApi data methods) has NO doc comment. Two consequences: (1) `// Deprecated: This operation is deprecated.` on the primary FindPetsByStatus/GetPetById methods is not attached, so staticcheck SA1019 and gopls never flag callers; only the *WithHTTPInfo variants (which emit a correct `//` + `// Deprecated:` paragraph) are flagged. (2) Even attached, the marker sits mid-paragraph (line 678 directly after the summary, with no `//` separator line). Go's convention and staticcheck's parser only recognise a paragraph that STARTS with `Deprecated: `. The same mid-paragraph form appears on deprecated Options fields (`/* Status ... */` immediately followed by `// Deprecated:`), so FindPetsByStatusOptions.Status is not recognised as deprecated either. This contradicts the AGENTS T2-5 claim that go marks every public variant with a `// Deprecated:` doc paragraph. Fix: make the examples line standalone (or put the loop inside a single section), emit `//` before `// Deprecated:` as the WithHTTPInfo branch already does, and do the same in options.mustache. Lock it with a go test that parses pet_api.go with go/parser + go/doc and asserts FuncDecl.Doc is non-nil and contains a `Deprecated:` paragraph.

T` gives nil) raise the 'Expected a response body for getPetById but received none' ApiError. go returns a zero-valued Pet with a nil error, and go's own TestBaseApi_SkipsDeserializationForNonJSON locks that behaviour in. The tests disagree too: rust's equivalent test accepts any outcome, swift asserts data==nil, and java/kotlin/csharp/python only test a String return type. findings.title: A response with no Content-Type on a byte/binary operation (getPetAvatar, downloadPetDocument, getPetAvatarThumbnail) decodes differently everywhere
findings.description: Every transport treats an absent Content-Type as text and returns the UTF-8-decoded string. The API layers then disagree. For a format:binary operation such as getPetAvatar: java base64-decodes that text and throws a raw IllegalArgumentException (see the separate java finding). kotlin, csharp and ruby return the UTF-8 bytes. dart tries base64 first and falls back to UTF-8. python, node, go, swift and elixir assume JSON and raise SerializationError. rust parses it as JSON and returns an EMPTY Vec on failure. php json_decode()s it to null, then settype(null,'string') gives "", which is returned as the bytes with no error. For a format:byte operation such as getPetAvatarThumbnail, whose body is a JSON string literal: python, ruby, node, php, go, rust, swift and elixir default to JSON and decode correctly. kotlin, csharp and dart return the UTF-8 bytes of the QUOTED literal, which are wrong bytes. java throws IllegalArgumentException. The dart result contradicts AGENTS 'dart defaults an absent/empty response Content-Type to JSON … matching swift/node' for byte returns. Root cause: binary and byte returns collapse to one native type, and the base layer is not told which format the operation declared. Fix: have the generator pass isBinary/isByteArray to the base layer and apply one rule. Add unit tests for both operations with no Content-Type.

findings.title: Malformed base64 in a top-level format:byte response (getPetAvatarThumbnail): 3 raw platform exceptions, 2 silent decodes, contradicting AGENTS T1-10
findings.description: getPetAvatarThumbnail returns a JSON string literal holding base64. If that string is not valid base64, the error contract says every decode failure is a SerializationError. python, ruby, php, go, swift and elixir raise it. java and kotlin call java.util.Base64.getDecoder().decode(inner) outside any wrapper, so a raw IllegalArgumentException leaks. csharp's Convert.FromBase64String leaks a raw FormatException, and dart's base64Decode(inner) does the same. node uses `Buffer.from(json as string, 'base64')`, which silently drops non-alphabet characters: I confirmed that "!!not*base64??" decodes to 6 garbage bytes. rust does `.decode(...).unwrap_or_default()` and returns an EMPTY Vec. AGENTS.md (Resolved) says 'python and node reject malformed base64 on decode (node decodeBase64 validates …) matching ruby/php/elixir/go/rust'. The node top-level byte path never calls decodeBase64, and rust's top-level path is lenient, so the code contradicts that document. R7-T3 covers only model fields, not this operation-return path. Fix: route these decodes through each SDK's strict decoder or SerializationError wrapper, and add a malformed-thumbnail unit test in all 12.

findings.title: java BaseApi treats an empty Content-Type as base64-binary while its own transport treats it as text
findings.description: Java's DefaultApiClient.isTextContentType("") returns true, with the comment 'A response with no Content-Type defaults to text handling', so the body is a UTF-8 String. BaseApi.isTextResponseContentType("") returns false, and its comment says 'Mirror the transport: an absent/empty Content-Type is treated as binary (base64-encoded by the transport)'. That is false. findings.description: Kotlin routes void operations (deletePet, setPetAvatar, setPetAvatarThumbnail) through invokeApiForResult<Unit>, and that function decodes any non-empty body. Other primitives go through settype() ("x"->true for bool). findings.title: swift depth-cap test uses 50-deep 'within' (peers 500-600) and its comment contradicts the source and AGENTS; Foundation's ~512 nesting limit makes swift's effective cap <1000
findings.description: Ten SDKs assert a 600-deep payload decodes and 1500-deep is rejected (rust 500/1500). swift asserts only nestedObjects(50) decodes. findings.title: Space-encoding assertions accept either `+` or `%20` in 7 SDKs, so the authorize-URL `%20` and token-body `+` contracts are not locked
findings.description: The resolved contract is `%20` in the authorize URL (php T1-1) and `+` in the x-www-form-urlencoded token body. For the authorize URL, php, ruby, node, dart and swift assert `scope=read%20write` exactly. java, kotlin and elixir accept `+` or `%20`, and csharp also accepts a raw space. python parses the URL with parse_qs, so `+` and `%20` look the same. go and rust check only `scope=read`. For the token body (`sendsScopes`), csharp, php, ruby and rust assert `scope=read+write`. java, kotlin, python and elixir accept either encoding (python also a raw space). dart, go and swift check only `scope=read` plus `write`. node compares the decoded value, which cannot tell the encodings apart. A regression to a default RFC 1738 encoder in the authorize URL, the T1-1 bug class, would pass in 7 SDKs. findings.title: oneOf/discriminator failure tests accept any error, or test an internal path, in java/kotlin/swift/rust/go/php
findings.description: The error contract says every decode failure is a SerializationError. csharp, ruby, elixir, node, dart and python assert exactly that for an unknown, missing or empty PetFood discriminator. java asserts `.isInstanceOf(Exception.class)` (ComposedSchemaTest lines 64, 87, 97 and 319). kotlin skips the SDK ObjectSerializer and calls `json.decodeFromString`, then turns any exception into null with `runCatching{}.getOrNull()` before `assertNull`. swift calls `JSONDecoder` directly and expects `(any Error).self`. rust asserts only `is_err()`. go asserts a non-nil error plus a message substring. php calls the internal `PetFood::build()` and asserts `\InvalidArgumentException`; the public `ObjectSerializer::deserialize` wraps that into SerializationException, so the php test checks the internal type, not the contract. None of these six would notice if the SDK began leaking a library exception or the wrong error type for a malformed union. Fix: decode through the public SDK serializer and assert the SDK SerializationError type exactly.

findings.title: Component-level enum defaults on a $ref property: ignored by java/kotlin/php/python, emitted as an untyped string literal by 8 others
findings.description: java, kotlin, php and python resolve the default through ModelUtils.unaliasSchema. Upstream keeps a $ref to an enum schema unchanged there (ModelUtils.java:1409 `isEnumSchema(ref) ... return schema`), so getDefault() returns null and the enum component's default is dropped. csharp, dart, elixir, go, node, ruby, rust and swift resolve it through ModelUtils.getReferencedSchema and do pick up the default. Because such a property has isEnumRef rather than isEnum, fixEnumDefaultValue and updateCodegenPropertyEnum never turn it into an enum member. The result is a plain string literal assigned to an enum-typed field: node `'medium'` to an enum (TS2322), dart `'medium'` (type error), swift `"medium"` (type error), rust `String::from("medium")` (E0308), and csharp the bare token `medium` under the `global::...Models.` prefix (csharp/models/model.mustache:491). Only go (untyped string constant), ruby and elixir (`:"medium"`) come out correct. Not exercised by petstore, which has no $ref'd enum with a default.

findings.title: Digit-leading property/param names give invalid identifiers in python/dart/php/rust and an unexported (silently dropped) field in go
findings.description: AbstractBetterCodegen.toVarName and toParamName send any name matching ^\d to escapeReservedWord, which was written to escape keywords. The base implementation prefixes `_`, giving `_1st`, which works for java/kotlin/node/swift/ruby/elixir. python, dart and php override it to append `_`, producing `1st_`, which is a syntax error in all three (php `$1st_`). rust overrides it to prefix `r#`, producing `r#1st`, which is not a legal raw identifier. go turns off reserved escaping but the digit branch still yields `_1st`, an unexported struct field that the alias-based MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON (go/pkg/models/pet.go:114-125) skips, so the property is silently dropped in both directions. csharp also gets `_1st`, which its own comment says CA1707 rejects under the analyzers. A property or query parameter such as `2fa` or `1stPlace` therefore produces six different results.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Digit-leading names need a separate prefix path from keyword escaping.

findings.title: Model-name collisions with built-in or SDK types are guarded only in node (e.g. a schema named Error breaks swift)
findings.description: AbstractBetterCodegen.toModelName applies a collision prefix only when getModelNameCollisionPrefix() is non-empty and the PascalCase name is in languageSpecificPrimitives. Only node sets a prefix ("Model"). In the other 11, a schema named `Error` shadows `Swift.Error` across the whole PetstoreClient module. The SDK itself uses it unqualified (DefaultApiClient.swift:723 `private struct UndecodableBody: Error`, SerializationError.swift:19 `cause: Error?`), so swift stops compiling. Likewise, schemas named `String` or `Object` shadow java.lang types inside the java and kotlin models package. php forbids `String` as a class name. rust model files `use super::*`, so a model named `Result` or `String` shadows the prelude. `Error`, `Date` and `Result` are common schema names. Only node renames the colliding model.

findings.title: Numeric default literals compile in java only: kotlin/csharp/rust/node/python emit literals that do not type-check, or corrupt them
findings.description: java's toDefaultValue adds the `L` and `F` suffixes and wraps a format-less number or decimal in `new java.math.BigDecimal("...")`. The other SDKs emit the raw default verbatim, with these results. kotlin maps number to BigDecimal and float to Float, so `val x: BigDecimal? = 1.5` and `val f: Float? = 1.5` do not compile. csharp maps number to decimal and float to float, so `decimal? X = 1.5` is CS0664 (needs the `M` suffix) and float needs `f`. rust maps number to f64, so an integral default `3` gives `Some(3)` in an Option<f64>, error E0308. node maps a format-less number to the branded `Decimal` string type, so `x: Decimal = 1.5` is a TS type error. python's fixEnumDefaultValue override has no isEnum guard: it prefixes the class name onto any default containing `.` that is not a quoted string, so `default: 1.5` becomes `Defaults1.5`, which is invalid Python (the base implementation and php both check prop.isEnum). The only petstore defaults are `retries: 3` (int32) and enum or string values, so none of this is exercised.

findings.title: format: uri is a validated typed URI in 6 SDKs and an unvalidated plain string in 6, despite stdlib URI types existing
findings.description: The typeMapping for URI differs across the 12, and so does what each SDK accepts for Pet.homepageUrl. java maps it to java.net.URI, which rejects malformed syntax on decode. kotlin uses io.ktor.http.Url, which is lenient. csharp uses System.Uri. php uses Uri\Rfc3986\Uri, and UriNormalizer throws on an invalid value. python uses UrlStr, an HttpUrl validator that also rejects relative and non-http(s) URIs such as `mailto:x` or `/a`. node uses a type-only brand with no runtime check. dart, swift, go, ruby, rust and elixir keep a plain String and accept anything. The golden shows the split: java Pet.java:124 `URI`, kotlin Pet.kt:80 `Url`, csharp Pet.cs:161 `Uri`, php Pet.php:58 `\Uri\Rfc3986\Uri`, python pet.py:46 `UrlStr`, node pet.ts:60 `URI`, versus dart pet.dart:66, go pet.go:75, ruby pet.rbs:14, rust pet.rs:50, swift Pet.swift:33 and elixir pet.ex:25, all String. dart (`Uri`), swift (`URL`), go (`net/url`), ruby (`URI`) and elixir (`URI`) all have stdlib URI types, so no language feature forces the split, and AGENTS.md does not record it.

findings.title: Operation-level server URLs and server-variable enum values are HTML-escaped in all 12 SDKs, which changes bytes on the wire; global servers emit them raw
findings.description:
Every operation-server template writes the URL literal as `"{{url}}"` and each server-variable enum constant as `"{{value}}"`, both double-brace and therefore HTML-escaped. The global server path writes `{{{serverUrl}}}` and `{{{.}}}` raw in all 12.

An operation server such as `https://h.example.com/v1?api-version=2024-01-01` therefore compiles to `https://h.example.com/v1?api-version=2024-01-01`. I confirmed this by rendering the java fragment. Any `&`, `'` or `=` in an operation-server URL or enum value is corrupted on the wire, identically in all 12 languages, while the same URL declared as a global server is sent correctly. The current goldens are unaffected only because the fixture URLs contain no such characters.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None.

findings.title: Package-manifest description is escaped differently per language: entity-encoded in 4 manifests, raw XML or raw strings in others
findings.description:
appDescription (escapeText'd info.description) reaches the published package metadata in three different ways:
- HTML-escaped `{{appDescription}}`: node package.json, php composer.json, python pyproject.toml, rust Cargo.toml. A description like `Pets & owners' API` is published to npm, Packagist, PyPI and crates.io as `Pets & owners' API`.
- Raw into XML: java pom.xml `<description>{{{appDescription}}}</description>` and csharp csproj `<Description>{{{appDescription}}}</Description>`. A `&` or `<` makes the XML ill-formed, so the Maven and MSBuild builds fail.
- Raw into a string literal: ruby gemspec `'...'` (an apostrophe is a syntax error, and the escapeText `\"` stays a literal backslash), kotlin `"..."` (`$` interpolates), elixir `"..."` (`#{` interpolates), and dart pubspec as an unquoted YAML scalar (`: `, a leading `&`/`*`/`#` breaks parsing, and `\"` stays literal).

The same info.description thus yields correct, entity-garbled or unbuildable package metadata depending on the language.

evidence.quote: <description>A simplified Pet Store API for integration testing.</description>

findings.title: Raw tag and externalDocs prose skips escapeText, so a multi-line or '*/' description breaks compilation in some SDKs but not others
findings.description:
injectTagMetadata stores `tag.getDescription()` and the tag externalDocs description raw. Model and operation externalDocs are raw ExternalDocumentation objects. None of them pass through escapeText, so newlines are not collapsed and the `*/` to `*_/` guard in AbstractBetterCodegen.escapeUnsafeCharacters never runs on them.

What breaks depends on the comment style:
- A multi-line tag description (a common `description: |` block) lands as `// line1\nline2` or `/// line1\nline2`. The second line is bare code, so go, rust, swift, dart and csharp fail to compile, and ruby (`# `) fails too.
- java, kotlin, php and node survive the newline inside `/** */`, but a `*/` in the same raw text closes their block comment early.
- python and elixir place it in `"""` docstrings or heredocs, where only a literal `"""` or (in elixir) `#{` breaks.

The same spec text therefore compiles in some SDKs and not in others. I rendered go's `{{#tagDescription}}\n// {{.}}` with a two-line value and got an uncommented second line.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Operation notes and model descriptions are already normalised through escapeText.

findings.title: Spec prose is HTML-escaped by {{...}} in 5 languages' API docs and left raw by {{{...}}} in the other 7, for the same doc slot
findings.description:
The main templates go through openapi-generator's MustacheEngineAdapter. It uses jmustache's default compiler, and AbstractBetterCodegen does not override processCompiler, so `{{x}}` HTML-escapes its value while `{{{x}}}` emits it raw. I checked this with jmustache 1.16: `pet's "x" a<b & c=d` renders as `pet's "x" a<b & c=d`. Only renderOptionsTemplate sets escapeHTML(false).

The 12 API templates disagree on which form they use for the same spec-prose slots:
- Operation parameter description and per-parameter example summary/description: escaped in node, dart, go, rust and swift; raw in java, kotlin, csharp (escapeXml), php, python, ruby and elixir.
- Tag description and tag/operation externalDocs description: escaped in node, go, rust and swift (dart escapes only the tag description); raw in the others.
- Operation-server variant description: escaped only in go.
- Model externalDocs description and model plural-example summary/description: escaped in all 12. csharp model.mustache:421/649 escapes twice (`{{summary}}` inside `lambda.escapeXml`), so `&` reaches the docs as a literal `&` inside CDATA.

Result: a parameter described as `the pet's "nickname"` renders as `pet's \"nickname\"` in node/dart/go/rust/swift and as `pet's \"nickname\"` in the other 7. The named-entity part (`"`, `&`, `<`) fails generatedCodeShouldNotContainHtmlEntities in those 5 languages only. This undoes AbstractBetterCodegen.preprocessOpenAPI, which decodes `"` from buf/protoc specs precisely so it does not reach generated docs. The petstore golden is clean only because no parameter, tag or externalDocs prose contains `' " & < > = \``.

// param petId: ID of pet to return

findings.title: String default literals are escaped ad hoc per language: ruby/php keep stray backslashes, four SDKs break on an apostrophe, and python skips escapeText
findings.description:
toDefaultValue for a string schema is written separately in each codegen:
- ruby, dart and php use `"'" + escapeText(default) + "'"`; node uses `getQuoteChar() + escapeText(...) + getQuoteChar()`.
- java, kotlin, go, rust, swift, csharp and elixir use `"\"" + escapeText(...) + "\""`.
- python uses `"'" + val.replace("'", "\\'") + "'"`, with no escapeText at all.

Because escapeText escapes `"` and `\` but not `'`, the results differ:
1. A default containing `'` is a syntax error in ruby, dart, php and node, but fine in python and the 7 double-quote languages.
2. A default containing `"` becomes `\"`. In ruby and php single-quoted strings that backslash is literal (verified: ruby `'a\"b'.length == 4`), so the in-memory default, and the serialized wire value, is `say \"hi\"` instead of `say "hi"`. node, dart and python decode it correctly.
3. python alone keeps raw newlines (syntax error) and undoubled backslashes (`\n` becomes a real newline), because it bypasses escapeText.
4. kotlin `"$USD"` and dart `'$USD'` interpolate.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None.

findings.title: escapeUnsafeCharacters overrides do not match each language's real hazards: python's rule is dead, ruby's leaks '\#{' into comments, and elixir has no '#{' guard
findings.description:
python: the override replaces `'''` because Python 'uses triple-quote docstrings', but every python template docstring is `"""` (api.mustache:52,102; model.mustache), and escapeText has already turned `"` into `\"`. The rule never protects anything; it only rewrites `'''` in prose to `'_'_'`.

ruby: the override rewrites `#{` to `\#{` (and `=begin`/`=end`) for every escapeText'd string. ruby renders those strings in `#` comments and single-quoted literals, where `#{` is inert, so `\#{` leaks into the docs. unescapeDocComment only reverses `\"` and `\\`.

elixir: it actually interpolates `#{...}` inside `"..."` and `"""` heredocs, and puts escapeText'd prose straight into `@moduledoc "{{{description}}}"` and `@doc """ {{{summary}}} {{{.}}} """`. Yet it inherits only the base `*/` rule. An operation description like `Fetches /users/#{id}` compiles in the other 11 SDKs but breaks elixir (undefined variable `id` under --warnings-as-errors) or silently interpolates.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: Each language does need its own rule, but the current rules target the wrong hazards: python's and ruby's are dead or harmful, and elixir's is missing.

python.note: python half only: the '''-rewrite is dead and should become identity, but no petstore description contains ''' or */, so no golden can lock it. Needs a description such as: description: "Quote ''' and comment close */ stay verbatim" on an operation and a model property, plus a test asserting the generated docstring keeps both unchanged.

ruby.note: ruby override rewrites #{ to backslash-#{ and ruby only renders escapeText strings in # comments and single-quoted literals where #{ is inert, so the escape leaks. Petstore has no description containing that sequence so no generated test can lock a fix. Spec: add to any operation 'description: Fetches /users/#{id}' and assert the generated pet_api.rb comment contains #{id} without a backslash.

elixir.note: Elixir really has no '#{' guard in escapeUnsafeCharacters (api.mustache:23 and :99 interpolate), but the petstore spec has no description containing '#{', so no generated test can lock a fix. The python and ruby parts are other agents'. Fix: override escapeUnsafeCharacters in BetterElixirCodegen to also replace '#{' with '\#{'. Spec YAML: add to the getPetById operation  description: 'Fetches /pets/#{id} (interpolation must stay literal)'; with it, a unit test can assert the generated @doc contains '#{id}' as literal text.

findings.title: Dart and Go spec setup rewrites the golden before the checks run, so the dart format gate cannot fail and go.mod/go.sum drift is hidden
findings.description: SharedRuntimeContainer runs getSetupCommands() inside /work and then snapshots the result (`cp -a /work /work-snapshot`, SharedRuntimeContainer.java:223). DartSpec's setup ends with `dart fix --apply ...` and then `dart format .`, so DartFormattingSpec's `dart format --set-exit-if-changed .` always runs on a tree that was formatted a moment earlier. GoSpec's setup runs `go mod tidy`, which rewrites go.mod/go.sum before GoBuildSpec, GoLintingSpec, GoClientSpec and GoWasmSpec, so an untidy manifest or a missing go.sum entry is hidden. The DartSpec setup comment is also stale: it says '770 info-level findings remain ... they don't fail the spec', but DartLintingSpec runs `dart analyze --fatal-warnings --fatal-infos`. The setup's `dart fix` codes (always_use_package_imports, directives_ordering, document_ignores) are not enabled by `include: package:lints/recommended.yaml`, so that step does nothing.

every language's lint/format/type-check runs in **check mode** ... no write-mode-posing-as-check

findings.title: Generated tests get weaker compile and analysis strictness than sources in swift, csharp and java
findings.description: AGENTS.md says linters and type checkers run 'over sources **and** tests'. Most languages apply the same strictness to tests (rust clippy --all-targets -D warnings, go vet/staticcheck ./..., dart analyze --fatal-infos, node tsc -p tsconfig.jest.json, php phpstan level 9 over `.`, kotlin detekt over src/test). Three do not. (1) swift: Package.swift puts `-warnings-as-errors` only on the PetstoreClient library target. The PetstoreClientTests testTarget has no swiftSettings, and SwiftLintingSpec runs a plain `swift build` (sources only), leaving the tests to `swift test`, so test-code warnings are never fatal. This is not forced: the same `-Wwarning DeprecatedDeclaration` downgrade the library uses would work for the tests. (2) csharp: CSharpStaticAnalysisSpec builds PetstoreClient.Test.csproj with `--warnaserror`, but that project sets none of AnalysisLevel=latest-all, AnalysisMode=All or EnforceCodeStyleInBuild (the SDK csproj sets all three). The test code is therefore checked only against the default analyzer set, while the SDK gets every CA rule. (3) java: spotbugs-maven-plugin defaults to includeTests=false and the pom does not override it, so SpotBugs never sees src/test, though checkstyle sets includeTestSourceDirectory=true. (elixir's `mix test` also runs without --warnings-as-errors. The ElixirClientSpec comment gives a reason: deprecation warnings at call sites cannot be suppressed in elixir. findings.title: Form-body (x-www-form-urlencoded) encoding differs: java, ruby and node use the WHATWG set (* literal, ~ escaped); the other 8 do the opposite
findings.description: For setPetPreferences the form body is encoded with two different character sets. java (URLEncoder), ruby (URI.encode_www_form) and node (URLSearchParams) keep `*` literal and escape `~` as %7E. csharp (EscapeDataString with %20→+), php (rawurlencode with %20→+), python (urlencode/quote_plus), dart (Uri.encodeQueryComponent), go (url.Values.Encode), rust (form_url_encode), swift (CharacterSet `-._~`) and elixir (URI.encode_www_form) do the reverse. Kotlin is broken separately (first finding). For nickname="a~b*c", confirmed with runtime encoders: java/ruby/node send `nickname=a%7Eb*c` and the rest send `nickname=a~b%2Ac`. Both are valid form encodings, but the bytes differ, and the rust helper's comment says the escape set is meant to be identical across every SDK.

findings.title: JSON request bodies are escaped differently: php and swift escape / as \/, php also escapes non-ASCII as \uXXXX
findings.description: Most SDKs write `/` and non-ASCII characters as-is in JSON request bodies (verified: java, kotlin, python, ruby, node, dart, rust, elixir). php calls `json_encode($sanitized, $flags)` with flags 0, so it sends every `/` as `\/` and every non-ASCII character as `\uXXXX`: Pet{name:"café", photoUrls:["https://x/y.png"]} becomes `"café"` and `"https:\/\/x\/y.png"`. swift's JSONEncoder and JSONSerialization are configured without `.withoutEscapingSlashes`, so every photoUrls value and every base64 `format: byte` value containing `/` goes out as `\/` (confirmed with swift on macOS: `{"name":"café\/ü","photoUrls":["https:\/\/x\/y.png"]}`). swift's own test locks this in (ObjectSerializerTests.swift:985-989). Two smaller cases: go's encoding/json always escapes U+2028 and U+2029, even with SetEscapeHTML(false). csharp's `JavaScriptEncoder.UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping` still writes characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (emoji) as `😀` pairs, based on known .NET behaviour (I could not run .NET here). Every body-carrying operation is affected (addPet, updatePet, placeOrder, setPetAvatarThumbnail, …). AGENTS records that go's HTML-escaping was turned off so bytes go out literally "like every other SDK"; php and swift break that same rule. Fix: php `JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES | JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE`; swift `outputFormatting = .withoutEscapingSlashes` and `options: .withoutEscapingSlashes`.

findings.title: Query-value encoding differs in 2 languages: java escapes ~ but not *; node keeps ! * ' ( ) ~ literal
findings.description: Nine SDKs encode non-allowReserved query keys and values with the RFC 3986 unreserved set `A-Za-z0-9-._~`: csharp, php, python, ruby, dart, go, rust, swift, elixir. Kotlin is broken separately (previous finding). Two others differ on the same input. java uses `URLEncoder.encode(...).replace("+","%20")`, which escapes `~` as %7E and keeps `*` literal. node uses `encodeURIComponent`, which keeps `! * ' ( ) ~` literal; fetch's WHATWG URL parser then escapes `'` back to %27. For getPetByName(category="a~b*c!d'e(f)g"), confirmed against runtime encoders: python/elixir/ruby send `a~b%2Ac%21d%27e%28f%29g`, java sends `a%7Eb*c%21d%27e%28f%29g`, node sends `a~b*c!d%27e(f)g`. java already restores `%7E`→`~` in its path and allowReserved encoders (ValueSerializer.java:123, :183). PetApiTest.java:533-544 asserts that `~` must never become %7E, but only on the path. The plain query encoder was never aligned. node's own path encoder (value-serializer.ts:211-224) shows the intended canonical set. This is not covered by the R8-10 OAuth note, which is about the token, Basic and authorize paths only.

findings.title: dart: a multipart array of strings sends only its last element
findings.description: dart's multipart builder handles a non-binary List field by calling `_addMultipartField` once per element. For a String element that runs `request.fields[name] = value`, and `http.MultipartRequest.fields` is a Map, so each element overwrites the previous one and only the last survives. The code comment says the list "expands into one part per element (repeated keys, as for the urlencoded form)", which is what java (DefaultApiClient.java:888), python (default_api_client.py:868), node, go, rust, swift, ruby, php, csharp, kotlin and elixir actually do. The same happens for num/bool elements (`request.fields[name] = value.toString()`). This is latent in the petstore, which has no multipart string array (`files` is binary and goes through `request.files.add`), but any spec with a multipart array of scalars loses data silently.

findings.title: ruby: Faraday decodes and re-encodes the query string, which undoes allowReserved, sorts parameters and drops repeated keys
findings.description: Ruby builds the query string itself in base_api.rb `build_query_string`, then passes the full URL to `Faraday::Connection#run_request`. Faraday's `Request#url` parses that query with the connection's params_encoder (`QueryParamsEncoder.decode` → `NestedParamsEncoder.decode`), and `build_exclusive_url` re-encodes it with `NestedParamsEncoder.encode` plus `Utils.escape` (ESCAPE_RE `/[^a-zA-Z0-9 .~_-]/`). I ran the installed faraday-2.14.2 encoder on a query matching the golden output. (1) allowReserved is undone: `revision=v1.0/beta:rc1` goes out as `revision=v1.0%2Fbeta%3Arc1`, while all other SDKs send `/` and `:` literally (the petstore's own documented example). (2) Every query is reordered alphabetically (`@sort_params = true`), and deepObject sub-keys are sorted as well. (3) Repeated keys collapse to the last value (`m=1&m=2` → `m=2`), so any exploded array query parameter (OAS default style form, explode true) loses all but its last element. The petstore has no exploded query array, so (3) is latent. Ruby's only allowReserved test is the unit test of `encode_query_allowing_reserved` (value_serializer_test.rb:477); no ruby test checks the URL that Faraday actually sends. The QueryParamsEncoder was added only to turn `+` back into %20, and its comment wrongly says it leaves every other character as Faraday encodes it. Fix: pass params separately, or give the encoder an identity decode/encode that keeps the pre-built query unchanged.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: none; Faraday accepts a custom params_encoder whose decode/encode can pass the query through unchanged

ruby.note: Same root cause and fix as F005; the encoder's old comment claiming only spaces change is replaced.
ruby.test: test/default_api_client_unit_test.mustache: 'keeps allowReserved characters literal'

findings.title: AGENTS claims node and python preserve full decimal precision for `type: number`, but both decode weightKg through a binary float; both also accept a quoted string
findings.description: AGENTS.md:246 lists node ('branded Decimal + JSON.rawJSON') and python ('Decimal') among the FIVE precision-preserving SDKs. That holds only on encode. On decode, node's parseJson is a plain JSON.parse, and the constructor then does `String(this.weightKg)`. I checked: 12.34567890123456789 becomes "12.345678901234567", 1.0 becomes "1", and 1e400 becomes "Infinity". python's parse_json is json.loads with the default parse_float=float, so pydantic receives a float. I checked: Decimal('12.345678901234567'). java, kotlin and csharp read the number text exactly (I checked java: 12.34567890123456789). Wire acceptance also diverges: `"weightKg":"1.5"` (quoted) is rejected by java (I checked), kotlin, csharp and the 7 native-float SDKs. python's lax Decimal accepts it, and node accepts ANY string ("abc", "NaN") as the branded Decimal. node's README 'Decimal / format: number precision' section talks only about int64 and never mentions this loss. Fixes: JSON.parse with a reviver using context.source (available in the same runtime that has JSON.rawJSON) and `json.loads(parse_float=Decimal)` or pydantic's lossless JSON path. Otherwise correct AGENTS.

evidence.quote: FIVE preserve full textual precision — java/kotlin (`BigDecimal`), csharp (`decimal`), python (`Decimal`), node (branded `Decimal` + `JSON.rawJSON`)
this.weightKg = String(this.weightKg) as unknown as Decimal;

findings.description: Case: Order/Pet `id` (int64) or `quantity` (int32) carrying 1.5, 7.0 or 1e2. java: Jackson's ACCEPT_FLOAT_AS_INT is enabled by default and ALLOW_COERCION_OF_SCALARS does not override it. findings.title: go matches JSON keys case-insensitively: {"ID":7} sets Pet.Id, and {"name":"Rex","NAME":"Evil"} yields Name="Evil"
findings.description: go decodes models via `json.Unmarshal(data, aux)` (encoding/json v1). v1 falls back to a case-insensitive field match when no exact key matches. A response key that differs only in case from a declared property is therefore bound to that field. `{"name":"Rex","photoUrls":[],"ID":7}` gives Id=7 in go, while the other 11 ignore the unknown key and leave id null. With `"name":"Rex","NAME":"Evil"`, go's later case-folded key overwrites, giving Name="Evil" vs "Rex" everywhere else. The Gap AJ required check uses the exact-case raw map, so the presence check and the decoded value can disagree. This is not forced: UnmarshalJSON already builds the raw map and can reject or ignore non-exact keys, or use json/v2 case-sensitive matching.

findings.title: java coerces a JSON number/boolean into a String field ({"name":42} -> "42"); the other 11 reject
findings.description: Jackson's ALLOW_COERCION_OF_SCALARS=false covers only number, boolean and date targets. String (LogicalType.Textual) is excluded, so int->String, float->String and boolean->String coercion stays on. I checked this against jackson-databind 2.19.4 (the golden's version) with the golden mapper config: `{"name":42}` decodes to name="42" and `{"name":true}` to "true". kotlin rejects this and has explicit tests for it (unquotedNumberScalarOnStringFieldThrows). csharp (STJ), go, rust, swift (I checked: typeMismatch), python StrictStr, dart `as String`, php assertPrimitiveTypes, ruby/elixir strict 'String' clauses and node's typeof check all reject it. The java comment claims parity ('Matches the other SDKs, which reject wrong-typed primitives'), but its tests cover only the String->number and number->boolean directions. Fix: `coercionConfigFor(LogicalType.Textual).setCoercion(CoercionInputShape.Integer|Float|Boolean, CoercionAction.Fail)`, plus a test.

findings.description: Every model sets `ConfigDict(populate_by_name=True)` and responses decode via `klass.model_validate(data)`, so pydantic accepts BOTH the alias and the field name. findings.title: Configuration and TransportOptions print secrets (proxy password, Authorization default header) in 7 SDKs; every authenticator redacts
findings.description:
The SDK has a redaction policy: every authenticator in all 12 masks its secret in toString, repr, Debug or inspect as `***`. The same secrets also sit in two other public value types. First, the proxy URL holds `user:pass@` credentials by design (python, dart and elixir parse the userinfo into Proxy-Authorization, java pre-computes it, and python's comment says this matches the other 11). Second, the default headers of Configuration and TransportOptions hold credentials: the generated docs use `.defaultHeader("Authorization", "Bearer token")` as the example, and java's PetApiTest does exactly that. Those values print in plain text in 7 languages:
- python: the frozen-dataclass repr prints `proxy='http://user:pass@h'` and the default_headers mapping (verified in /tmp).
- rust: `#[derive(Debug)]` on both structs prints proxy and default_headers; TransportOptions also prints the CA PEM bytes.
- ruby: the default `inspect` dumps the instance variables.
- elixir: the struct `inspect` dumps them, although authenticators use `@derive {Inspect, except: [:token]}`.
- node: `util.inspect` and `console.log` dump the readonly fields, although authenticators define `[nodejs.util.inspect.custom]`.
- php: var_dump and print_r dump the readonly props, although authenticators define `__debugInfo`.
- go: `%+v` prints the defaultHeaders map contents. The proxy is a *url.URL, so only its address prints.
In java, kotlin, csharp, dart and swift the classes have no field-dumping representation (Object, Instance-of, or type-name default), so nothing leaks. Same object, same secret, different logging exposure: either redact (mask proxy userinfo and sensitive header values) in all 12, or never dump in all 12.

evidence.quote: type Configuration struct { baseURL string; defaultHeaders map[string]string }

findings.description: PARITY_TODO T2-10 says TransportOptions is builder-only "because it has validated invariants": the builder rejects a proxy URL that has no host or does not use http or https. That holds in java (package-private ctor), kotlin (private constructor), csharp (internal ctor), dart (TransportOptions._), swift (fileprivate init), go (unexported fields, Build() returns an error) and rust (private fields, build() returns Result). The same input is rejected up front in the other languages. None of these is forced: php and node can declare a private constructor, ruby can use `private_class_method :new`, and python's frozen dataclass can run the same proxy check in __post_init__. findings.title: Connection reuse differs: ruby never keeps a connection alive, python's pool holds one connection per host under its concurrent async facade, and go uses a zero-value http.Transport
findings.description: ruby: build_connection uses Faraday's default net_http adapter, which creates a new Net::HTTP per request and wraps it in http.start {...} (faraday-net_http 3.4.x net_http.rb: Net::HTTP.new at :54/:59, http.start at :112). Every ruby request therefore pays a fresh TCP and TLS handshake. The comment claiming the cached connection preserves 'the underlying socket pool / keepalive' is false, and close() has nothing to release. python: urllib3.PoolManager(**kwargs) uses the default maxsize=1 per host, while the async facade runs requests concurrently through asyncio.to_thread. Every concurrent request beyond the first opens a new connection and has it discarded on return, with a 'Connection pool is full' warning. go: buildHTTPClient starts from &http.Transport{} instead of http.DefaultTransport.Clone(). That gives no IdleConnTimeout (idle sockets are held until the server closes them), MaxIdleConnsPerHost=2, no dial or TLS-handshake timeout or TCP keep-alive, and no ProxyFromEnvironment. java, kotlin, csharp, node, rust, swift, php, dart and elixir use pooled keep-alive clients with library-default limits.

findings.title: OIDC rediscovery after the Cache-Control max-age expires throws away the exchanged authorization-code tokens (all 12); discovery is single-flight only in java/go

The access and refresh tokens from exchangeCode are discarded, and the next getAuthHeaders throws 'Must call exchangeCode() before making API requests' (or its equivalent), which cannot be recovered without a new user authorization. Refreshing the endpoints should carry the token state over. Separately, discovery is serialized only in java (synchronized getDelegate) and go (mutex held across fetch). kotlin/csharp/swift/python/ruby/node/dart/php/elixir fetch outside any lock: concurrent callers fire duplicate discovery requests, and the last writer replaces the delegate, which can silently discard a delegate that exchangeCode just populated. rust instead fails the concurrent caller (separate finding).

findings.title: dart's request timeout does not abort the in-flight request and does not cover the response body read
findings.description: The total deadline is Future.timeout around _httpClient.send(...), which only stops waiting for the response headers. The response body is then read with streamedResponse.stream.toBytes() with no deadline, so a server that sends headers and then stalls the body hangs a dart call forever. dart:io's connectionTimeout covers connect only, and idleTimeout applies to idle pooled connections, not an in-progress read. When the headers timeout fires, the underlying request is not cancelled: the socket stays open and the eventual StreamedResponse is never listened to (leaked). The other SDKs' deadlines abort the request and cover the body: go client.Timeout, node AbortSignal.timeout, rust reqwest timeout, csharp HttpClient.Timeout with buffered content, kotlin request/socket timeouts, swift resource timeout, elixir Task.shutdown, php max_duration, and the python/ruby read timeouts.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: package:http ^1.2 has no abort API. The body read can still be bounded with .timeout(), and the io client can be closed or aborted (newer package:http exposes Abortable requests), so this is not forced.

dart.note: Same root cause and fix as F009. The late response is now cancelled when the headers deadline fires, and the body read is cancelled at the deadline. A request that is still waiting for headers is not aborted: package:http has no abort for the plain Request used here.
dart.test: default_api_client_unit_test.mustache: 'a server that never answers throws NetworkTimeoutException' and the stalled-body test

findings.title: java alone retries any request, POST included, after it was fully sent (sendWithRetry), and the retry is untested
findings.description: sendWithRetry re-sends the request once whenever the IOException message contains 'header parser received no bytes'. The comment says 'zero bytes were exchanged, so the request never reached the server'. That is wrong: the JDK raises this when the connection hits EOF before any RESPONSE bytes, after the request was written. A server that processes a POST (createPet, the OAuth2 token POST with a single-use code or a rotating refresh_token) and then drops the connection gets the request twice. The other 11 do not retry at the SDK level: python sets Retry(total=0), elixir retry:false, and go's net/http replays a non-idempotent request only when nothing was written. No test exercises the retry path.

findings.title: node never consumes or cancels intermediate 3xx bodies in the redirect loop (undici connection leak); python skips release_conn on redirect-refusal paths
findings.description: node's AbstractApiClient follows each Location with a new fetch() and overwrites `response` without awaiting arrayBuffer() or body.cancel() on the previous 3xx. It does the same on the throw paths (non-HTTP scheme, HTTPS->HTTP replay refusal, too many redirects). undici keeps the socket busy until the body is consumed or GC runs, so every redirect hop leaks a connection out of the pool. kotlin explicitly consumes ('consume redirect body to release the connection'), dart drains (stream.drain), python reads and release_conn()s on the success path, csharp disposes, and java/php/ruby/elixir/rust/go read or drop fully. python has the smaller version of the same gap: the three ApiException raises inside _follow_redirects (non-HTTP scheme, downgrade refusal, too-many-redirects) fire without response.release_conn(), because the response was requested with preload_content=False, so that connection is held until GC.

findings.title: python redirect loop mutates the shared PoolManager.proxy_headers, so concurrent requests race and can lose proxy credentials permanently
findings.description: _follow_redirects snapshots self._pool_manager.proxy_headers, deletes Proxy-Authorization from that shared dict on a cross-origin hop, and restores it in finally. The pool manager is shared by every request on the client, and the async facade runs requests concurrently on worker threads (asyncio.to_thread). While one request is mid-redirect, every other concurrent request through the ProxyManager goes out without Proxy-Authorization and gets a 407. Two overlapping cross-origin redirects corrupt the state for good: A snapshots {PA} and strips it, B snapshots {} (already stripped), A restores {PA}, then B restores {}, and the client loses its proxy credentials for its lifetime. No other SDK mutates shared transport state per request: java/kotlin/csharp/etc. strip Proxy-Authorization from a per-request header copy.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: urllib3's ProxyManager keeps proxy headers on the manager. Building a per-hop ProxyManager or passing per-request headers avoids the shared mutation, so this is not forced.

python.note: Removed Guard 3 and the snapshot/restore of the shared pool_manager.proxy_headers from _follow_redirects. Proxy-Authorization authenticates the client to its proxy, never to the redirect target. The per-request Proxy-Authorization header is still stripped cross-origin by Guard 2 (_SENSITIVE_HEADERS). The old test asserting the mutation was rewritten to assert proxy_headers is untouched during and after the hop.

findings.title: swift's production session uses URLSessionConfiguration.default: a process-wide cookie jar and response cache that no other SDK has
findings.description: buildSession uses URLSessionConfiguration.default, which has httpShouldSetCookies=true with HTTPCookieStorage.shared and urlCache=URLCache.shared with useProtocolCachePolicy. A Set-Cookie from any response is stored process-wide and replayed as a Cookie header on later requests from every swift Client in the process (including clients for other tenants or credentials). Cacheable GET responses can be served from URLCache without reaching the server. The other 11 are stateless: csharp explicitly sets UseCookies=false ('The other 11 SDKs are stateless by default'), and none of java/kotlin/go/node/python/ruby/php/rust/dart/elixir installs a cookie jar or cache. The test-only seams build .ephemeral sessions, so the suites never see the production .default behaviour.

findings.title: Query and form parameter order on the wire varies: insertion, hash, random, or sorted
findings.description: For the same call, the 12 SDKs put query params on the wire in different orders. csharp, node, php, dart, kotlin (map side) and rust follow declaration (insertion) order. java collects into a `HashMap`, so the order is the hash order. go ranges over a `map[string]any`, which is randomized per iteration, so the same request can produce a different query each time. swift iterates a `[String: Any?]`, which is randomized per process. ruby is sorted alphabetically by Faraday. elixir is sorted by key (small Erlang maps). python moves every allowReserved param to the end. The Ktor transport also regroups repeated keys. deepObject sub-keys follow each language's map order, which is random in go, rust and swift. Form bodies: go sorts (`url.Values.Encode`), swift is random, java follows HashMap order, the rest use insertion order. The bytes are non-deterministic in go and swift. Use ordered containers (LinkedHashMap, slice of pairs, OrderedDictionary/array) so every SDK follows spec-declaration order.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None

findings.title: Unreserved/safe sets differ between SDKs: java and node in query values, and java, ruby and node in form bodies
findings.description: R8-10 aligned only the OAuth2 paths to RFC 3986 `-._~`. The regular query and form encoders were left alone. Query values (non-allowReserved): csharp, python, php, dart, go, rust, swift and elixir (and ruby, after Faraday re-encodes) keep exactly `-._~` literal. java uses `URLEncoder` plus `+`→`%20`, so `*` stays literal and `~` becomes `%7E`. node uses `encodeURIComponent`, which keeps `! * ' ( )` literal (WHATWG then turns `'` into `%27`). Form bodies: csharp, python, php, dart, go, rust, swift and elixir keep `~` and send `*` as `%2A`. java (`URLEncoder`), ruby (`URI.encode_www_form`) and node (`URLSearchParams`) keep `*` and send `~` as `%7E`. I confirmed node `k=a+b%7E*%21%27%28%29`, ruby `k=a+b%7E*%21%28%29%27` and python `k=a+b~%2A%21%28%29%27`. A compliant server decodes these the same way, but the bytes differ, which matters for signing and caching. Fix by sharing one RFC 3986 unreserved encoder per language, as the OAuth2 change did.

findings.title: rust (unforced) and go reject protobuf-valid durations above ~292 years
findings.description: google.protobuf.Duration allows ±315,576,000,000s. rust parse computes secs.checked_mul(1e9) into an i64 and builds chrono Duration::nanoseconds(total), so anything above 9,223,372,036s is 'out of range' even though chrono::Duration itself spans ±~292 million years (Duration::seconds + nanoseconds would work). go is bounded by time.Duration (int64 ns). java/kotlin/csharp/python/node/ruby/php/dart/elixir/swift accept e.g. "315576000000s". go's limit follows from its chosen stdlib type; rust's is an implementation artefact.

findings.title: swift ROUNDS the sub-millisecond part of a date-time on encode (can roll into the next second/day); every other SDK truncates
findings.description: The swift doc comment says 'any sub-millisecond component is truncated on encode', but DateFormatter with SSS rounds: Date(timeIntervalSince1970: 0.9996) -> "1970-01-01T00:00:01.000+00:00", 1704067199.9999 -> "2024-01-01T00:00:00.000+00:00" (crosses a year boundary), 0.1239 -> ".124" (verified Swift 6.2). java/kotlin (SSS formatter), csharp (fff), python (timespec=milliseconds), go, rust (%.3f), ruby (%3N), php (v), dart, elixir (div 1000) all truncate. Values decoded from the wire are already ms-truncated by ISO8601DateFormatter, so this bites caller-built Dates such as Date().

findings.title: Extra or missing multipart per-part headers: php adds text/plain + Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit, kotlin adds Content-Length, php Psr18 does not escape the field name
findings.description: php DefaultApiClient builds multipart through Symfony FormDataPart. In the bundled symfony/mime, FormDataPart::preparePart wraps every string field in `new TextPart($value, 'utf-8', 'plain', '8bit')`, and configurePart forces encoding '8bit' on every part. So every php text part carries `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8` and `Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit`, and file and JSON parts also carry `Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit`. RFC 7578 §4.7 says senders SHOULD NOT generate Content-Transfer-Encoding. The other SDKs, including php's own Psr18ApiClient, send text parts with Content-Disposition only, so php's two transports also disagree with each other. Kotlin's Ktor formData() appends a `Content-Length: N` part header to every ByteArray part (verified from the ktor-client-core 3.5.0 bytecode), which no other SDK sends. Separately, php Psr18ApiClient interpolates the field name raw into `name="…"` without backslash-escaping `"` or `\`. Every other SDK, and php's own Symfony path, escapes it.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: php: Symfony FormDataPart's defaults. They are not forced, because Psr18ApiClient already hand-builds parts without them.

kotlin.note: Kotlin side only (the php part is not mine). Ktor's formData appends a per-part Content-Length for byte parts. Dropping it would need InputProvider parts with unknown size, which makes MultiPartFormDataContent unsized and sends the request chunked. That is a bigger wire change than the header it removes. Ktor's multipart body is documented as a black box at AGENTS.md ~358.

php.note: php Psr18ApiClient only. The field name is now escaped for backslash and quote in all five part kinds, via a new AbstractApiClient::escapeMultipartFieldName. NOT done: Symfony FormDataPart still adds text/plain and Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit headers on the DefaultApiClient path, because removing them needs custom parts or a FormDataPart subclass. The kotlin Content-Length header is not touched.
php.test: tests/Psr18ApiClientUnitTest.mustache: 'psr18 multipart escapes a quote and a backslash in the field name'

findings.title: Multipart non-ASCII filename: ASCII fallback and RFC 5987 filename* encoding differ (python '?', elixir per-byte '__', ruby raw UTF-8 with no fallback, node keeps ' ( ) *)
findings.description:
This applies to real filenames, which come from file-handle parts: java File, go *os.File, ruby/php/python file objects, node Blob.name, swift URL, elixir {:file,…}. It is distinct from the closed 'field name as filename' item. For `résumé.pdf`:
- Most SDKs emit `filename="r_sum_.pdf"`: go, rust, node and php replace per code point; java, kotlin, csharp, dart and swift per UTF-16 unit or unicode scalar.
- python emits `filename="r?sum?.pdf"` (encode('ascii', errors='replace')).
- elixir emits `r__sum__.pdf` because it replaces per BYTE.
- ruby emits NO ASCII fallback and puts the raw UTF-8 in `filename="résumé.pdf"`, which the other SDKs deliberately avoid.
- Emoji filenames produce `__` in the UTF-16 languages and `_` in the code-point languages.
The filename* value is also encoded with different safe sets. go, php, kotlin, csharp, dart, rust, python and elixir keep only `-._~`. java (URLEncoder) and ruby (encode_www_form_component) keep `*` and encode `~`. node (encodeURIComponent) keeps `! ' ( ) *`; `'`, `(`, `)` and `*` are not RFC 5987 attr-chars, and `'` is the ext-value delimiter. swift keeps the attr-char set `!#$&+^`|`. Fix: one shared rule, using the go/php buildFilenameDirective as the canonical form. Unit test: assert the exact Content-Disposition for `résumé*(1).pdf` in each language.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None

findings.title: Multipart scalar part stringification differs: python bool 'True', php bool '1'/'' and swift Int64/Int32/Float sent as application/json parts
findings.description:
Scalar multipart fields are stringified differently. java (`"" + value`), kotlin (toString), go (%v), node (String()), dart ($value) and ruby (#{value}) send a boolean as `true`/`false` in a plain text part. The exceptions:
- python interpolates `{value}` in an f-string, so True becomes `True`.
- php uses strval(): true becomes `1` and false becomes `` (empty string), in both DefaultApiClient and Psr18ApiClient.
- swift only treats `String || Int || Double || Bool` as scalars. `value is Int` is false for Int64 and Int32, and `is Double` is false for Float (I checked this with swift). So an int64 or int32 field, which is how swift maps `format: int64`, goes to the model branch and is sent with `Content-Type: application/json`.
It is latent because the fixture's multipart companions are strings only (documentType, notes). Petstore extension: add a boolean and an int64 companion to uploadPetDocument (e.g. `isPrimary: boolean`, `pageCount: integer/int64`), and assert the exact part bytes in all 12.

} else if (value instanceof String || value instanceof Number || value instanceof Boolean) {

findings.description: Every other SDK builds the form body field by field. It stringifies each scalar through ObjectSerializer.stringify/toFormValue and skips null array elements. Ruby instead calls `URI.encode_www_form(body.compact)`. compact only drops nil top-level fields. A nil element inside an array is still emitted (ruby 2.6 output: `tags=a&&…`, an empty pair), where java, kotlin, csharp, python, node, dart and rust skip it. Non-string scalars use Ruby's #to_s rather than the SDK wire form, so a Time becomes `2024-01-02+03%3A04%3A05+UTC`, not ISO 8601. The fixture's renewalDate is a Date, whose to_s happens to be correct. Fix: use the same explicit pair loop with ObjectSerializer.stringify that the other 11 use.

findings.title: A bare 'utf-16' body with a little-endian BOM decodes to garbage in csharp, swift and elixir
findings.description: java/kotlin, python, ruby, go, dart, rust, node and php honour a BOM for a bare 'utf-16' label and default to big-endian only without one. csharp returns new UnicodeEncoding(bigEndian: true, byteOrderMark: false), which does no BOM detection. swift maps it to .utf16BigEndian; I verified that FF FE 41 00 decodes to U+FFFE U+4100. elixir passes it to :unicode.characters_to_binary(:utf16), which is big-endian with no BOM handling. A LE-BOM body therefore gives a leading U+FFFE plus byte-swapped text. A BE BOM also leaves a stray U+FEFF in csharp/swift/elixir.

evidence.quote: return new UnicodeEncoding(bigEndian: true, byteOrderMark: false);

findings.note: done in csharp; still open for elixir, swift

elixir.note: Elixir side only. A bare utf-16/utf16 label now sniffs FF FE (little-endian) and FE FF (big-endian), drops the mark, and defaults to big-endian without one. utf-16le/be and utf-32 are unchanged.

findings.title: Declared-charset coverage differs: windows-1252 / shift_jis / iso-8859-x bodies decode correctly in some SDKs and as mojibake in others
findings.description: java/kotlin (all JVM charsets), csharp (with CodePagesEncodingProvider), python, ruby, php (mbstring), node (ICU TextDecoder) and rust (encoding_rs) decode any registered charset. go hard-codes utf-8/ascii/latin1/windows-1252/utf-16. swift hard-codes about 16 labels. dart supports only latin1/ascii/utf-16 and falls back to a lenient UTF-8 decode. elixir supports only latin1/utf-16/utf-32 and returns the raw bytes. So 'text/plain; charset=windows-1252' with byte 0x80 decodes to '€' in 10 SDKs but U+FFFD (dart) or invalid raw bytes (elixir). 'charset=shift_jis' also fails in go/dart/elixir.

findings.title: Follow-up request headers after a 301/302 POST->GET demotion differ: go keeps Content-Type; python/rust send Content-Length: 0 on the GET
findings.description: go deletes Content-Type/Content-Length only when prevStatus == 303. net/http's header copier re-copies the ORIGINAL request's headers onto each hop, so a 301/302-demoted GET carries Content-Type: application/json with no body. python's drop_body_headers requires current_body is not None, so a body-less POST (which got the Content-Length: 0 workaround) that is 302'd to GET still sends 'Content-Length: 0'. rust deliberately keeps a literal Content-Length: 0 even when next_body is None. java/kotlin/csharp/php/ruby/node/dart/swift/elixir strip both entity headers whenever the follow-up has no body.
