findings.title: Redirect-refusal error messages were never harmonized: three messages with up to six wordings each
findings.description: Several templates call these the 'harmonised cross-SDK canonical' messages, but they are not. Non-http scheme: 'Refusing to follow redirect to non-HTTP(S) URL:' (java/kotlin/python/node), '...non-http(s) URL:' (csharp/ruby/dart/rust), 'Redirect to unsupported scheme '<s>' in Location:' (php), '...non-HTTP(S) Location:' (swift), 'refusing ... non-http(s) Location (<status> redirect from a to b)' (elixir), go 'refusing to follow redirect to non-HTTP scheme "x"'. Too many: 'Too many redirects (exceeded maxRedirects) following <url>' (java), '...(exceeded maxRedirects=N)' (kotlin/php/node), '...(exceeded max_redirects=N)' (python), 'Exceeded maximum number of redirects (N)' (csharp/ruby/dart/swift), 'too many redirects (exceeded N)' (rust/elixir), go 'stopped after N redirects'. Downgrade: 12 distinct strings (e.g. java '...HTTPS->HTTP redirect: <next>', kotlin/rust '...: <cur> -> <next>', python '...HTTPS -> HTTP downgrade redirect (307) to', ruby 'Refusing to replay body across HTTPS -> HTTP redirect (TLS downgrade):'). R8-7 harmonized other messages; these were missed. Only go's lowercase is forced (ST1005).

findings.title: Response headers drop content-encoding/content-length after decoding in rust and csharp but keep them in the other SDKs
findings.description: rust explicitly removes 'content-encoding' and 'content-length' from the returned header map after manual decompression. csharp's AutomaticDecompression strips both from Content.Headers, and swift on Apple strips Content-Encoding. java, kotlin, python, ruby, php, node, dart, go and elixir return the wire content-encoding and the compressed content-length. ApiHttpResponse.headers / ApiException.responseHeaders for the same gzip response therefore differ, and a caller comparing content-length with body length sees a mismatch only in some SDKs.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: csharp/swift are runtime-driven, so the remaining 9 could match by stripping, or rust could stop stripping.

rust.note: Rust side only. The stripping is deliberate: after manual decompression the headers must describe the decoded body (default_api_client.mustache comment). Which side of the rust/csharp/swift versus nine-SDK split moves is a cross-SDK ruling; the previous batch skipped it too.

csharp.note: csharp drops content-encoding and content-length because HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression strips them from Content.Headers (default_api_client.mustache:140); the handler does this itself, so the wire headers are not recoverable without manual decompression.

swift.note: swift side only. Apple URLSession strips Content-Encoding itself, and which side of the rust and csharp stripping should move is a cross-SDK ruling. Batch 1 already skipped it (see the outcomes field).

findings.title: csharp alone enables online certificate-revocation checking
findings.description: HttpClientHandler is built with CheckCertificateRevocationList = true. With verifySsl=true and no caCertPath, .NET fetches CRL/OCSP on every new TLS connection. If the revocation endpoint is unreachable (air-gapped/egress-restricted hosts), chain building reports RevocationStatusUnknown and the handshake fails, while the same endpoint works in the other 11, none of which check revocation. The caCertPath branch sets RevocationMode.NoCheck, so behaviour also differs within csharp.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None (it may be there for an analyzer rule such as CA5400, which can be suppressed with a rationale).

csharp.note: Tried removing CheckCertificateRevocationList = true: run 1 failed every csharp build and analysis spec with 'error CA5400: HttpClient may be created without enabling CheckCertificateRevocationList' (DefaultApiClient.cs:239, --warnaserror, AnalysisMode All). Reverted; the property must stay, and no generated file may carry a suppression per editorconfig.mustache policy.

findings.title: Named status errors do not always pin their status: the csharp (message, inner) constructor gives StatusCode 0, and dart, swift and rust accept any status
findings.description: In java, kotlin, php, python, ruby, node and elixir, each leaf (BadRequest through InternalServerError) hard-codes its status, for example java `super(400, …)` and elixir `status_code: 400`. (go leaves cannot be constructed outside FromResponse.) The exceptions are as follows. In csharp, every leaf's (string message, Exception innerException) constructor chains to ApiException(message, inner), which never sets StatusCode, so `new NotFoundException("x", inner).StatusCode == 0`. In dart, every leaf takes `required super.statusCode`, so `BadRequestException(statusCode: 500, …)` is legal. swift leaves are empty subclasses that inherit ApiError.init(statusCode:…), defaulting to 0. In rust, BadRequestError::from(ClientError) accepts any inner status. A NotFoundError reporting status 0 or 500 breaks the type/status invariant the factory guarantees.

findings.title: OAuth2TokenError messages and cause retention were never harmonised across the 12
findings.description: The canonical strings, used by java, csharp, python, ruby, node and dart, are 'Token response is not valid JSON: <detail>' for an unparseable 2xx body, 'Token response is not a JSON object' for valid non-object JSON, and 'Token response missing or empty access_token field'. The outliers are: rust 'failed to parse token response: <e>' and a lowercase 'token response missing or empty access_token field', with a JSON array body (`[]`) reported as the missing-access_token message; swift and elixir 'Token response is not a valid token JSON object' for both the invalid-JSON and non-object cases; kotlin 'Token response is not a JSON object: <detail>' for invalid JSON; php 'Token response is not a JSON object' for invalid JSON (json_decode returns null); go reports a non-object body as 'Token response is not valid JSON: json: cannot unmarshal array…'. Cause retention also differs. java, kotlin, csharp and python (and ruby's implicit cause) keep the parser exception. The node, dart, go, rust and elixir OAuth2TokenError types and the swift enum have no cause slot at all, and php does not pass $previous. R8-7 harmonised the sibling OIDC/bearer messages but not these.

message: "Token response is not a valid token JSON object"
throw OAuth2TokenException("Token response is not a JSON object: ${e.message}", e)
throw new OAuth2TokenException("Token response is not valid JSON: " + e.getMessage(), e);

findings.title: The 'Response headers:' line of the rendered error uses 12 different map syntaxes, and java's order is nondeterministic
findings.description: The rendered error string otherwise uses identical labels, but the headers value is each language's native map dump: java/kotlin/csharp `{k=v}`, php/node JSON `{"k":"v"}`, python `{'k': 'v'}`, ruby `{"k" => "v"}`, dart `{k: v}`, go `map[k:v]`, rust Debug `{"k": "v"}`, swift `["k": "v"]`, elixir `%{"k" => "v"}`. Log scrapers and the cross-SDK rendering tests therefore cannot share one expected string. java is also non-deterministic. The constructor stores Map.copyOf(responseHeaders), whose ImmutableCollections.MapN iteration order is salted per JVM run, so the same error renders headers in a different order from run to run. kotlin's toMap() and csharp's Dictionary preserve order. A canonical `k: v` join, or JSON in insertion order, would make this uniform.

findings.title: fromResponse error-body parsing skips the BOM strip that the success path applies (BOM-prefixed body: only java and swift populate errorBody)
findings.description: Every success-path deserializer except node's strips a leading U+FEFF (each carries the 'RFC 8259 §8.1 … Windows-generated payloads' comment). The error-body parse in fromResponse mostly does not. java goes through ObjectSerializer.deserialize, which strips. swift's JSONSerialization tolerates a BOM (confirmed by script). kotlin parseToJsonElement, csharp JsonDocument.Parse (its own ObjectSerializer comment says System.Text.Json throws on a string BOM), php json_decode, python/ruby/node/dart parse_json, go unmarshalErrorBody, rust serde_json::from_str and elixir parse_json are all called raw, so they leave errorBody null. I confirmed with scripts that python json.loads, node JSON.parse and ruby JSON.parse each reject a BOM. node has no BOM strip anywhere, so its success-path deserialize also rejects a BOM payload that the other 11 accept. Fix: strip the BOM inside each parse_json/parseJson helper, which both paths share.

findings.title: kotlin and go parse the OAuth2 §5.2 error object differently from the other 10 (non-string fields)
findings.description: java, csharp, php, python, ruby, node, dart, rust, swift and elixir require `error` to be a non-empty JSON string, and type-check error_description and error_uri independently, setting a non-string value to null. kotlin uses `root["error"]?.jsonPrimitive?.contentOrNull`, which coerces a numeric or boolean `error` (`{"error":400}`) into the code "400", where the others report code=null and the raw-body message. The same class of coercion was fixed for refresh_token in T2-12. kotlin also calls .jsonPrimitive on description and uri: a non-primitive description throws, the catch-all fires, and the whole parse falls back to code=null and the raw body. go decodes into a struct with string fields, so any non-string description or uri makes json.Unmarshal fail and also discards a valid code. Example: `{"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":{"en":"x"}}` gives the message '…: invalid_grant' in 10 SDKs and '…: {raw body}' with code=null in kotlin and go. go additionally treats an empty description "" as absent, so the message omits ' -- ', where the others render '… -- '. This is forced only to the extent that go's getters return string, not *string.

kotlin.note: Kotlin part only. A new jsonStringOrNull helper requires a JSON string for error, error_description and error_uri. A numeric error no longer becomes code '400'. A non-string description or uri is dropped independently and the valid code is kept. The go part was not touched.

findings.title: rust's per-status error wrappers render a different, context-free string from ApiError and from the other SDKs
findings.description: ApiError::from_response returns a Box holding BadRequestError, NotFoundError, ClientError and so on. Each wrapper has its own Display, for example 'Not found (404): API returned status code 404', 'Client error (418): …' or 'Network error: …'. These drop the 'HTTP status code' / 'Response headers' / 'Response body' lines that ApiError's Display (and every other SDK's string form for the same typed error) renders. ApiErrorKind adds a third format, 'API error (status N): …'. So err.to_string() for a 404 from any rust operation differs from java toString, python str, go Error() and the rest, and loses the response body in logs. Fix: have each wrapper's Display delegate to the inner ApiError's Display.

findings.title: swift OAuth2TokenError does not conform to LocalizedError: localizedDescription is the generic Foundation text
findings.description: Every other swift SDK error conforms to LocalizedError (ApiError, SerializationError, OAuth2ServerError and ConfigurationError), and every other language's OAuth2TokenError renders its message. swift's OAuth2TokenError is a bare enum (missingAccessToken(String) / invalidResponse(String)) with no errorDescription and no message accessor. I confirmed with a swift script that error.localizedDescription is "The operation couldn’t be completed. (….OAuth2TokenError error 0.)" and that the message text never appears. Its shape (two cases) also differs from the single-message type in the other 11. Minimal fix: add `extension OAuth2TokenError: LocalizedError` that returns the associated string.

findings.title: 'Whitespace-only' detection uses each language's native trim, so the 12 SDKs accept and reject different API-key values
findings.description: Every SDK rejects an empty or whitespace-only key or token, but each uses its own stdlib whitespace set: java Character.isWhitespace, kotlin isBlank, .NET IsNullOrWhiteSpace, php trim (" \t\n\r\0\x0B", which includes NUL and not \f), python str.strip, ruby strip (ASCII plus NUL), JS trim, go TrimSpace, dart trim, rust trim, swift .whitespacesAndNewlines, elixir String.trim. I checked java, kotlin-on-JVM, python, ruby, node, rust and swift locally. For a QUERY or COOKIE API key, where non-ASCII is allowed, the results are: "\f" is accepted only by php (sent as the credential); "\x1f" is rejected as empty by java, kotlin and python and accepted by the other 9; U+00A0 is accepted by java, php and ruby (elixir probably too) and rejected by kotlin, csharp, python, node, go, dart, rust and swift; U+0085 is accepted by java, kotlin, php, ruby and node and rejected by the rest; "\0" gives 'must not be empty' in php and ruby but 'contains forbidden control characters' elsewhere. For Bearer the input is always rejected but the message differs, e.g. "\f" gives 'printable ASCII' in java and php and 'must not be empty' elsewhere. Fix: define one whitespace set, e.g. ASCII SP/HTAB/CR/LF/VT/FF or the Unicode White_Space property, and implement it explicitly per language instead of calling the native trim. Add a shared table test.

findings.title: In all 12 SDKs, a token that is only the 'Bearer ' prefix passes the empty-token guard and sends a credential-less Authorization header
findings.description: The constructors reject an empty or whitespace-only token so that 'Authorization: Bearer ' is never sent. Prefix de-duplication runs later, in getAuthHeaders, so the token "Bearer " (or "bearer    ") is not whitespace-only and passes construction. Stripping the 7-char prefix then emits `Authorization: Bearer ` or `Authorization: Bearer    `, the exact unauthenticated request the guard exists to prevent. The behaviour is the same in all 12 (so not a parity gap), but the guard is ineffective in every SDK. The likely real-world case is an env var templated as `Bearer ${TOKEN}` with TOKEN unset. Fix: in every constructor, strip the prefix first and then apply the empty and ASCII checks. Unit test: `BearerAuthenticator(host, "Bearer ")` must raise 'Bearer token must not be empty'.

findings.title: Per-scheme wrapper authenticators print differently across languages: java falls back to Object.toString, rust has no Debug, node/go/elixir print the base class name
findings.description: AGENTS records authenticator debug field-sets as uniform, but the generated per-scheme wrappers (SessionCookieAuthenticator, AdminBasicAuthenticator, ...) break this. java wraps by composition (forced by `final` bases and SpotBugs CT_CONSTRUCTOR_THROW, as the template says) but never delegates `toString()`. `new SessionCookieAuthenticator(h,k).toString()` therefore gives `com.example.petstore.auth.SessionCookieAuthenticator@1b6d3586`, with no host, keyParamName or location. kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, dart, swift and php show `SessionCookieAuthenticator(host=..., keyParamName=SESSION_ID, apiKey=***, location=COOKIE)`. The rust newtype `pub struct X(ApiKeyAuthenticator)` has no Debug impl, so `{:?}` does not compile and any user struct that derives Debug cannot hold a wrapper. node's inspect hook hard-codes `ApiKeyAuthenticator(` / `BearerAuthenticator(` instead of `this.constructor.name`, so wrappers print as the base class. go (embedding) and elixir (whose `new/2` returns the base struct) also show the base name. Secrets stay masked; only the non-secret field-set and type name drift. Fix: java wrapper template should override toString using the delegate's fields and the wrapper's simple name; rust should add a Debug impl that delegates; node should use `this.constructor.name`.

findings.title: The apiKey scheme name is pasted into each language's string literal without escaping, so legal header names can break or silently change some SDKs
findings.description: Each Better<Lang>Codegen builds the wrapper's super-call by concatenating `spec.keyParamName()` inside a hard-coded quote character, with HTML escaping disabled: single quotes in php, node, ruby and dart; double quotes in java, kotlin, csharp, python, go, rust, swift and elixir. RFC 7230 tchar allows `'`, `$` and backquote in header and cookie names, and OpenAPI query names may contain anything. So: a header named `X-Api'Key` gives a syntax error in php, node, ruby and dart but compiles in the other 8. A name containing `$ident` becomes Dart or Kotlin string interpolation; `$apiKey` would even splice the secret into the header name. A query name containing `"` or `\` breaks the double-quote languages. The same unescaped value feeds the redirect strip-list templates. Fix: escape per target language (one helper per codegen). Extend the probe spec with an apiKey scheme whose name contains `'` and `$` so the build and lint specs exercise it.

findings.title: elixir omits secret fields from inspect output instead of showing '***' as the other 11 do
findings.description: elixir uses `@derive {Inspect, except: [:token]}` (likewise :api_key and :password). The secret field therefore disappears from `inspect/1` output rather than appearing as a masked field. The other 11 render it as `token=***` / `apiKey: ***` / `'password' => '***'`, and their tests assert the `***` marker, which elixir's tests cannot. Secrets do not leak. Note that `inspect(auth, structs: false)` bypasses the Inspect protocol entirely and prints the raw map with the secret. A hand-written `defimpl Inspect` that emits `token: "***"` would match the other 11 and close the `structs: false` hole.

elixir.note: Replaced @derive {Inspect, except: ...} with a defimpl Inspect that masks the secret fields as "***" (nil stays nil) in all 8 authenticators: bearer, api_key, basic, implicit, auth_code, client_credentials, password and OIDC. The finding's claim that this closes the inspect(structs: false) hole is wrong, because that option bypasses the Inspect protocol entirely, so that hole remains.

findings.title: go and rust auth error texts differ from the canonical strings in ways ST1005 does not require (contradicts the R8-7 'harmonised' claim)
findings.description: Canonical texts are `API key value for 'X' must not be empty`, `Bearer token must not be empty` and `Basic auth username must not contain ...`. go wraps sentinels so the canonical phrase changes shape: `invalid API key: value for 'X' must not be empty` and `invalid bearer token: token must not be empty`. ST1005 only forbids a capitalised first word. It accepts a leading initialism such as 'API', and it would allow `bearer token must not be empty`. go's own required-parameter sentinel ('missing the required parameter ...') shows the sentinel can keep the canonical wording. go's Basic messages are canonical apart from forced lowercase. rust's BasicAuthenticator adds an extra rust-only prefix inside InvalidArgument: `invalid HTTP Basic credentials: Basic auth username must not contain ':' ...`. rust's ApiKey/Bearer and swift's Basic do not have it, and the rust test locks it in. The go bearer test asserts only the suffix 'token must not be empty', so the drift went unnoticed. Fix: use canonical (lowercased-only-where-forced) phrasing after the sentinel, and drop the rust Basic prefix.

findings.title: python authenticators compare and hash by value, including the secret; every other SDK except elixir and php's loose == uses identity
findings.description: ApiKey/Basic/Bearer (and the OAuth ones) are `@dataclass(frozen=True)` with the default `eq=True`. Two separately built authenticators with the same host and secret are therefore `==`, and they hash equal, which makes them usable as set or dict keys by value. Equality also compares the secret. java, kotlin, csharp, swift, dart, node, ruby and go (pointers) use reference identity, and rust implements no PartialEq. elixir structs (BEAM, forced) and php `==` (language, forced) are structural. python can turn value equality off with `@dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False)`, so its difference is not forced. Decide on identity (the majority) and add a test that two equal-credential authenticators are not `==`.

python.note: All five authenticator dataclasses (ApiKey, Basic, Bearer, OAuth2 client-credentials, OAuth2 password) are now @dataclass(frozen=True, eq=False), so they compare and hash by identity. The secret is no longer compared or hashed by value.

findings.title: ruby per-scheme wrappers take keyword arguments while their base authenticators (and every other SDK's wrappers) take positional ones
findings.description: `SessionCookieAuthenticator.new(host:, api_key:)`, `AdminBasicAuthenticator.new(host:, username:, password:)` and `ServiceTokenAuthenticator.new(host:, token:)` are keyword-only. The bases they subclass are positional (`ApiKeyAuthenticator.new(host, key_param_name, api_key, location)`, `BearerAuthenticator.new(host, token)`). So `ServiceTokenAuthenticator.new('h','t')` raises ArgumentError, while the matching base call works. In java, kotlin, csharp, php, python, node, go, rust, swift and elixir the wrappers are positional like their bases. dart is named everywhere, which is consistent within dart. The RBS sig matches the code, so steep does not catch the mismatch, and no test constructs a ruby wrapper. Fix: pick one convention for ruby and use it for both base and wrapper.

findings.title: rust appends authenticator query params instead of overriding, so a same-named query parameter is sent twice
findings.description: The other 11 SDKs merge `getQueryParams()` into a map keyed by name (java put, python update, go map assign, dart addAll, elixir Map.merge, ...), so the authenticator's api_key replaces any same-named operation query parameter and the URL carries exactly one `api_key=`. rust keeps a Vec of tuples and `push`es the authenticator's entries, so the URL carries both `api_key=<user>&api_key=<secret>`, and which value wins depends on the server. This is latent: no petstore operation has a query parameter named after the apiKeyQuery scheme (`api_key`). To pin it, add a petstore or probe operation secured by apiKeyQuery that also declares an optional `in: query, name: api_key` parameter, and assert a single occurrence. Fix: remove any existing entry with the same key before pushing.

rust.note: Same defect as F256, fixed by the same change.

findings.title: Sync auth-header accessor on token-based OAuth flows: csharp throws, node/dart (and go/rust's infallible variants) silently return {}
findings.description: Among the value-wrapped-async SDKs, csharp's GetAuthHeaders() on the CC/password/auth-code/OIDC authenticators throws InvalidOperationException ('use GetAuthHeadersAsync() instead'). node getAuthHeaders() and dart authHeaders() return an empty map, and dart's auth-code authenticator returns {} even after exchange. go AuthHeaders() and rust auth_headers() also swallow errors into {}; go's auth-code variant logs while its CC variant does not. A caller using the sync/infallible accessor gets fail-loud behaviour in one SDK and a silently unauthenticated request in the others. AGENTS documents the method shape, not this behaviour.

findings.title: Token-request body and authorize-URL parameter order differ (java hash order, go/elixir sorted, rust/swift random per process)
findings.description: Same input, different bytes. kotlin/csharp/php/python/ruby/node/dart emit insertion order (grant_type, client_id, client_secret, scope). java builds params in HashMap and iterates hash order: grant_type, scope, client_secret, client_id (computed). go url.Values.Encode() and elixir URI.encode_query(map) sort keys (client_id, client_secret, grant_type, scope; authorize URL client_id, redirect_uri, response_type, scope, state). rust (HashMap with RandomState) and swift (Dictionary with per-process seeded hashing) change the order between runs, so their token bodies are non-deterministic. Semantically equivalent for a form decoder, but it violates the byte-identical rule and makes byte-level golden assertions impossible. Use insertion-ordered containers (LinkedHashMap, ordered slice, Vec, KeyValuePairs, keyword list).

findings.title: expires_in string grammar differs (hex, type suffixes, newline trimming)
findings.description: Quoted expires_in values are parsed with each runtime's own number grammar. For "0x10", ruby Float(), JS Number() and swift Double() return 16 while the other languages give 0 (stale). java's Double.parseDouble accepts "3600d"/"3600f" (probed: 3600). swift trims only .whitespaces, so "3600\n" becomes 0 where every other SDK gets 3600. Use one decimal-digits(+fraction) grammar in all 12.

findings.title: An unreadable caCertPath with verifySsl=false is rejected by 7 SDKs and accepted by 5
findings.description: java, kotlin, csharp, php and python check the CA only in the `else if (caCertPath != null)` branch after `!verifySsl`, so with verifySsl=false a missing or garbage CA path is ignored. ruby, node, elixir and swift validate at construction regardless of verifySsl, dart calls setTrustedCertificates before checking verifySsl, and go/rust read the file in TransportOptions build(). Those 7 throw a configuration error for the same input. A shared rule is needed (validate whenever the field is set, or never when verification is off).

findings.title: The 'not already set' checks for User-Agent and X-Request-ID are case-sensitive in all 12, so the wire result varies by HTTP library
findings.description: Every client merges transport defaults and request headers into a case-sensitive map, then checks the exact strings `User-Agent` and `X-Request-ID` before injecting (java/kotlin/python containsKey/`in`, csharp a default-comparer Dictionary, php isset, ruby `||=`, node a property lookup, go/swift/elixir map keys, dart containsKey). A caller who sets `user-agent` or `x-request-id` in lower case through Configuration.defaultHeader or TransportOptions.defaultHeader gets a second, injected header. What reaches the wire then depends on the library (inferred from library semantics, not run here): java/python send two header lines; node's Headers joins them into `MyApp, petstore-client/1.0.0 (node)`; go (http.Header canonicalisation), rust (HeaderMap) and swift (URLRequest.setValue) keep whichever was written last, which follows randomised map iteration order and so is non-deterministic. The caller's override should win in all 12, so the lookup should be case-insensitive.

findings.title: The default User-Agent product token comes from a different identifier in different SDKs
findings.description: Each Better<Lang>Codegen builds userAgentDefault differently. java/kotlin use invokerPackage (`com.example.petstore/1.0.0 (java)`), not the spec-derived Maven artifactId `petstore-client` that R?-T3-7 introduced for parity. php uses the PHP namespace (`PetstoreClient`), not the composer package. python uses the import name `petstore_client`, not the distribution `petstore-client`. node uses npmName (`petstore-client`), ruby gemName, and csharp/dart/elixir/rust/swift/go their packageName. The token goes on the wire with every request, so server-side analytics see unrelated names for the same SDK family. Pick one source (the published package name) for all 12.

findings.title: kotlin and php reject an upper-case proxy scheme (HTTP://...) that the other 10 accept
findings.description: kotlin hand-parses the scheme and checks `scheme !in listOf("http", "https")` case-sensitively. php compares parse_url()['scheme'], which keeps the original case, with !== 'http'. The other 10 accept it: java uses equalsIgnoreCase, csharp/python/node/dart/go/rust/elixir parsers lowercase the scheme (python/node/ruby verified locally), ruby downcases, and swift lowercases. RFC 3986 schemes are case-insensitive. kotlin's ad-hoc parser also differs elsewhere: a string with no '://' gets a distinct '(missing scheme)' message, and `http://@:3128` passes its host check while java's URI-based check rejects it. Ktor's common io.ktor.http.Url is available, so the hand parser is not forced.

findings.title: php, python, node and ruby let callers skip proxy validation through a public TransportOptions constructor
findings.description: Proxy validation lives only in the builder's proxy() method. java (package-private ctor), kotlin (private), csharp (internal; PARITY_TODO T2-10 says TransportOptions is builder-only 'because it has validated invariants'), dart (TransportOptions._), swift (fileprivate init), go (unexported fields) and rust (private fields) make the builder the only way in, and elixir validates inside new/1. php's TransportOptions::__construct is public with defaults, python's frozen dataclass has a public __init__ and __post_init__ only freezes headers, node's constructor is public, and ruby's initialize is public. findings.title: python and dart share mutable, process-wide Servers constants; go AllServers is a mutable slice
findings.description: go's own docs explain the goal: the generated Server* values are shared package-level values, so immutability stops one caller corrupting the configuration for the whole process. java (Map.of/List.copyOf), kotlin (toMap), csharp (ReadOnlyDictionary + collection-expression IReadOnlyList), node (Object.freeze), ruby (frozen), php (fresh instance per call), rust/elixir (fresh values) and swift (value types) all meet it. python's ServerConfiguration/ServerVariable are frozen dataclasses but their `variables: Dict` and `enum_values: List` are plain mutable containers, and SERVER_0/SERVER_1/ALL are module-level, so `SERVER_1.variables['version'].enum_values.append('evil')` changes validation for every caller. dart's top-level `final server1 = ServerConfiguration(variables: {...})` uses non-const map/list literals and the constructor does not copy them, so `server1.variables[...]` and `enumValues.add(...)` mutate the shared value; `allServers` is a growable list. go's AllServers is an exported []*ServerConfiguration whose elements can be reassigned.

evidence.quote: a mutable variable would let one caller corrupt the configuration for the whole process

dart.note: Dart half only. servers.mustache now emits const server0, server1 and const allServers, so the maps, enum lists and the list cannot be mutated.

go.note: Go has no immutable package-level values. ServerConfiguration and ServerVariable are already immutable and copy on read (server_configuration.mustache:15-25). Only reassigning a package variable or slice element remains, which is an explicit act, and making Server* and AllServers functions would break the public API.

findings.title: AGENTS' reason that swift's date-time decoding 'cannot be made strict' is false: swift maps `format: date` to String, not Foundation.Date
findings.description: AGENTS.md:365-370 closes date-time input strictness by saying swift 'maps both `format: date` and `format: date-time` to one `Foundation.Date`, so it needs the date-only parse fallback'. In fact BetterSwiftCodegen.java:74 maps `date` to `String`, and only `DateTime` maps to `Date`. The `.custom` dateDecodingStrategy, including the `yyyy-MM-dd` fallback in ObjectSerializer.swift:69-79, therefore only ever runs for date-time fields. Swift accepts `"2024-01-01"` as a date-time (midnight UTC) for no reason any language forces, unlike the stricter SDKs. The date-only fallback could be removed.

findings.title: Integer-enum members ignore the language's enum casing in csharp, node, go, rust and swift
findings.description: String-enum members follow each language's convention (csharp/node/rust `OnHold`, go `AvailabilityOnHold`, swift `onHold`). Integer-enum members come out as the raw `NUMBER_1`: csharp Priority.cs:20, node priority.ts, go `PriorityNUMBER_1` (priority.go:22), rust `NUMBER_1` (which needs Cargo.toml `non_camel_case_types = "allow"`), swift `case NUMBER_1` instead of `number1`. dart (`number1`) and elixir (`:number_1`) apply their convention to int enums too. java/kotlin/php/python/ruby use UPPER_SNAKE for all enums and are consistent.

findings.title: Over-broad reserved-word mangling renames legal identifiers: swift `_type`, dart `type_`, php `$and_/$or_/$class_/$return_`, ruby `_and/_or/_not`
findings.description: loadReservedWords lowercases every entry (AbstractBetterCodegen.java:1446-1460). swift.txt lists `Type`, `Self`, `Any` and `Protocol`, so the plain field name `type` is escaped: ApiResponse is `_type` (ApiResponse.swift:13), although `var type` is legal Swift (only `.Type` is special). dart.txt lists `type` and `Function`, giving `type_` (api_response.dart:12), although neither is a reserved word in Dart. php escapes `and/or/class/return` to `$and_`, `$or_`, `$class_`, `$return_` (EdgeCases.php:36-48), although a `$`-sigiled property and PHP 8 named arguments both allow keywords. ruby escapes `and/or/not` to `_and`, `_or`, `_not` (edge_cases.rb:79-81), although `obj.and` is valid Ruby. Only `class` is a real clash, with Object#class. Meanwhile java, kotlin, csharp, go, node, python (where it is a real keyword) and elixir keep `type` and `and`. The extra renames change the public field name with no language feature forcing them. The prefix-versus-suffix escape style also differs among languages that do escape.
findings.note: done in dart, swift; still open for php, ruby

dart.note: dart side only: BetterDartCodegen.shouldEscapeReservedVarName now keeps type and function as plain variable names (neither is a Dart reserved word, and the list is matched case-insensitively), so ApiResponse.type_ is now type. swift, php and ruby sides not touched.

findings.title: `format: int32` range is enforced by 5 SDKs; swift (Int), python, dart, php, ruby, elixir and node accept and re-send values outside int32

findings.title: elixir's model-level `@deprecated` attaches to the next function (defstruct's __struct__), not to the module
findings.description: elixir/models/model.mustache:332-334 (and :490-492) emit `@deprecated "This schema is deprecated."` just before `@type t` and `defstruct`. In Elixir, @deprecated is a function attribute: it applies to the next `def`, and defstruct expands to `def __struct__/0,1`. The deprecation therefore lands on __struct__ (or the next generated function), which users never call directly; `%Tag{}` expands at compile time and gives no warning, and the module is not marked deprecated in docs. The idiomatic module-level marker is `@moduledoc deprecated: "…"` (doc metadata), which is close to the R6-3 moduledoc approach. The other 11 SDKs mark the type itself. This is plausible from reasoning; elixir is not available locally to verify.

elixir.note: model.mustache now emits 'moduledoc deprecated:' right after defmodule for deprecated struct models (both the hasVars and no-vars branches) instead of the function attribute that landed on __struct__; the module is now marked in the docs metadata and __info__(:deprecated) is empty. Verified failing before the fix.

findings.title: python raises a runtime DeprecationWarning whenever a deprecated field is set, including when the SDK decodes a server response
findings.description: Pet/PetWithOwner get `@field_validator("status") def status_warn_deprecated` (pet.py:76-85), which calls `warnings.warn(..., DeprecationWarning)` whenever the value is non-None. A validator runs on model_validate, so every Pet response that contains `status` emits a warning, even if the caller never touches the field. Under the common `-W error` or pytest `filterwarnings = error`, deserializing a normal server response raises. The other 11 SDKs warn only at compile or doc time when user code references the member. pydantic's own `Field(deprecated=...)` warns on attribute access, which is the closer equivalent. findings.title: ruby (Types::Any) and elixir models do no type or enum validation on construction, and go enums never validate on encode, so wrong-typed values reach the wire
findings.description: Every optional ruby attribute is `Types::Any.optional` (e.g. pet.rb:81, order.rb:68-77). Required ones are `Types::Required`, which only checks non-nil. Only INLINE enums use `Types::String.enum`, and $ref enums (favorite_color, availability) are Any. So `Pet.new(name: 123, photo_urls: [1])` or `Order.new(quantity: 'x')` builds and serializes `"name":123` with no error. OPENAPI_TYPES checking runs only on deserialize. elixir structs are untyped, and sanitize_for_serialization emits whatever is stored: an unknown inline-enum atom goes out as its name, and an unknown standalone-enum atom hits a FunctionClauseError in value/1. go enum types have UnmarshalJSON validation but no MarshalJSON, so `OrderStatusEnum("bogus")` is sent. python validates on construction and assignment (validate_assignment), node in the constructor, php through typed properties, and the static languages through their types.

findings.title: ruby request bodies send a DateTime in non-canonical form because `when Date` matches DateTime first
findings.description: In sanitize_for_serialization, `when Date` (object_serializer.rb:275) comes before `when Time, DateTime` (:282). DateTime is a subclass of Date, so a DateTime value takes the Date branch and is sent as `object.to_s`, i.e. `2024-01-01T12:30:45+00:00` with no `.000`, instead of DEFAULT_DATETIME_FORMAT `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3N%:z`. Verified with ruby: `case DateTime.new(...) when Date` matches. The DateTime half of the second arm is dead code. Model attributes are `Types::Any`, so a DateTime assigned to a date-time field such as Order.ship_date reaches this path. The parameter path (stringify, :187) has no Date arm and is correct.

ruby.note: Moved the Time/DateTime arm ahead of the Date arm in sanitize_for_serialization, because DateTime is a Date subclass and was sent as Date#to_s without .000.

findings.title: rust's derived `Default` on discriminated variants leaves the discriminator empty (`foodType: ""`), unlike `new()`
findings.description: DryFood and WetFood keep `#[derive(Default)]` (dry_food.rs:9), so `DryFood::default()` has `food_type: String::new()`, while `new()` sets 'dry' (dry_food.rs:27). `DryFood { weight_kg: 1.0, ..Default::default() }` therefore sends `"foodType":""`, which a discriminated server rejects. The Defaults/Order models already have a hand-written Default 'so that default() agrees with new()' on schema-default fields. Discriminator defaults were left out of that fix. java (field initializer), kotlin (`= "dry"`), swift and dart (init defaults), python, node, ruby and elixir all default to 'dry'. go's zero struct has the same empty value, which is idiomatic there.

findings.title: uniqueItems arrays (Pet.photoUrls) go on the wire in insertion order in 6 SDKs and in hash or sorted order in the others
findings.description: photoUrls maps to an unordered set in rust (`std::collections::HashSet`, RandomState: order differs between runs, pet.rs:38), swift (`Set<String>`, per-process seeded hashing), python (`Set[StrictStr]`; str hash randomization changes order per process, pet.py:38) and elixir (MapSet, enumerated sorted). csharp HashSet keeps insertion order only as an implementation detail. java LinkedHashSet, kotlin mutableSetOf, php Ds\Set, ruby Set, node Set, dart's default LinkedHashSet and go's slice-backed Set[T] all keep insertion order. For the same Pet, the bytes of an addPet body differ between languages, and between runs in rust/swift/python, which breaks request signing, caching and byte-exact tests. Use an insertion-ordered set (rust IndexSet, swift OrderedSet or array plus dedupe, python list plus dedupe) or sort on encode everywhere.

findings.title: ApiResult.headers immutability differs: copied and read-only in java/csharp/rust/node; mutable and uncopied in python/dart/go/kotlin; ruby freezes the transport's own hash in place

findings.title: swift: everything after `@available(*, deprecated)` is dropped from a deprecated data method's documentation (externalDocs, Parameters, examples), and blank lines split doc blocks
findings.description: The swift api template emits `@available(*, deprecated, …)` right after the summary/notes and BEFORE the externalDocs, `- Parameters:` and example lines. Swift takes a declaration's doc comment from the trivia before its first token, which is the attribute. Every `///` line after the attribute is therefore ignored. Verified by building a module with swiftc -emit-symbol-graph from the golden getPetById block: the docComment is only ["Find pet by ID", "Returns a single pet"]. The `- petId:` parameter doc and both examples are gone, and findPetsByStatus loses its externalDocs link and parameter list. Separately, the `{{#allParams}}{{#vendorExtensions.pluralExamples}}` line emits blank lines between example blocks, and Swift keeps only the LAST contiguous `///` block. Verified: a test function with a summary, a blank line and an example block documented only the example heading. Today this only bites the two deprecated ops, but any non-deprecated op with param examples would lose its summary. Other languages put the deprecation marker after the full doc (java/kotlin/csharp/dart) or in the doc itself. Fix: emit `@available` after the last `///` line (as the WithHTTPInfo variant already does) and make the example loop line standalone.

findings.title: Form-urlencoded and multipart field order on the wire differs (hash order, sorted, or random per process)
findings.description: setPetPreferences fields are nickname, tags, note, renewalDate in spec order. kotlin, csharp, python, ruby, node, php, dart and rust emit them in spec/insertion order. java builds the body in a HashMap, so the order is note, nickname, renewalDate, tags (verified on the JDK). go's url.Values.Encode and elixir's small-map Enum both sort keys: nickname, note, renewalDate, tags. swift iterates a [String: Any], which is randomly seeded per process. For multipart (uploadPetDocument: file, documentType, notes): java sends file, notes, documentType; elixir sorts; go (`range formFields` over a map), rust (HashMap<String, MultipartValue>) and swift ([String: Any]) are non-deterministic per call or per process. The governing rule asks for the same bytes on the wire. Ordered multipart matters to streaming servers that expect metadata before the file. kotlin, csharp and rust tests assert the exact order; java, swift, php, node and dart only assert contains(). Fix: use LinkedHashMap, ordered pairs or an ordered dict, and assert the exact body in every language.

findings.title: csharp sends `application/json; charset=utf-8` (and form `; charset=utf-8`) where the other 11 send the bare declared type
findings.description: csharp's DefaultApiClient wraps string bodies, meaning every JSON and form-urlencoded request, in `new StringContent(text, Encoding.UTF8, contentType)`. On .NET 8 that sets Content-Type to `<type>; charset=utf-8`. The override that applies the declared type explicitly excludes strings (`body is not string`). The multipart JSON part (`new(json, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json")`) and the redirect-replay path behave the same way. Every other SDK puts the declared type on the wire verbatim. The file already strips StringContent's default Content-Type from multipart text parts 'to keep the multipart wire bytes identical across languages', so this is not forced. Tests capture headers at the IApiClient seam, before HttpClient, so they never see the charset. Fix: set Headers.ContentType = new MediaTypeHeaderValue(contentType) after construction.

findings.title: ruby form-urlencoded body stringifies values with to_s instead of ObjectSerializer
findings.description: Ruby's serialize_body sends form bodies through `URI.encode_www_form(body.compact)`, which calls to_s on each value, and the operation layer passes raw values (for example `request_body['renewalDate'] = options.renewal_date`). The other 11 stringify form values through their canonical helper: java toFormValue, kotlin/csharp/python/node/dart/go/swift/elixir stringify, php's formatDateOnly pre-format, and rust serde values. Ruby's own query path uses ObjectSerializer.to_query_value, so ruby is inconsistent with itself as well. It is latent in petstore because Date#to_s happens to be YYYY-MM-DD. A date-time form field would go out as `2024-01-01 12:00:00 UTC` instead of the canonical `.SSS+00:00`, and a BigDecimal as `0.15e1`. A nil element inside an array produces a bare `tags` key, where the others skip it. Expand setPetPreferences with date-time, number and boolean fields to cover this.

Only java (garbagePemCaCertPathThrowsIllegalArgumentException, which also asserts the message names the path) and dart (ArgumentError containing 'CA certificate', no TlsException leak) test a readable file with garbage PEM. findings.title: Codegen classes build generated source text in Java (StringBuilder/concatenation) instead of templates, with unescaped spec strings
findings.description: CLAUDE.md forbids building file content with StringBuilder or string concatenation in Java. Current violations: ruby builds the Options `initialize` signature, the attr_accessor list, `require_relative` lines, the RBS signature, and the nested `module ... end` blocks and RBS parent modules with StringBuilder (BetterRubyCodegen.java:406-424, 1063-1123, 1201-1222). python builds full import statements as strings (BetterPythonCodegen.java:53-79, 986-1001, 1215-1308). All 12 build the per-scheme authenticator `super(...)` argument lists and scope literals as raw source (formatJavaScopes / formatKotlinScopes / formatNodeScopes / formatRubyScopes / formatPhpScopes / formatDartScopes / formatSwiftScopes / formatPythonScopes / formatCSharpScopes, plus build*SuperArgs). Those builders interpolate tokenUrl, refreshUrl, authorizationUrl, openIdConnectUrl, keyParamName and scope names into quotes without escaping, so a `$` in a URL or scope interpolates in kotlin and dart, and a `'` breaks the single-quoted node/ruby/php/dart/python literals. In addition, postProcessFile runs whole-file regex rewrites: go `, \)`→`)` and python `\{ ('.*?') }`→`{$1}` (BetterGoCodegen.java:628, BetterPythonCodegen.java:1191). These can also alter string literals inside generated code.

findings.title: Whitespace-only / symbol-only enum values: php alone avoids an empty identifier
findings.description: In AbstractBetterCodegen.toEnumVarName, sanitizeName(" ") gives "_", and stripping the leading and trailing underscore then leaves "". An enum value made only of spaces, or one that sanitizes to nothing (for example `@@`, or non-ASCII text without allowUnicodeIdentifiers), therefore gets an empty constant name and the generated SDK fails to compile in 11 languages. Only BetterPHPCodegen.toEnumVarName handles a subset of this, mapping whitespace-only values to `SPACE_<n>`. There is no shared fallback such as `VALUE_<index>`, and no language disambiguates enum constants that collide after casing (`a-b` vs `a_b`).
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. The php fix belongs in the shared base.

findings.title: java reserved-word list deliberately omits true/false/null, which are illegal Java identifiers
findings.description: reserved-words/java.txt has no `true`, `false` or `null`. src/test/resources/scripts/JavaKeywords.java filters them out explicitly as "not language keywords", but they are reserved literals and cannot be used as identifiers. JavaReservedWordsSpec only asserts that the resource is a superset of the runtime keywords, so adding the literals would not break it.

findings.title: swift maps int32 to platform Int (64-bit), accepting out-of-range values that java/kotlin/csharp/go/rust reject
findings.description: Swift's typeMapping maps `integer` (int32 or no format) to `Int`, which is 64-bit on every supported platform, even though Swift has `Int32`; it also maps `short` to Int. The other statically typed SDKs map int32 to a 32-bit type: java Integer, kotlin Int, csharp int, go int32 (order.go:65 `*int32`), rust i32 (order.rs:43). Their decoders reject 3000000000 for Order.quantity, while swift decodes it (Order.swift:24 `public var quantity: Int?`). Dynamically typed SDKs accept it as well, so the accepted input set differs by language for no forcing reason.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: None. Int32 is a Swift stdlib type.

findings.title: dart README claims jsonDecode turns integers above 2^53 into double; on the Dart VM they stay exact 64-bit ints
findings.description: The dart caveat says 'For JSON numbers above 2^53 the parser silently picks `double`, so `format: int64` values larger than 9 007 199 254 740 991 ... lose precision'. On the Dart VM (Flutter mobile/desktop, server, the README's 'Native' platform), jsonDecode returns an exact 64-bit `int` for any integer literal that fits in int64. Only dart2js/web, where every number is a JS double, loses precision. The caveat warns native users about a loss that does not happen, and it does not scope the real loss to the web target. go/rust/swift/java etc. correctly state that int64 is unaffected.

findings.title: Spec comments claim the gates match the generated Makefile, but the elixir, php and swift Makefiles disagree
findings.description: elixir: ElixirLintingSpec says it runs 'The generated Makefile's build, lint and dialyzer targets: compile with warnings as errors'. The Makefile's build target is plain `mix compile`, and mix.exs sets no `elixirc_options: [warnings_as_errors: true]`, so a client's `make build` or `make lint` never enforces what the spec gates. php: PhpModernizationSpec says rector runs 'exactly as a client's `make format` runs it'. The php Makefile's format target is `vendor/bin/phpcbf || true`: no rector, and `|| true` swallows failures. Its lint target runs only phpcs, while PhpFormattingSpec also gates `php-cs-fixer check`. swift: the Makefile's `analyse` target (`swift build -Xswiftc -warnings-as-errors -Xswiftc -strict-concurrency=complete`) is never run by a spec. Package.swift's own comment says the generated code is not Sendable-clean ('aren't Sendable-compatible without significant refactor. Keep on v5 mode'), so this client-facing target very likely fails on the golden. That is likely but unverified, since swift-format and the SwiftPM build were not run.

findings.title: SwiftFormattingSpec runs swift-format lint without --strict, so it exits 0 on any formatting finding
findings.description: swift-format lint reports findings as warnings and exits non-zero only when `--strict` is passed. SwiftFormattingSpec.generatedCodeShouldBeProperlyFormatted runs `swift-format lint --recursive Sources Tests` without it, so the test cannot fail on a formatting violation. Every other language's formatting spec exits non-zero on drift (`--check`, `--set-exit-if-changed`, `--check-formatted`, `test -z $(gofmt -l)`). Formatting is still covered, because SwiftLintingSpec runs `swift-format lint --strict`. The formatting spec itself is just a check that always passes, and a swift formatting regression is reported as a linting failure, not a formatting one.

findings.title: Multipart JSON part headers differ: csharp and dart add `; charset=utf-8` and change header order; kotlin adds a per-part Content-Length
findings.description: For addPetPhotos, the `metadata` part (encoding contentType application/json) is sent by java, python, ruby, php, node, go, rust, swift, elixir and kotlin as `Content-Disposition: form-data; name="metadata"` followed by `Content-Type: application/json`. csharp builds it with `new StringContent(json, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json")`, which sets `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`. Because Content-Disposition is removed and re-added afterwards, the Content-Type header also comes first. csharp already avoids this default for scalar parts (a comment in DefaultApiClient explains it), but not for the JSON part. dart uses `http.MultipartFile.fromString(..., contentType: MediaType('application','json'))`, and package:http always adds a charset parameter there, so dart also sends `application/json; charset=utf-8`. package:http also writes content-type before content-disposition and gives non-ASCII text fields an extra `content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8` and `content-transfer-encoding: binary`. kotlin: Ktor's formData adds a `Content-Length` header to each binary part (checked with ktor-client-core 3.5.0: `[Content-Disposition=[form-data; name="files", filename="files"], Content-Type=[image/png], Content-Length=[2]]`). No other SDK sends a per-part Content-Length. AGENTS closes only the multipart filename and MIME type and kotlin's test depth, not these header bytes.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: dart: package:http MultipartFile.fromString always adds a charset (fromBytes with an explicit MediaType avoids it); csharp: none (set Headers.ContentType explicitly); kotlin: Ktor formData adds Content-Length (borderline, library behaviour)

kotlin.note: Kotlin side only (csharp and dart are not mine). Same cause as F252: Ktor formData adds Content-Length to byte parts, and removing it forces chunked multipart. Library behaviour, noted as borderline in the finding itself.

dart.note: Dart half only. The multipart JSON part is built with MultipartFile.fromBytes(utf8.encode(json)) and an explicit MediaType, so the part type is a bare application/json. The header order (content-type first) comes from package:http and is forced. The csharp and kotlin parts were not touched.
dart.test: default_api_client_unit_test.mustache: 'multipart JSON part declares application/json without a charset'

csharp.note: The csharp charset suffix on the JSON part was already fixed earlier (CreateStringContent). The remaining drift was header order: Content-Type was written before Content-Disposition. A new SetPartDisposition helper puts Content-Disposition first for byte, stream and JSON parts. dart and kotlin sides are other agents'.

findings.title: Query, form and multipart parameter order is not the declared order in 7 languages: hash order, random or sorted
findings.description: Kotlin, csharp, php, node, dart (query and form) and rust (query and form) send query parameters, form fields and multipart parts in declaration order. The other 7 do not, and four of them send different bytes on different calls. java uses `new HashMap<>()` for queryParams, formBody and multipart, so getPetTag sends `filter,sizes,colors,revision`, setPetPreferences sends `note,nickname,renewalDate,tags`, addPetPhotos sends `metadata` before `files`, and uploadPetDocument sends `file,notes,documentType` (Java HashMap order computed). go ranges over a `map[string]any`, so query and multipart order is randomized per call; its form body is sorted by url.Values.Encode. swift iterates `[String: Any?]` dictionaries, so query and form order is randomized per process (two runs gave different orders). ruby is re-sorted alphabetically by Faraday (previous finding). elixir iterates small maps in sorted key order (query, form and multipart). rust multipart uses `HashMap<String, MultipartValue>`, which is randomized. python sends every allowReserved parameter after all the others. dart's http.MultipartRequest writes every text field before every file or JSON part. Ordered containers exist in every one of these languages (LinkedHashMap, slices, Vec, KeyValuePairs, keyword lists), and rust already uses an ordered Vec for query and form, so no language feature forces the difference.

findings.title: allowReserved characters are re-escaped by the HTTP client in node and rust (') and swift ([ ])
findings.description: The allowReserved encoders all restore the same reserved set `: / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; =`, but some HTTP clients re-parse the URL and change those bytes before sending. node passes the URL to fetch, whose WHATWG parser escapes `'` as %27 in an http(s) query (checked: `new URL('http://h/p?k=a'b')` → `k=a%27b`). rust passes it through `reqwest::Url::parse`, which implements the same WHATWG rule. swift's `URL(string:)` escapes `[` and `]` in the query (checked on macOS: `revision=a[b]` → `revision=a%5Bb%5D`). php builds the request through a PSR-7 Uri, and nyholm/psr7 query filtering escapes characters outside unreserved, sub-delims and `:@/?`, so `[` and `]` are likely escaped there too (not executed here). java, kotlin, csharp, python, go, dart and elixir keep their own bytes; ruby re-escapes everything (separate finding). findings.title: ApiResult equality and header mutability differ across the 12
findings.description:
ApiResult is the public return type of every `*WithHttpInfo` call, and its equality and immutability differ by language.
- Value equality: java (record), kotlin (data class), python (frozen dataclass), elixir (struct), php (loose ==).
- Reference equality: csharp (plain primary-ctor class, not a record), ruby, dart.
- No equality at all: rust (no PartialEq derive), swift (no Equatable conformance), node (plain interface object), go (map field makes == invalid).
- Headers: java and csharp take a read-only defensive copy, ruby freezes, rust, swift, php and elixir are immutable. python keeps a mutable `Dict` inside a `frozen=True` dataclass, so `hash(result)` raises TypeError and `result.headers[...] = ...` mutates it; python's own Configuration uses MappingProxyType for the same purpose. dart stores the mutable `response.headers` map as-is. kotlin stores the caller's map without copying.
None of this is forced: csharp can use `record`, rust can `derive(PartialEq)` (bounded on T), swift can add a conditional `Equatable where T: Equatable`, dart can override ==, and python/dart can wrap the headers read-only.

Both depend on scale: `1.5` and `1.50` are unequal and hash differently, so Pets decoded from `{"weightKg":1.5}` and `{"weightKg":1.50}` (Jackson keeps the text's scale) are not equal. node's Decimal is a branded string compared by `===`, so a user-built `Decimal("1.50")` does not equal a decoded `1.5` (JSON.parse canonicalises it to "1.5"). csharp (`decimal` equality and hash), python (verified: `Decimal('1.5') == Decimal('1.50')` with equal hashes) and the seven native-float SDKs treat them as equal. Not forced: java and kotlin can compare with `compareTo == 0` and hash `stripTrailingZeros()`, and node can normalise the Decimal string.

findings.title: dart's barrel exports the no-auth sentinel (`noAuth`, `NoAuthAuthenticator`) as public API; the other SDKs hide it
findings.description: The NO_AUTH sentinel is meant to be internal: operations declared `security: []` pass it to suppress the client authenticator. python's docstring says it "never leaves the generated client; callers never see it", and ruby, php and elixir say the same. It is hidden in kotlin (`internal object NoAuth`), csharp (`internal sealed class NoAuth`), java (`protected static` in BaseApi), go (unexported), rust (`pub(crate)`), swift (internal) and node (not re-exported from the package root), and elixir marks it `@doc false`. dart declares `class NoAuthAuthenticator` and `const Authenticator noAuth` in src/auth/authenticator.dart, and the package barrel exports that file without `hide`. Dart consumers therefore get `noAuth` as a documented public symbol they can pass as a per-call `auth` to strip credentials from any operation, which no other strongly-encapsulating SDK allows. The fix is `export 'src/auth/authenticator.dart' hide noAuth, NoAuthAuthenticator;` or a library-private name. (php's public `Auth\NoAuth` and python's and ruby's public names come from those languages' lack of package-private visibility, though `@internal`, a leading underscore and `private_constant` are available.)

findings.title: Timeout budget across a redirect chain: whole chain in go/node/swift, per hop in the other 9
findings.description: The same `timeout` gives different total budgets once redirects are followed. go's http.Client.Timeout covers the whole Do() including redirects. node builds one AbortSignal.timeout and spreads it into every redirect fetch. swift's timeoutIntervalForResource covers the whole URLSessionTask including delegate-followed redirects. java (redirectBuilder.timeout per hop), kotlin (per request), csharp (HttpClient.Timeout per SendAsync), python (urllib3 Timeout per request), ruby, php (max_duration per request), rust (per send) and elixir (a new Task per recursive hop) re-arm the deadline on every hop. With timeout=5s and up to 20 redirects, a call fails at about 5s in go/node/swift but can run about 105s elsewhere.
findings.suspected_forced_reason: go's Client.Timeout and swift's resource timeout are whole-transfer by library design. Either side could be made to match: per-hop with a per-request ctx/timeout in go and node, or a total budget in the manual-loop languages.

findings.title: Unsynchronized mutable auth state in the implicit and authorization-code authenticators (java/go/swift/csharp); kotlin uses @Volatile and rust a Mutex
findings.description: OAuth2ImplicitAuthenticator.accessToken and OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.tokenExchanged are written by setAccessToken/exchangeCode (typically on a callback thread) and read by getAuthHeaders on request threads. kotlin marks both @Volatile and rust wraps both in Mutex. java uses plain fields, which gives no happens-before, so a request thread can keep seeing null or false. go uses plain fields, a data race that `go test -race` flags and a torn read of a string header. swift's classes declare @unchecked Sendable over plain `var accessToken: String` and `var tokenExchanged: Bool`, a data race on a refcounted String. csharp uses plain fields. dart, node, php, ruby, python and elixir are not exposed: single-threaded, GIL-protected or immutable.

csharp.note: OAuth2ImplicitAuthenticator._accessToken and OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator._tokenExchanged are now volatile, and the implicit GetAuthHeaders reads the token once into a local. A reflection test checks the IsVolatile modifier. java, go and swift are other agents'.

java.note: OAuth2ImplicitAuthenticator.accessToken and OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.tokenExchanged are now volatile. The implicit getAuthHeaders reads the field once so the null check and the header agree. Java side only.

go.note: OAuth2ImplicitAuthenticator.accessToken is now guarded by a mutex and OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.tokenExchanged is an atomic.Bool. The tests are race-detector tests: they only fail under make test, which uses -race, and GoClientSpec does not pass -race. The java, swift and csharp parts are not mine.

swift.note: swift side only. OAuth2ImplicitAuthenticator.accessToken and OAuth2AuthorizationCodeAuthenticator.tokenExchanged are now guarded by an NSLock, with the same accessor names. The tests are concurrency stress tests; I did not show them failing without the lock.

findings.title: Use-after-close: six different messages, and several doc comments still promise an SDK ApiException/ApiError
findings.description: The error types correctly follow the AGENTS built-in-state-error rule, but the message is not uniform: 'ApiClient has been closed' (java, csharp); '... and can no longer send requests' (kotlin, php, ruby, swift); '... and can no longer be used' (python, node, elixir); 'Cannot send request: the API client has been closed' (dart); 'API client has been closed and can no longer send requests' (go); 'ApiClient is closed' (rust). Several comments contradict the code and AGENTS by saying use-after-close raises an SDK error: php DefaultApiClient::close ('surfaces an SDK-typed ApiException', but AbstractApiClient throws \LogicException), php Psr18ApiClient::close ('raises an SDK-typed ApiException'), node AbstractApiClient.close ('raises an ApiError', but it throws Error), dart close() ('raises a typed ApiException', but it throws StateError), rust struct doc ('fails fast with an ApiError', but it returns ConfigurationError::InvalidState), and elixir/go ('raises an SDK error').

evidence.quote: throw new IllegalStateException("ApiClient has been closed");
throw StateError('Cannot send request: the API client has been closed');
errors.New("API client has been closed and can no longer send requests")
flip the closed flag so a subsequent sendRequest() surfaces an SDK-typed ApiException
a subsequent {@link sendRequest} raises an {@link ApiError}

findings.title: rust DefaultApiClient::close() only sets a flag and releases nothing, despite its docs
findings.description: The trait impl documents close() as 'Releases the underlying transport'. It only stores closed=true. The reqwest::Client, with its pool, idle sockets and hyper connections, lives until the last Arc<dyn ApiClient> is dropped. The Client facade, every *Api and every HTTP-aware authenticator hold clones, so in practice it lives until all of them are dropped. java (HttpClient.close), go (CloseIdleConnections), python (pool clear), csharp (Dispose), kotlin (HttpClient.close), node (dispatcher.close), dart (client.close), swift (finishTasksAndInvalidate) and php (reset) do release their pools on close. elixir documents that its pool is global, and ruby has no pool (see the pooling finding). rust can hold Mutex<Option<reqwest::Client>> and take() it on close.
findings.note: template/README text, not a rule document: still open

findings.note: reported by the rust fix agent, unverified

rust.note: Cause: with_creation_lock removed its lock file only after the body returned, so the panic from a failed container start leaked it. Every later test then waited up to 240 s for the lock, and each re-ran initialisation because OnceLock stayed empty. Now a Drop guard releases the lock and the initialisation outcome is cached as a Result, so later callers fail at once with 'fixture containers are unavailable: <reason>'. Measured with no Docker socket: 25 tests still running after 250 s before; failing in 4 s after.
rust.test: testcontainers_helper.mustache (in-file cfg(test) module, since the helper has no test file): creation_lock_is_released_when_the_guarded_body_panics, creation_lock_is_released_when_the_guarded_body_returns, panic_message_reports_str_and_string_payloads
